Uniform Title: Śaivasiddhāntaparibhāṣā Secondary Title: Śaivasiddhāntaśaivaparibhāṣā Author: Śivāgrayogin

Description: This electronic text has been transcribed from the Devanāgarī edition of the Oriental Research Institute (Sanskrit Series no. 90). Notes: Transcribed by the staff of Muktabodha under the supervision of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski. Revision 0: November 11, 2005.

Country of publication: India. Abbreviations:
a = adhyāya.
*ahaṃ* = egoity (*ahaṃkāra*) *kira* = *kiraṇāgama* (the scripture of rays) *pa* = chapter (*paṭala*)
Parāśaropapurāṇa = Chapter on the Lord (Patipaṭala) = Quarter (Pāda)
puṃ = the principle of the individual (puruṣatattva);
pau = the Pauṣkarāgama;
pra = valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa).
bra = Brahmā;
mataṅga = Mataṅgāgama;
mṛ = Mṛgendra.
*vā* or *co* = *sū* = *vi* = *vidyā* [the White Horse] = *Śvetāśvatara* = *Śvetāśvatara-upaniṣad*
ślo = śloka sarva = Sarvajñānottara si sā = Siddhāntasārāvalī
Sūtra || Śrīḥ ||
Homage to the venerable gurus.
The First Chapter of the Śaiva-Paribhāṣā: I bow to that Supreme Lord, whose characteristics are existence, consciousness, and bliss.
The imperishable Lord of bound souls, the master of the fivefold cosmic acts beginning with creation.
Bowing to Gaṇeśa, the six-faced Kārttikeya, Sāmba, the Lord of the Assembly of Consciousness, and my Guru,
I speak in the Śaiva language for the delight of the devotees of Śiva.
1) Indeed, among the four aims of human life (puruṣārtha)— namely, dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa—

liberation (mokṣa) is the supreme aim. And since that liberation is attained only through the direct realization of non-difference from the Lord (paty-ananyatā-sākṣātkāra), which consists in the manifestation of one's own Śiva-nature within the bound soul (paśu) upon the removal of fetters (pāśa) by means of initiation (dīkṣā) and other such means;

Since even such direct realization is to be accomplished through the thorough knowledge of the three categories designated as Pati, Paśu, and Pāśa, and since that thorough knowledge depends upon the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), one must first [establish] pramāṇa by means of its enunciation (uddeśa), definition (lakṣaṇa), and examination (parīkṣā).
It is being examined.
2) In this context, *uddeśa* (enumeration) is the mere mention of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of categories by means of their names;

*lakṣaṇa* (definition) is the unique property (*asādhāraṇadharma*); and *parīkṣā* (examination) is the investigation as to whether the definition established for a category is logically tenable or not. Among these, the enumeration of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is: perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), and verbal testimony (*śabda*)—these three.

Regarding the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it has been said: "In the Śāṅkara [system], there are perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*), together with verbal testimony (*śabda*)."

3) Regarding that, the general definition of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the power of self-consciousness (*ātmacicchakti*), which is distinct from doubt, error, and memory. As it has been stated in the venerable *Pauṣkara*:
"The power of consciousness (cicchakti), when entirely free from doubt and other such [impurities], is called the means of knowledge (māna). Thus [it is said].

(4) Among these, doubt (*saṃśaya*) is a cognition that, upon perceiving a common property, oscillates between two alternatives, such as "Is it a post or a person? and so forth. Error (*viparyaya*), however, is the cognition of something as being what it is not.

For example: "silver in mother-of-pearl," and so forth. Memory (*smṛti*) is a cognition produced by latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) generated by a prior experience, such as the direct perception of a beloved woman by a lover.
Consciousness-power (*cicchakti*) itself, distinct from these three, is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
As it is stated in that very same work:
"Doubt is a cognition that hangs between two [alternatives] due to the perception of a common form;
error is knowledge otherwise, which is not established in the actual nature of the object."
"Recollection (smṛti) is said here to be a cognition whose object is something previously experienced;
the power of consciousness (cicchakti), when devoid of these [mental modifications], is accepted as the means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa)."

(Pau Pra Pa Ślo 5–6) 5) And this power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) is precisely the cognition whose object is the thing-in-itself (*padārtha*). Its fruit consists of the rejection or acquisition of its own object and so forth. And it is said in the Pauṣkara:
The supreme object of cognition is held to be the result, which consists of the operations of avoidance and so forth.
That there are no defects such as over-extension (*ativyāpti*) and so forth has been established in that very [work].
Here, defects such as under-extension (*avyāpti*) can never possibly occur.
In the case of the means of valid cognition such as perception, there is no fault of non-pervasion due to [the presence of] pervasion.
There is no over-extension [of the definition] to objects of cognition, because it does not apply to various non-existent things;
nor is there any lack of pervasion, provided that such is the nature of the means of valid cognition.
Therefore, the statement regarding the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) has been correctly illustrated. Thus [it is said].
(From *Pramāṇaparīkṣā*, verses 9–11) 6) The Tathāgatas, however, characterize valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in this way:
"Valid cognition is non-deceptive knowledge; it is the stability of causal efficacy (*arthakriyāsthiti*)."
Non-deceptiveness. Thus [it is said].

That is incorrect; for it lacks pervasion (*avyāpti*) regarding inferences concerning past and future objects, since there is no causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) whatsoever for those [objects] that are non-existent as past or future.
Furthermore, it suffers from over-pervasion (*ativyāpti*) regarding memory-cognition and conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka-jñāna*), for one does not act on the basis of those two.

Someone might argue that [the cognition] is contradicted; yet this is not an acceptable consequence, because according to their view, only non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpa*) is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), precisely because it has a pure object as its domain.
7) Regarding those that illuminate: valid cognition is experience; it is other than memory.
Memory, moreover, is said to be a cognition produced solely from the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of a previous cognition.

Thus they describe it. But even that is not so, because there is a contradiction between what you previously established— namely, the intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*) of the knowledge of the meaning of Vedic sentences preceded by the recollection of word-meanings— and what you now assert, namely, that perception (*anubhūti*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by way of excluding memory (*smṛti*).

Furthermore, the intended validity of memories and cognitions with respect to their own objects and their own nature would not be established, because memory lacks the status of direct experience (*anubhūti*) due to its impossibility of being distinct from memory itself.
8) The Bhaṭṭas maintain that a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that which determines an object as it truly is, which has not been previously apprehended.
As they say:
"Therefore, that which has arisen with firmness and does not require corroboration..."
"Let that cognition be recognized as a valid means of knowledge by means of another cognition."
(Ślokavārttika,
Sūtra 40) That too is not at all satisfactory; for there are defective sense organs that produce accidental coincidences,
such as the delusions regarding smoke and other inferential marks when mist and the like are mistaken for smoke.

Furthermore, this would result in the validity of the words of those who are deluded or deceitful, and it would entail the consequence that the entire Veda lacks authority; for since the meaning of the Veda has been understood by everyone in some birth or other, there would be no state of being previously unknown (*anadhigatapūrvatva*). Moreover, in this view—
The validity of the second and subsequent cognitions in a continuous stream would not exist.

9) The Naiyāyikas, however, state that a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that which, while being either the instrument or the locus of the act of cognition, is pervaded by valid cognition (*pramā*). As they have said:
"In this context, a means of valid cognition is that which is pervaded by valid cognition and is the instrument for the attainment of knowledge (*pramiti*)."
Alternatively, valid cognition (pramā) is a correct experience that is either the locus of validity or pervaded by it. Thus [it is said].

That too is not correct; for instruments (karaṇas) lack the status of means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) because they are themselves objects of cognition (prameya), or else, if they were indeed means of valid cognition, it would follow that lamps and the like would also possess that status. As it is said in the venerable Pauṣkara:
"But surely, how could that which is the instrument for the production of valid knowledge (pramiti) not itself be a means of valid cognition?"
Therefore, because it would follow that lamps, eyes, and so forth are themselves means of valid cognition, that which is a means of valid cognition is not itself an object of cognition;
thus, the absence of an object of cognition remains established.
In that case, sound and the other [objects] are inferred by means of cognition because they possess the nature of being objects;
for that which is an object of measurement is not itself the instrument of measurement, since it is measured by an instrument of measurement.
In the world, the conventional usage "I see" is established on the basis of utility;
for there is no object whatsoever for which valid cognition occurs without it.
Therefore, that alone should be accepted as the means of valid cognition (māna), and not the eye and so forth, which are not of such a nature.
(From *Prauḍhaprakāśa*, verses 11–14) 10) Since it is impossible for the sense organs, such as the eye, to perceive objects other than their own respective domains,
some means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that perceives everything must be admitted. And that is none other than the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*).
As it has been said:
"The eye is not for the cognition of sound, nor is the ear for the perception of form;
consciousness alone is the apprehender in all cases, and therefore it is considered the means of valid cognition."

(Prabodhapariśodhanī, verse 15) 11) But then, since the establishment or non-establishment of all objects follows the positive and negative concomitance of the intellect, and since that [intellect]...
If it is argued that consciousness (*buddhi*) alone is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) here because it grasps all objects, we say no;

for, like the eyes and other senses, it is equally material (*prākṛta*) and thus lacks the nature of pure consciousness (*cidrūpa*), and furthermore, it is itself an object of knowledge (*vedya*) due to its being characterized by pleasure, pain, and so forth. Therefore, [the existence of] consciousness is necessarily...
Validity does not exist [inherently], and it has been said: "That upon whose establishment this [cognition] is established, and without whose establishment nothing at all is established—
why is that final cognition not accepted as a means of valid knowledge?"

Because there is no distinction in their being composed of primordial matter (prakṛti), and because vision and the other faculties are likewise undifferentiated, cognition lacks the nature of consciousness; therefore, the intellect does not possess the status of a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa).
Furthermore, cognition is itself known in the form of pleasure, pain, and so forth;
therefore, the absolute validity of cognition as a means of knowledge is not accepted.

(Pau Pra Pa Ślo 16–18) 12) Now, if it is argued that since valid cognition (*pramā*) arises only when the totality of factors beginning with the cognizer (*pramātṛ*) and ending with the object of cognition (*prameya*) is present, and does not arise when it is absent, the causal totality of valid cognition itself is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), we say: no; for if that were the case...

Because it would follow that the conventional usage of the knower (*pramātṛ*), the object of knowledge (*prameya*), and so forth would be annihilated; because there is no causal complex (*sāmagrī*) apart from the knower and the rest; and because the universal concomitance (*vyāpti*)—that "whatever is distinct from something must be different from it"—would be contradicted.
Therefore, it is established that the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) alone, when free from doubt and other such defects, is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Likewise:
And it has been said:
"But surely, who would not accept the causal totality (*sāmagrī*) for the establishment of the object of cognition?
For it is only when the cognizer and so forth, ending with the jar, are present that there is the ascertainment of the jar."
Therefore, that [objection] is not [valid], because it would entail the abolition of the conventional usage of the knower, the object of knowledge, and so forth,
since the knower, the object, and the means of knowledge are established as being included within that [consciousness].
Furthermore, apart from those [individual factors], no causal totality (sāmagrī) is perceived;
for whatever is distinct from something else is, by its very nature, different from it.
"But let the power of consciousness, though differentiated by doubt and so forth, be considered the means of knowledge."

(From *Pauṣpaślokī*, verses 19–22) 13) If it is objected: "But even in your system, if the self’s power of consciousness (*ātmacicchakti*) is the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), then the same defect applies—the undesirable consequence that a single entity would possess both the status of the means of knowledge and the status of the knower (*pramātṛ*)"; we reply: No, because [the distinction is made] through ignorance (*avidyā*), passion (*rāga*), and so forth.

The cognitive power (*cicchakti*) directed toward objects while being turbid is indeed the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), not the knower (*pramātṛ*). The cognitive power directed toward the Self while being free from turbidity is indeed the knower, not the means of knowledge. As it has been stated in that very same work:
"And the cognitive power is nothing other than consciousness itself which is dependent on another."
"His knowledge is not directed toward that [object], for the mother [cognition] is oriented toward the measure (māna) and toward another. Thus [it is said].

(Pau Pra Pa Ślo 7) 14) Therein, first, the definition of perception (*pratyakṣa*) is stated: perception is valid cognition that is direct (*sākṣātkārin*). It is of two kinds, distinguished as non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) and conceptual (*savikalpaka*). [The non-conceptual...]

Non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*) is knowledge that penetrates the mere object, devoid of association with name, genus, and so forth. Conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*), however, is qualified knowledge consisting of the association with name, genus, and so forth. And it is said in that very same work:
"Due to its connection with conceptualization, that power, though one, is said to be twofold."
The apprehension of the mere essential nature of an object is non-conceptual (nirvikalpaka).
"Conceptual cognition is accompanied by the connection with names, universals, and so forth. Thus [it is said].
(From *Prauḍhaprakāśa*, verses 27–28) 15) Furthermore, that perception (*pratyakṣa*) is threefold by another classification:

sensory perception (*indriyapratyakṣa*), mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*), and the perception of consciousness (*citpratyakṣa*) which is independent of the senses and the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). As it has been said:
"Direct perception is said to be threefold, by virtue of the senses, the mind, and consciousness. Thus [it is stated].
And in the Pauṣkara:
"This [perception] is held to be of three kinds: dependent on the senses, likewise independent, and dependent on the internal organ."
(From the *Pauṣkaraprāmāṇyaśloka* 28) 16) Therein,

it is the direct knowledge of one's own self (*svātmāparokṣajñāna*) arising from the eternal connection of the Self with the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), which has cast off all bonds and is independent of the senses and the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). As it has been said:

"In that state, yoga is considered innate because it is independent of the senses, because all bonds have been completely abandoned, and because of the union with the infinity of the power of consciousness."

However, the experience of objects presented by the external senses depends upon the internal organ, namely the mind (*manas*). This has been stated in that very same work: (pau pra pa ślo 29) The experience of objects brought forward by the external senses is dependent upon the internal organ;
this has been stated in that very same [text]:
"The connection of the power of consciousness with the object of meditation depends upon the external collection of sense organs,
which in turn depend upon the internal organ."
(Pratyabhijñāhṛdaya, verse 31) Even though it is dependent upon the senses, for the sake of removing the veil of impurity,
there is the perception of objects through the door of the senses by the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) in dependence on the senses. That too is stated in that very same work:
Furthermore, there would be another [means] dependent on the senses for the sake of removing the covering;
by virtue of its power, it perceives the object through the medium of those senses. Thus [it is said].
(Pratyabhijñā-hṛdaya, verse 30) 17) Now,

it has been stated that perception is the connection of the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) with objects through the gateway of the senses; however, since that [power], being established in itself, lacks orientation toward an object, how could there be [perception] for it without some instrument (*karaṇa*)?

If it is asked how there is a connection with objects, the answer is: it is true that, although she (consciousness) is established in herself, she is manifested by a fraction [of her nature] due to the power of the veil of impurity; being turned toward objects by ignorance, colored by passion, and acting through the medium of the internal organ and the external senses, she proceeds toward external objects for the sake of the self's experience.

18) However, perception is not, as stated by others, knowledge produced merely by the contact of the sense organs with their objects; for that [contact], being devoid of conjunction with the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), is ineffective. As it has been said:
"Perception is the conjunction of the power of consciousness with the object through the path of the sense organs."
For the power of consciousness itself does not indeed turn toward objects.
How can there be a connection between that [consciousness] and objects of meaning without an instrument?
True, it is established as residing in itself alone due to being veiled by impurity.

When [the mind], joined with the instruments such as the *kalās*, is engaged with objects at any time, that is called perception (*pratyakṣa*); it is the sense organ (*akṣa*) that operates upon the object.

Nor is the mere conjunction of the sense organ and its object accepted as perception, because those [objects] devoid of conjunction with consciousness are incapable of producing any effect. Thus it is said.
And in the *Svāyaṃbhuvatantra* (Pauṣkara, Praśna, Śloka 23–26):
"Consciousness, intensified by *kalā*, has its objective field revealed by *avidyā*."
"And being colored by passion, it is also joined with the instruments such as the intellect. Thus [it is said].

19) Therein, the connection of the sense organs (*akṣasaṃbandha*) is sixfold: conjunction (*saṃyoga*), inherence in the conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*), inherence in that which inheres in the conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavetasamavāya*), inherence (*samavāya*), inherence in the inherent (*samavetasamavāya*), and the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*). This has been stated in the Pauṣkara:
The sixfold relationship, known as direct perception (pratyakṣa), occurs through the sense-faculties (akṣa).
The cognition of substances such as a jar arises from mere contact with the eye;
the cognition of their qualities and universals arises from inherence in that which is conjoined.
The cognition of "quality-ness" arises from the inherence in that which is conjoined with and inherent [in the substance];
the perception of sound is established as being due to its inherence in the auditory organ.
The nature of sound (śabdatva) is perceived through its inherence in an object that itself inheres [in something else];
it is an established principle that absence and inherence are perceived as qualifiers.
Or rather, the cognition of inherence in the absence [of a thing] stands as the qualificandum. Thus [it is said].
Elsewhere also [it is said]:
"The universals of the jar, its blueness, blueness-ness, sound, and sound-ness..."
"And non-existence and inherence are to be grasped from among the six types of relations. Thus [it is said].
Thus concludes the means of valid cognition known as direct perception.

20) Now, inference (*anumāna*) is defined. Inference is the valid cognition of an imperceptible object through the ascertainment of pervasion (*vyāpti*). The phrase "through the ascertainment of pervasion" is included to exclude [the case of] verbal cognition.
The term "imperceptible" is used to avoid over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to perceptual cognition that follows a doubt.

Here, according to the derivation based on the state of being (*bhāvavyutpatti*), inference (*anumāna*) is the cognition of an object beyond the senses produced by the knowledge of the presence of the middle term in the subject as qualified by pervasion (*vyāpti*); thus, it is the power of consciousness (*cit-śakti*) delimited by the mental modification (*vṛtti*) that constitutes inference.
However, its instrument—the consideration of the mark (*liṅgaparāmarśa*)—is not itself inference, because it is an object of knowledge (*meyatva*). And it has been said:
"Inference is that which brings about the cognition of an imperceptible object through a firm pervasion."

(Pau Pra Pa Ślo 37) 21) In this context, pervasion (*vyāpti*) is defined as the relation between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*) that is free from limiting conditions (*anaupādhika*).
As it has been said:
"The concomitance of the probans with the probandum per se is called pervasion (vyāpti). Thus [it is said].

(Verse 41) 22) An *upādhi* is that which, while not pervading the probans (*sādhana*), does pervade the probandum (*sādhya*). For example, when smoke is to be proven by means of fire, the contact with moist fuel (*ārdrendhanasaṃyoga*) and so forth [is an *upādhi*]. For that [contact] pervades the probandum, namely smoke...

It is pervasive, because it exists everywhere where there is smoke; it is non-pervasive with respect to the probans, fire, because it does not exist in things such as red-hot iron balls which possess fire. And this is a certain (niścita) upādhi. An example of a suspected (śaṅkita) upādhi is the unseen factor when "darkness" is to be proved by the reason "being the son of Mitrā. This pervasion (vyāpti), moreover, is of two kinds.

This is due to the distinction between positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). Positive pervasion (*anvayavyāpti*) is the general relationship between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*), as in: "Wherever there is smoke, there is fire, as in a kitchen.
Negative pervasion (*vyatirekavyāpti*) is the relationship between those two by way of their absence, as in: "Where there is no fire..."
In that case, there is no smoke either, just as in a great lake. As it has been said in that very same place:
"And that pervasion (vyāpti) is to be known as twofold, consisting of negative concomitance (vyatireka) and positive concomitance (anvaya)."
"Positive pervasion (anvaya-vyāpti) is to be known by way of the presence [of the reason] in similar instances;
the other, the pervasion between the probandum and the probans, is by way of absence (abhāva). Thus it is said.
And elsewhere [it is said]:
"Indeed, whatever kind of relationship between the pervaded and the pervader is desired between two entities..."
Therefore, from the absence of those two, the opposite is perceived. Thus [it is said].

23) Furthermore, this inference is of two kinds: for oneself (*svārtha*) and for others (*parārtha*). That which is for oneself is the cause of one's own comprehension. And that occurs, for instance, on a mountain and so forth, immediately after the apprehension of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between fire and smoke in a kitchen or similar location.

Inference [for oneself] (*svārthānumāna*) is the inference of fire and so forth from the perception of a pervaded mark (*liṅga*). However, when one, having inferred fire for oneself from smoke, employs a five-membered statement (*pañcāvayavavākya*) to inform another, that is inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*). And those members are as follows:

There are five [members], distinguished as the proposition (*pratijñā*), the reason (*hetu*), the example (*udāharaṇa*), the application (*upanaya*), and the conclusion (*nigamana*). Among these, "the mountain possesses fire" is the proposition; "because of possessing smoke" is the reason; "whatever possesses smoke possesses fire, such as a kitchen" is the example; and "and this [mountain] likewise possesses smoke" is the application.
Therefore, "it possesses fire alone" is the conclusion (*nigamana*). Thus, from a statement endowed with these five characteristics, even another person understands the fire;
that is inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*). And so it has been stated in the venerable *Pauṣkara*:
And that [inference] here consists of five members: the proposition and the reason.
These two are the example and the application; then the fifth is the conclusion.
The statement of the desired object is the proposition, while the reason is the statement possessing its pervasion.
The example is of two kinds, and the reason is examined accordingly;
the application (upanaya) is the extension of the pervasion between the example and the subject.
Furthermore, the conclusion (*nigama*) would be a restatement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) together with its reason (*hetu*). Thus [it is said].

(pau pra pa ślo 37–40) 24) And that reason (*hetu*) is of two kinds, distinguished as the "reason based on perceived means" (*dṛṣṭasādhanasādhana*) and the "reason based on general observation" (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭasādhana*). Among these, the former is that which leads to the inference of objects not accessible to the senses. For example: [the inference of] a potter from the act of making a jar.
And having seen [a jar] in one place, because a jar is also seen elsewhere, one concludes, "This jar was made by a potter.

The second type, however, is that which infers an object not accessible to direct perception (*pratyakṣāyogya*). For example, another person's speech is the inferential mark for another person's cognition. In that case, the probandum (*sādhya*) is...
The knowledge of another person is not perceptible;

rather, it is that which is delimited by the nature of knowledge as defined by the property to be proven (*sādhyatāvacchedaka*). One's own knowledge of that same class is perceptible; therefore, this is indeed an inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*). The same applies to the activity of the world (*prapañcakṛtya*).

And not having observed its creator in any single instance, the means of proof known as *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*—based on the commonality of being an effect—infer a creator of the world who is beyond the scope of the knowledge of bound souls (*paśu*) and their fetters (*pāśa*).
This same reasoning should be applied to the bound soul, the fetter, *māyā*, karma, and so forth. As it has been said:
Inference is of two kinds: that based on what is perceived (*dṛṣṭa*) and that based on what is perceived through general correlation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*).
Among these, the former is the means of inferring an object that is not accessible to the senses.
"Anything else [besides direct perception] is an indicator of an object that, though existent, is not perceived. Thus [it is said].
(From *Pramāṇapārāyaṇa*, verses 43–44) 25) Where the probandum (*sādhya*) or that which belongs to the class of the probandum is not suitable for perception,
that is a "remote" (*para*) reason whose probandum is known solely through verbal testimony (*śabda*). For example, [the reason] that infers prior merit (*pūrvapuṇya*).

The specific object of enjoyment at present is that which is to be accomplished through merit and the like; since it is not known without verbal testimony, it is known solely through the word (*śabda*). Furthermore, that probans (*hetu*) is of three kinds, distinguished as: positive-negative (*anvaya-vyatirekin*), purely positive (*kevalānvayin*), and purely negative (*kevalavyatirekin*).
26) In that regard, the reason (hetu) characterized by both positive and negative concomitance is endowed with five features (rūpa). These features are:

presence in the subject (pakṣadharmatva), existence in the similar class (sapakṣe sattva), exclusion from the dissimilar class (vipakṣād vyāvṛttiḥ), the state of having an uncontradicted object (abādhitaviṣayatva), and the state of having no counter-argument (asatpratipakṣatva). Among these, the subject (pakṣa) is that which possesses the property to be proven (sādhyadharma) in a state of doubt.

The *sapakṣa* (similar instance) is that which possesses the probandum (*sādhya*) as something ascertained. The *vipakṣa* (dissimilar instance) is that which possesses the absence of the property of the probandum as something ascertained. Among these, the "property of being a feature of the subject" (*pakṣadharmatva*) of the reason is its occurrence in the subject, such as a mountain. Its "presence in the similar instance" (*sapakṣe sattvam*) is its occurrence in a similar instance, such as a kitchen. Its "exclusion from the dissimilar instance" (*vipakṣād vyāvṛttiḥ*) is its absence in a dissimilar instance, such as a great lake.

The non-deviation of the reason [from the subject]. The state of having an unsublated object (*abādhitaviṣayatva*) means the absence of sublation by another means of valid cognition regarding the probandum (*sādhya*), such as fire, in the subject (*pakṣa*), such as a mountain. The state of having no counter-probans (*asatpratipakṣatva*) means the absence of another reason that establishes a probandum contrary to the intended probandum. Thus, it is endowed with these five characteristics.
Thus, it is the positive-negative concomitant (anvayavyatirekin) that establishes the probandum.

27) A reason that is empty of the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) is a purely positive (*kevalānvayin*). One that is empty of the similar example (*sapakṣa*) is a purely negative (*kevalavyatirekin*). Both of these establish their respective probandum only when they are endowed with the four characteristics. Their examples follow in order: "The mountain possesses fire, because it possesses smoke, just as..."

The kitchen. The universe is dependent upon an agent because it is an effect, just as clay is dependent upon a potter. Every effect exists [prior to its production] because it is being produced; that which is not so is not so, like the horn of a hare.
And so it has been said: "The positive-negative (anvayavyatirekin), the purely negative (kevalavyatirekin),
and the purely positive (kevalānvayin)— it is characterized by these forms in succession."
The property of the subject (pakṣadharma) exists in the similar class (sapakṣa) and is excluded from the dissimilar class (vipakṣa);
it is uncontradicted and lacks a counter-argument, and consists of both positive and negative concomitance.
The subject (pakṣa) is that which possesses the property to be proven; the similar instance (sapakṣa) is that which is endowed with properties similar to it;
the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa) would be that which possesses properties contrary to it; and sublation (bādha) arises from another means of valid cognition.
In the case of the probandum, the two [types of reasons] possess the three characteristics; therefore, through that knowledge, there is the status of being a counter-example (vipakṣa).
A positive reason (anvayin) is one that lacks a counter-example, while the other is likewise one that lacks a similar example (sapakṣa).
A place containing fire is inferred from the presence of smoke, just as a kitchen is;
likewise, the universe must be presided over by someone, because it is an effect by virtue of its substantial existence.
Just as clay is dependent upon the potter, this positive concomitance (anvaya) further shows that an effect arises only from what already exists, because of the reason that it is being produced.
"A portion of a phenomenon that was previously non-existent is produced, like the horn of a rabbit. Thus [it is said].

(From *Pramāṇapārāyaṇa*, verses 44–50) 29) Among the stated forms, such as the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and so forth, those that lack even one of these forms are non-reasons (*ahetu*). Because they possess some of these forms, they appear like reasons; thus, they are pseudo-reasons (*hetvābhāsa*). These are...

And [the fallacies] are fivefold, due to the distinctions of the unestablished (*asiddha*), the contradictory (*viruddha*), the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), the unascertained (*anadhyavasita*), and the mistimed (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*).
Among these, the definition of the unestablished is as follows: the cognition of the pervaded (*vyāpya*) as a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) is called "establishment" (*siddhi*).
"There would be non-establishment due to its absence; the reason (hetu) possessing that [absence] is of many kinds."

And that [unestablished reason] is of ten kinds: unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddha*), partially unestablished (*bhāgāsiddha*), unestablished in its locus (*āśrayāsiddha*), unestablished in its qualifier (*viśeṣaṇāsiddha*), unestablished in its qualificand (*viśeṣyāsiddha*), unestablished in both (*ubhayāsiddha*), unestablished due to ignorance of the reason (*hetvajñānāsiddha*), unestablished due to ignorance of the locus (*adhikaraṇājñānāsiddha*), unestablished for one of the two parties (*anyatarāsiddha*), and unestablished in its pervasion (*vyāpyatvāsiddha*). Furthermore, the unestablished in its pervasion...
It is of two kinds: one due to the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes pervasion (*vyāpti*), and the other due to the presence of a limiting condition (*upādhi*).

Thus, taken together, there are eleven types of unestablished reasons (*asiddha*). Among these, an example of an unestablished reason in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddha*) is as follows: "The jar and so forth must be of the nature of atoms, because they are eternal, like the self (*ātman*) according to the Pāñcarātra doctrine. Here—
In an impermanent jar, which is agreed upon by both disputants, the reason "permanence" is unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddha*). Or, for example:
"Sound is permanent, because it is visible. Here, visibility is unestablished in sound, the subject (*pakṣa*).

An example of *bhāgāsiddha* (partial unestablished) is: "The individual soul (*jīva*) and the body are non-eternal, because they are products, like a jar. Here, the property of being a product (*kāryatva*) is unestablished with respect to the *jīva* among the two things—the *jīva* and the body—that constitute the subject (*pakṣa*). An example of *āśrayāsiddha* (unestablished locus) is:
"A sky-lotus is fragrant, because it is a lotus, like a pond-lotus. Here...

A sky-lotus cannot exist. An example of [an inference] where the qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*) is unestablished (*asiddha*) is: "Sound is eternal, because it possesses the quality of being visible (*cākṣuṣatva*), like color. In this reason (*hetu*), the qualification "being visible" is unestablished. An example of [an inference] where the qualified (*viśeṣya*) is unestablished is: "Sound is eternal..."

"Because it is a substance while being an object of knowledge, like a pot. In this reason (*hetu*), there is the non-establishment (*asiddhi*) of "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*), which serves as the substantive element (*viśeṣya*). An example of that which is unestablished for both [the proponent and the opponent] is: "A pot is eternal, because it is supersensible while being a quality (*guṇa*). In this reason, "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*), which serves as the adjectival element (*viśeṣaṇa*), is unestablished.

The transcendence of the senses (*atīndriyatva*), which serves as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), is also unestablished. An example of a reason being unestablished due to ignorance (*ajñānāsiddha*) is as follows:

"Devadatta possesses much wealth, because he is the substratum of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) which is the cause thereof, like Yajñadatta. Here, the reason—being the substratum of unseen merit—is unestablished due to ignorance, since we have not perceived such a substratum.

An example of [the fallacy] unestablished due to ignorance of the locus (*adhikaraṇājñānāsiddha*) is as follows: "Now, in this space here, an atom is at some time the initiator of a substance, because it is an atom, like an atom that initiates a jar.
In this case, the locus...
The reason is unestablished due to ignorance of its locus, because an atom whose substratum is space is not known; that is, there is ignorance regarding its support (*āśrayājñānāsiddha*).
An example of one being unestablished for either party (*anyatarāsiddha*) is: "Sound is non-eternal, because it is produced, like a jar.
Here, in the view of the other party, the Mīmāṃsaka, the state of being produced (*kṛtakatva*)...

Because the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*), this is a "reason unestablished for one of the two parties" (*anyatarāsiddha*). An example of a "reason unestablished in its pervasion" (*vyāpyatvāsiddha*) is: "Everything is momentary, because it exists, like a water bubble. Here, because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to apprehend the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between existence and momentariness, this is the first [type of *vyāpyatvāsiddha*].

The reason (*hetu*) is unestablished due to lack of pervasion (*vyāpyatvāsiddha*). An example of unestablished pervasion due to a limiting condition (*aupādhika-vyāpyatvāsiddha*) is as follows: "The child in the womb is dark-complexioned, because he is the son of Maitra, like the previously born sons of Maitra. Here, while darkness is the property to be proven (*sādhya*), there exists a limiting condition (*upādhi*) consisting precisely in the difference in the digestion of food such as vegetables; therefore, it is an instance of unestablished pervasion due to a limiting condition.
This reason is unestablished (asiddha).

31) Now, the contradictory (*viruddha*). Its definition is: being pervaded by the opposite of the probandum (*sādhya*), or having as its probandum that which is pervaded by the opposite of the probans (*sādhana*). For example: "Sound is eternal, because it is a product, like space. Here, the reason "being a product" is pervaded by non-eternality, which is the opposite of its own probandum.

[This is] pervaded. However, an example where the probandum is pervaded by the opposite of the probans is as follows: "The mind is non-eternal, because it is conscious, like the self. Here, the probandum in the form of non-eternality is pervaded by its own opposite probans, namely, lack of consciousness.
32) The inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) reason is that which deviates. It is of two kinds:
the common inconclusive (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*) and the uncommon inconclusive (*asādhāraṇānaikāntika*). Among these, the first is as follows:

"The self (*ātman*) is eternal, because it is an object of cognition (*prameyatva*). Here, the reason of being an object of cognition exists both in the subject (*pakṣa*), the self, and in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*).

It exists in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), such as a jar, and in the subject itself. As for the second type—for example: "Earth is eternal, because it possesses odor"—here the reason, "possessing odor," is excluded from the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) such as the self (*ātman*) and from the counter-examples such as water, and it exists only in the subject (*pakṣa*).

33) A reason that does not determine the probandum (*sādhyāniścāyaka*) is the "unascertained" (*anadhyavasita*). For example: "The universe exists continuously, because it is a real entity (*vastutvāt*). Here, the reason "being a real entity" does not determine its own probandum, namely continuous existence;
therefore, it is unascertained. A reason that is sublated by another stronger means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the "mistimed" (*kālātīta*). It...
Thus, it is called "having its object sublated. It is fivefold due to the distinctions among the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Among these, sublation by perception (*pratyakṣabādha*) is, for example: "Fire is not hot, because it is an entity (*padārtha*). Sublation by inference (*anumānabādha*) is, for example: "The entire universe is without a material cause (*nirupādānaka*), because it is adventitious (*āgantuka*). Sublation by scripture (*āgamabādha*)...
For example: "Sacrifices and the like do not bring about heaven, because they are actions, like fruitless actions.

An instance of sublation by presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is as follows: "Devadatta, who lives for a hundred years, is neither in the house nor outside, because he is not perceived by direct perception. And so it has been stated in the venerable *Pauṣkara*:
In this Śiva-āgama, five refutations of logical reasons (hetu) are stated:
the first is the non-establishment (asiddhi) of the reason when its presence in the subject (pakṣavṛtti) is not certain.
Because atoms are eternal, the reason [that they are causes] is unestablished in its essential nature;
it is likewise unestablished in its various aspects due to the non-establishment of the qualifier, the qualified, and so forth.
A present [reason] would be contradictory with respect to both the subject (pakṣa) and the counter-subject (vipakṣa),
whether it be pervasive or non-pervasive, due to the reason that it is not spatially delimited.
That which exists in all three states of the [three] propositions is the inconclusive (anaikāntika) reason;
O twice-born ones, "the self is eternal because it is knowable" is cited as an example of this.
An unproven non-implicative reason is that which is indeterminate with respect to the subject itself;
for example, it has been stated: "The universe exists as a continuum because it is a real entity."
"But the 'mistimed' [reason] is that which contradicts the means of knowledge regarding the probandum in the subject;
for example: 'The universe is without a material cause, because its effects are adventitious.'"

(From *Pramāṇapaddhati*, verses 51–56) 34) Those who, however, include the "undetermined" (*anadhyavasita*) within the "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*), consider the "neutralized" (*prakaraṇasama*) to be a fifth [type of inconclusive reason]. Its definition, moreover, is: that for which there exists a counter-reason of equal strength that establishes the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*).

A reason that exists [but is countered] is called *satpratipakṣa* (counter-balanced) or *prakaraṇasama* (neutralized by the context), as for example: "Sound is eternal, because it is devoid of subverting evidence"; and "It is non-eternal, because it is devoid of proving evidence. Thus it has been stated in the venerable *Pauṣkara*: "Non-sublation and being counter-balanced [constitute the requirements of a valid reason]."

By stating that the absence of a counter-argument is a quality of a logical reason (*hetu*), Śiva himself has indicated that a reason possessing a counter-argument is a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*). There are four types of fallacious subjects (*pakṣābhāsa*): in some cases due to the absence of a subject, and in others due to the absence of the property of being a subject-feature (*pakṣadharmatva*).

In some cases, because both the presence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and its concomitance with the property to be proven (*paksasapakṣadharmatva*) are absent; and in other cases, even though both are present, there is an absence of pervasion (*vyāpti*).
35) Here follow the examples in order: "The sky-flower is fragrant, because it is a flower. In this case...

The subject itself does not exist [as a locus for the reason], as in: "The self is impermanent, because it has the nature of an atom. Here, since there is no nature of an atom, the property of being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) is absent. "The horn of a rabbit is fragrant, because it is composed of earth. Here, both the subject and the property of being a property of the subject do not exist. "Earth is eternal, because it is visible. Here...

Even though the presence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and its existence in the subject (*pakṣasattva*) may be established, there is no pervasion (*vyāpti*) between the probandum and the probans.

(36) Furthermore, these fallacious subjects (*pakṣābhāsa*) are subsumed under the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddha*), the unestablished nature (*svarūpāsiddha*), and the unestablished pervasion (*vyāpyatvāsiddha*); therefore, they are not defined separately here. As for the fallacious examples (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*):

They are of two kinds: due to defects of meaning (*arthadoṣa*) and due to defects of expression (*uktidoṣa*). Among these, the defect of meaning is fourfold: the deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*), the deficiency of the probans (*sādhanavaikalya*), the deficiency of both, and the deficiency of the essential nature (*svarūpavaikalya*) of the similar instance (*sādharmyadṛṣṭānta*). As for the dissimilar instance (*vaidharmyadṛṣṭānta*), however, there is the deficiency of the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāvavaikalya*).
It is fourfold: deficiency of the means of accomplishment and deficiency of the essential nature.

37) For example: "The universe is an effect, because it is perceptible; by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), like the self (*ātman*)," and in that same context, "like unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*)," "like illusion (*māyā*)," and "like a sky-flower (*khapuṣpa*). Or again: "The subject of dispute is an effect, because it is imperceptible; by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), like the self," and in that same context, "like unseen merit."

The fault of expression regarding both the positive example (*anvaya-dṛṣṭānta*) and the negative example (*vyatireka-dṛṣṭānta*) consists in stating them in reverse order— such as saying "like an illusion" or "like a sky-flower"—
and in stating the positive and negative pervasions (*anvaya-vyatireka-vyāpti*) in reverse order; this occurs in that very same context.

In positive inference (*anvayānumāna*), there are five types: (1) stating the probandum and the probans in reverse order; (2) stating the probandum as the probans; and (3) stating the probans as the probandum. Likewise, there are five types in negative inference (*vyatirekānumāna*), making ten types in total. For example, in the positive formulation: "The mountain possesses fire, because it has smoke."

Having stated the positive concomitance (*anvayavyāpti*) as "just as in a great lake," and having shown the negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*) in that very same context, [he then states] the positive concomitance again as "just as in a kitchen" (meaning:
wherever there is fire, there is smoke, just as in a kitchen), and in that very same context, the mountain...
"In 'smoky because of possessing fire,' [the following are] examples of the opposite of the probandum (*sādhyaviparyaya*), the opposite of the probans (*sādhanaviparyaya*),
and [furthermore] the opposite of the probans; thus,
by virtue of defects in the word and its meaning, as well as by virtue of positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*), there are eighteen fallacious examples (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*)."

If it is asked, "Since these pseudo-examples (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*) are not defined in the treatises on logic (*tarkaśāstra*), how are they defined here?", [the answer is: because they can be subsumed under the fallacies of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*), such as non-establishment (*asiddhi*) and so forth, they were not mentioned separately there. However, since they are mentioned separately in this Śaiva Āgama, they are proclaimed here as distinct categories.
This has been stated in the venerable Pauṣkara:
"When a proposition such as 'fire is not hot' is asserted along with its reason,
[it involves] the first two of the five members of inference."
The contrariety has been pointed out; now the illustration is being stated:
"The self is eternal because of its omnipresence, just like space."
"The example may be deficient in the probandum, and likewise in the probans," and so forth.
(Pau Pra Pa Ślo 58–60) 38) In this context, *chala*, *jāti*, and *nigrahasthāna* are defined. Among these, the definition of *chala* is as follows:
"When a statement is employed with a specific meaning in mind,
the attribution of an unintended meaning to it and the subsequent negation of that [intended] meaning is considered *chala* (quibble)."

And that [quibble] is threefold: quibble regarding speech (*vākchala*), quibble regarding generality (*sāmānyacchala*), and quibble regarding metaphorical usage (*upacāracchala*). Among these, the definition of quibble regarding speech is:
"The subversion of an intended meaning by means of a distortion of the expression."

For example: in the argument "This man is wealthy because he has nine blankets," there is a negation based on superimposing a numerical sense onto the word *nava*, which is used here in the sense of "new. [The objection asks: "Where are his nine blankets?
Only one blanket is established by direct perception."
The definition of the quibble based on generality (*sāmānyacchala*) is as follows: "This is the quibble based on generality,
which consists in the subversion of an intended meaning by means of a connection with a generality, through a reversal of the intended purport."
Someone might utter the statement, "Oh, this Brahmin is a learned scholar," merely on the basis of the possibility that the Brahmin is a learned scholar;
then, a quibbler (chala-vādī), superimposing upon it the intended sense that being a Brahmin is the cause for being a learned scholar, [objects].
An objection is raised: being a Brāhmaṇa is not the cause for being a learned reciter (anūcāna), because it is inconclusive with respect to those who merely claim to be Brāhmaṇas.

The definition of quibble regarding metaphorical usage (*upacāra-chala*) is as follows: "In the employment of metaphorical and indicative expressions, that sublation which occurs because the primary meaning is impossible is indeed quibble regarding metaphorical usage."
Just as in the expressions "a hamlet on the Ganges" and "the boy is a lion," how can there be a dwelling of a hamlet on the Ganges, or how can a boy be a lion? Such is the objection raised.

When a disputant employs a statement involving quibble (*chala*) with respect to the opponent's investigation, if the opponent does not recognize it or the members of the assembly do not expose it, the fault lies with the opponent; conversely, if they do expose it, the fault lies with the disputant.

39) Now, regarding *jāti* (futile rejoinders): these are [the following types]: *sādharmya* (similarity), *vaidharmya* (dissimilarity), *utkarṣa* (exaltation), *apakarṣa* (depreciation), *varṇya* (the subject to be praised), *avarṇya* (the subject not to be praised), *vikalpa* (alternative), *sādhyasama* (equivalence of the probandum), *prāptisama* (equivalence of attainment), *prasangasama* (equivalence of consequence), *pratidṛṣṭāntasama* (equivalence of a counter-example), *anutpattisama* (equivalence of non-arising), *saṃśayasama* (equivalence of doubt), *prakaraṇasama* (equivalence of the point at issue), *hetusama* (equivalence of the reason), *arthāpattisama* (equivalence of presumption), *aviśeṣasama* (equivalence of non-distinction), *upapattisama* (equivalence of proof), *upalabdhisama* (equivalence of perception), *anupalabdhisama* (equivalence of non-perception), *nityasama* (equivalence of the eternal), and *anityasama* (equivalence of the non-eternal).
Regarding the term *kāryasamā*: here, the word *sama* (equal), which is heard at the end of the *dvandva* compound, is connected with each member individually. Their general definition is as follows:
when a reason for establishing [a position] has been employed, the response is incapable of refuting it.
Others, however, say that "rejoinder" (uttara) is that which contradicts itself. Thus [it is said].
In that regard, the definition of the genus (*jāti*) for both the similar (*sādharmya-sama*) and the dissimilar (*vaidharmya-sama*) [futilities] is as follows:

"The counter-positioning (*pratyavasthāna*) against a reason (*hetu*) employed by a proponent for the purpose of establishing one's own view, by means of similarity or dissimilarity, is [the fallacy known as] *tatsama* (the equal)."

Among these, the *sādharmyasama* (balancing through similarity) *jāti* is as follows: when it is stated in the conclusion that "sound is non-eternal because it is produced," [the opponent objects]: "This is not so; for there is also a similarity with space (*ākāśa*) in its formlessness (*amūrtatva*). Why, then, should it not be eternal like that? There is no distinction."

The *vaidharmyasamā* (balancing the heterogeneity) sophistry is as follows: regarding the same aforementioned conclusion, one might ask, "Since it possesses properties heterogeneous to a jar—namely, audibility—why should it not be eternal? In this manner, other varieties of *jāti* (futile rejoinders) are also to be inferred.
40) The definition of the points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*): "The crushing of another's ego by one whose own ego remains unshaken—that is 'defeat' (*nigraha*).
The ground for that [defeat] is called a 'point of defeat' (*nigrahasthāna*). Thus it is said.
And these are: abandonment of the proposition, shifting the proposition, contradiction of the proposition,

renunciation of the proposition, shifting the reason, shifting the meaning, the meaningless, the understood meaning, the irrelevant, the mistimed, the deficient, the redundant, the repetitive, and failure to restate.

Ignorance, lack of ingenuity, distraction, admission of an opponent's view, overlooking what requires censure, censuring what does not require censure, deviating from one's own tenet, and fallacious reasons— these are the twenty-two points of defeat.

The definition of the loss of the proposition (*pratijñāhāni*): When that which was initially stated by someone in the debate— such as the thesis (*pakṣa*) and so forth— is subsequently abandoned by that same person, it is called the loss of the proposition.

And that [rejection] is of six kinds due to the abandonment of the probandum, the probans, the subject, and their respective particulars. Among these, the rejection of the thesis regarding the probandum (*sādhyapratijñāhāni*) is as follows: when it has been stated, "Sound is impermanent because it is perceptible by the senses," [the opponent objects] that "generality (*sāmānya*), though perceptible by the senses, is seen to be permanent."

If it is replied that [the reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), then one might argue that sound (*śabda*) would also be eternal; in this manner, other definitions of points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) should also be inferred.

41) Now, verbal testimony (*śabda-pramāṇa*) is defined. Knowledge produced by the words of a reliable person (*āpta*) is verbal testimony. A "reliable person" is an individual who perceives things as they truly are and teaches accordingly.
His "words," however, are a collection of terms possessing mutual expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), semantic competency (*yogyatā*), and proximity (*sannidhi*). By means of that—

"A pot," "objectness," and "bringing" and "effort" are deficient in expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*); "one should sprinkle with fire" is incompatible (*ayogya*); and that which is uttered with an interval, such as "cow... bring," is not a sentence.
Expectancy is the desire to know on the part of the cognizer. Compatibility is the absence of certainty regarding a lack of syntactic connection (*ananvaya*).

Proximity (*sannidhi*) is the presence [of words] without interruption. Therefore, a sentence is a collection of words possessing expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), compatibility (*yogyatā*), and proximity. That is of two kinds: the worldly, such as "There are five fruits on the bank of the river," and the Vedic, which is the speech of the supreme authority, the venerable Sadāśiva. And that—

It is twofold: the Veda and the Śaiva Āgama. The Vedic statement is well known; the Śaiva Āgama statement, however, is as follows: "Having attained [the means] for liberation, one should resort to those virtuous ones and the abode of Śiva," and so forth. Therefore, regarding the Veda and the Śaiva Āgama...
Because they were composed by the supreme and most trustworthy Sadāśiva, those two alone provide a correct understanding;
only the knowledge produced by them is valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

42) However, the authority of the Vedas is established because their originator has not been specified, because they are not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*), and for that very reason they are eternal, as well as being accepted by great people (*mahājana*). But since the scriptures (*āgama*) are the opposite of that— having fallen outside the path of the revealed word (*śruti*)— they are included within the system of the Tantric path, and so forth.
If it is asked, "How can there be authority [for the Vedas] given that faults are heard regarding their performance?"— this is true;

however, for those who accept the authority of the *smṛtis* of Manu and others composed by seers (*ṛṣis*), how could there be any suspicion of lack of authority regarding the *āgamas* composed by the Lord who is worshipped by them?

[This is] the opportunity [for refutation]. Now, if you think that their authority is due to being rooted in an impersonal, eternal Veda, that is untenable; for instance, is the eternity of the Veda in terms of its own nature (*svarūpataḥ*) or in terms of its continuity (*pravāhataḥ*)? Not the first; because its nature consists of sound, it perishes as soon as it is uttered, and thus [cannot be perceived] through direct perception (*pratyakṣataḥ*).

This is because of the observation of impermanence, and because recognitions such as "this is that very letter *ga*" lack the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding the permanence of the nature of sound, since they have only a universal (*sāmānya*) as their object. Nor is the second [alternative] tenable; for even if there were permanence in the form of a continuous stream, this would consist merely in the non-interruption of the tradition between teacher and student.

Because conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) is characterized by arising and destruction, and because the Veda is included within that [proliferation], it is indeed non-eternal. Therefore, [the Veda's authority] is established solely on the basis of its being composed by the Supreme Lord, the supreme authoritative person (*paramāpta*), who is eternal, stainless, omniscient, free from partiality, a perceiver of things as they truly are, imperishable, perfect, independent, and the destroyer of both the bound souls (*paśu*) and their fetters (*pāśa*).

The authority of the Vedas and the Āgamas [is established]. If it is asked, "Since the Veda is heard to be self-existent (*svayaṃbhū*) and eternal (*nitya*), how can it possess origination and destruction?", that is not so;
for it is an effect (*kārya*) by virtue of being composed by the Supreme Lord, the self-existent and supreme authority.

Because the status of being the cause is metaphorically attributed [to it], and because its self-existence and eternity—due to its persisting until the dissolution of the universe—are heard of in various places. If it is argued that, since the authority of the Āgamas is accepted on the grounds that they were composed by the Supreme Lord, it would follow that the Vāma and other such [Tantras] must also be authoritative, this is true; yet...
By the Lord himself, for those entitled to Vedic rites, [the means] are supplemented by the Vedas;
whereas for those such as the twice-born who were seized by the curse of the six sages, [liberation occurs] through the performance of rituals according to independent Āgamas in another birth.

Other systems, such as Vāma and the rest, were taught by me solely for the purpose of establishing eligibility for Vedic Śaiva rites and for the purpose of deluding the Asuras and others; therefore, these independent Āgamas, which contradict the Vedas, should not be practiced by my devotees who are disciplined.
Because it has been stated thus, each of those [scriptures] possesses authority only with respect to its respective qualified practitioner, and not with respect to everyone.
As it is said in the Kāmika:
"The Śaiva Āgama is also considered to be of two kinds: that which is based on direct revelation (śrauta) and that which is not based on direct revelation (aśrauta)."
That which consists of the essence of the Vedas is considered Śrauta, while the other is regarded as Svatantra.
Furthermore, other treatises in this world that contradict the teachings of the Vedas have indeed been proclaimed by me for the purpose of delusion.
"The Vāma, the Pāśupata, the Vātula, and the Bhairava—
these are said not to be practiced, as they are outside the Vedas and likewise other such [systems]."

43) Therefore, even the prohibition of tantric practice refers exclusively to those tantras that contradict the Vedas. If it is argued that since knowledge and liberation are possible through other scriptural traditions (āgamas), Vedic (ārṣa), and divine sources, those very scriptures are sufficient, we say no; for in those...

Because it describes only the twenty-four principles that have descended from primordial nature (*prakṛti*), and because it fails to describe the supreme liberation that transcends the thirty-six principles, and because [the two systems] are mutually contradictory;
therefore, knowledge and liberation [are attained] only through the scriptures composed by the Supreme Lord, who is distinguished by omniscience and other attributes.
Thus, everything regarding "attainment" (*siddhi*) is clarified. As it is stated in the *Pauṣkara*:

"Alternatively, those objects within the sphere of Śiva that have not been attained by the virtuous through faith, others—namely, the objects within the spheres of primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and so forth—have been attained by other good people."
The word of the ṛṣis is not [contradicted] by human speech, nor is the divine word [of the gods] by the ṛṣis;
the word of Brahmā is not [contradicted] by the gods, nor the word of Viṣṇu by the lotus-born [Brahmā].
Likewise, the Raudra [tantra] is not sublated by the Hara [tantra], nor is that spoken by Śiva sublated by the Raudra;
because of the progressive superiority of each higher level, the lower is sublated by the higher.
All scripture is established in accordance with the Śiva-āgamas,
not in contradiction with other scriptures, nor merely by way of agreement with them.
The Śiva-śāstra must be established, because it is that which establishes [all else];
for whatever extent of pervasion is desired for any given scripture, [that is found therein].
O Brahmins, the authority of each of those [means of knowledge] is limited to that very extent;
that scripture which consists of the words of a reliable person is also the sole means for establishing objects that are beyond the reach of the senses.
He who declares an object with complete certainty—whether through direct perception or through inference—is an authoritative person (āpta); therefore, Śiva is the most authoritative of all.
With his entire collection of sense-faculties perfectly serene, he is omniscient and has all things as his domain;
free from partiality, he always perceives things exactly as they are.
He is imperishable, perfectly complete, independent, and the destroyer of the bonds of bound souls;
His word alone is the sole authority, ever true and a treasury of the highest good.
Immediately after creation, the Lord, by the mere touch of His own rays, makes those souls whose domain is the pure path (śuddhādhvan) intense in their vision and action.
The Lord Sadāśiva also, having entered into the form of Sound (nāda),
[manifests] knowledge consisting of the six categories as well as manifold meters.
"The treasure-house of compassion taught them the ten-fold division of Śiva previously mentioned, as well as another, the eighteen-fold division of Raudra. Thus [it is said].
44) Here,

by the word "means of knowledge" (*pramāṇa*), the word [itself] is denoted, either through the etymological derivation based on the instrument (*karaṇa*) or through the metaphorical identification of the word with its meaning; in all cases, it is the power of consciousness alone.
Because its authority has been established. Thus it is stated in the venerable Pauṣkara:
"But the word, through a traditional lineage, is the inferential indicator of the knowledge of Śiva."

(Prapañcasāra, verse 74) 45) A *pada* is a collection of phonemes (*varṇa*). Since phonemes are momentary and thus lack the capacity to convey meaning, the *sphoṭa*— so called— is [posited] within the phonemes for the purpose of conveying meaning.

Some category of entity must be admitted as eternal. Thus, the threefold nature of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is established. Within these very three means of valid cognition, all others—such as analogy (*upamāna*) and so forth—are included as appropriate. For instance, presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is included within inference (*anumāna*).
How so?
Presumption (*arthāpatti*) is the postulation of another fact that makes a given fact possible, based on the perception of a fact that would otherwise be impossible.
For example, having observed the absence of the living Devadatta from his house, one postulates his presence outside.

This [inference] is indeed nothing but inference (*anumāna*), because it is produced by the knowledge of "presumption" (*arthāpatti*) insofar as that presumption consists in an inseparable relation (*avinābhāva*).
For "presumption" is the impossibility of a living person's absence from the house without his being outside;
this is precisely the inseparable relation itself: Devadatta, being absent from the house while being alive for a hundred years, must be present outside.
Because it is the counter-positive of the absence of being at home; for that which is not so is not thus, just as, for example, Yajñadatta when he is not alive at home.

46) Analogy (*upamāna*) is also nothing but inference (*anumāna*); it is not a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). To explain: if analogy is the cognition of similarity, then it is simply perception (*pratyakṣa*), because the apprehension "this is similar to that" is possible through perception. However, if the cognition "that is similar to this" is analogy, [it is likewise reduced to inference].
Then, [the cognition] "this is similar to that" arises because this is the counter-correlate of the similarity residing in that;
for whatever is the counter-correlate of the similarity of something is similar to it, just as is commonly accepted—this is indeed an inference.
Now, immediately after hearing the sentence of transfer (*atideśavākya*), through the recognition of its meaning, of that...

Even then, the determination of denotability belongs to the individual object through the sentence; the determination that a universal residing in the individual is the ground for the application of the word follows from the mark of parsimony (*lāghava*). Therefore, comparison (*upamāna*) is not a separate means of knowledge.

47) Possibility (*saṃbhava*) also does not exceed the scope of inference (*anumāna*). For "possibility" is the ascertainment of the existence of a hundred based on the fact that "a hundred is possible within a thousand. And since that [ascertainment] is produced by grasping the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) of the hundred with the thousand, it is nothing but inference. Furthermore, it is established that if tradition (*aitihya*) is in accordance with reality, it is simply verbal testimony (*śabda*).

48) Even non-existence (*abhāva*) is not distinct from perception (*pratyakṣa*). For instance, the non-existence of a jar or the like is apprehended by the sense organ, because the cognition thereof conforms to the presence and absence (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of that [sense organ].
Nor is it established otherwise [than as perception] by the apprehension of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) and its dependence thereon, as is the case with the cognition of fire and so forth.

It is logical that [the cognition] conforms to that [object]. For otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that a person with closed eyes could perceive the absence of blue and so forth in a jar or other object presented to the sense of touch.
If it is argued that the cause is the cognition of the locus (*adhikaraṇa-jñāna*) produced by the sense organ that perceives the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), we say no; for...
Otherwise, since air is not perceived by the eye, it would follow that one could perceive the absence of color in it.

Furthermore, since defects in the sense organs and so forth are observed when there is a cognition of absence, its being produced by the senses must be admitted even on that basis. Nor is it the case that there is no contact such as conjunction with an absence.

How its status as being perceived by the senses (*aindriyikatva*) is to be explained must be stated; for it is logical to postulate the sense-object contact (*sannikarṣa*) of "qualifier-ness" (*viśeṣaṇatā*) in accordance with its being perceived by the senses. Nor is there a mutual dependence between the postulation of its being perceived by the senses and the postulation of the sense-object contact; for [the postulation of the contact] follows from the postulation of its being perceived by the senses.
Because it is not required; for sensory contact is required for something to be perceived by the senses, but the postulation of that [contact] is not required for the postulation of that [object].

49) The method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*) is also nothing but inference. For instance, when it is stated, "The thief is among these ten; these nine are not the thief," there arises the certain cognition: "This one is the thief. [The formal argument is: The state of being a thief resides in such-and-such a person, because, while residing in any one of those present before us, it does not reside in any other than such-and-such a person.

This is indeed an inference, such as "because of being so-and-so. Even though there was no prior apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) regarding specific instances like "being so-and-so," it is possible to apprehend pervasion in a general sense. Thus, the threefold nature of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is established.

50) The validity (*prāmāṇya*) of these [cognitions] is both apprehended and produced intrinsically (*svataḥ*). In this context, "being apprehended intrinsically" means being apprehended by every cognizer of its own substratum at a time when no sublation (*bādhā*) has occurred.
And in this matter, the proof is the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) itself; for by that which apprehends the cognition, the cognition [is apprehended].
That which is delimited by an object is apprehended; and the object includes both the qualifier and the qualified, as well as their relation.

For this very reason, the after-cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) "I know the jar precisely as a jar" is observed. Nor should it be argued that, in this case, doubt regarding validity would be impossible, since such doubt is incompatible with what has been ascertained; for even when an object is ascertained...
For doubt is established through the doubt that knowledge might be produced by defects; otherwise,
even for one who maintains the extrinsic nature of validity (*paratastva*), there would be no doubt regarding validity,
since the object's actual state is ascertained by the primary cognition (*vyavasāya*) even if it is not ascertained by the subsequent reflective cognition (*anuvyavasāya*).

Furthermore, because doubt regarding validity culminates in doubt regarding that [object] itself; otherwise, there would result a doubt regarding validity even with respect to an object that has been well-ascertained. And intrinsicness (*svatastva*) in the production [of knowledge] consists in being produced by whatever causal complex produces its own substratum-knowledge, provided that it is produced by the causal complex of knowledge.

The self-validity (*svatastva*) of valid cognition (*pramā*) consists in its not being produced by causes other than those [constituting the causal complex of knowledge]. And there is an inference for this:

"The subject under dispute, valid cognition, while being produced by the causal complex of knowledge, is not produced by anything additional to that, because it does not possess the property of invalidity (*apramātva*), like a jar. Nor is it the case that the subject under dispute is valid cognition...

One might suspect that Udayana’s inference—that "valid cognition (pramā) is dependent on a cause over and above the causes of [ordinary] cognition, because, while being an effect, it is a specific kind of that [cognition], like invalid cognition (apramā)"—is a subverting argument (*bādhaka*). [However, this is not so, for one may counter:
"Valid cognition is not produced by anything other than the causes of cognition distinct from defects, because it is a cognition, like invalid cognition."

Because it is seized by the planet of the counter-argument (*pratisādhana*), and because, since the production of valid cognition is possible from the mere collection of causal conditions for knowledge (*jñānasāmagrī*) alone,
there would follow the fault of conceptual over-elaboration (*kalpanāgaurava*) in postulating an additional cause such as a "quality" (*guṇa*) or the "absence of defects" (*doṣābhāva*).

51) If it is argued that since a defect (*doṣa*) is the cause of invalid cognition (*apramā*), it is difficult to avoid the conclusion that the absence of such a defect must be the cause of valid cognition (*pramā*), we reply: no, because the absence of a defect is otherwise accounted for (*anyathāsiddha*) as being merely the non-obstructer of invalid cognition. Invalid cognition, however, arises and is known only extrinsically (*parataḥ*). For that [invalid cognition], there exists [a cause] distinct from the causal complex of cognition (*jñānasāmagrī*).

This is because [error] is the cause for the arising of a defect; and regarding its cognition, there is the possibility of another means of knowledge (*māna*)—distinct from the causal complex that grasps the cognition itself—acting as its grasper. As for its definition, it is either "the state of being a cognition whose qualifier does not reside in the qualificandum" (*viśeṣyāvṛttyaprakārakajñānatva*), or "the state of being a cognition whose qualifier resides in what is not that [qualificandum]" (*atadvati tatprakārakajñānatva*).
Furthermore, such erroneous cognition does not consist of two cognitions—one of perception and one of memory—as asserted by the Prābhākara school;

for this contradicts the manifestation of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the form "this is silver. Nor is there a single cognition in the case of "this is silver" [that could account for the error].

It cannot be said that silver arises as something indefinable (*anirvacanīya*) within the mother-of-pearl, because the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) for its production is absent. Nor can it be maintained that the silver arises as something non-existent (*asat*), for it is impossible for that which is a mere void (*tuccha*) to undergo either production or cognition. Furthermore, it cannot be said that the silver merely appears within the self (*ātman*).

For if that were the case, it would follow that there would be the cognition "I am silver. Therefore, since the other theories of error (*khyāti*) lack any basis in valid authority (*prāmāṇika*), it is established that erroneous cognition is indeed *anyathākhyāti* (the theory of misapprehension).

Thus ends the "Exposition of the Means of Valid Cognition" (*pramāṇanirūpaṇa*) in the *Śaivaparibhāṣā*, composed by the venerable Jñānaśivācārya, the foremost lord of yogins, protector of the Śaivas, and teacher who transcends the [ordinary] castes and stages of life (*ativarṇāśramācārya*).
The First Chapter.
The Second Chapter:
1) Now, the object of knowledge (*prameya*) is investigated. That is threefold: the Lord (*pati*), the bound soul (*paśu*), and the fetter (*pāśa*).
As it has been said:
"The Lord, the bound soul, and the bond—these three categories have been declared. Thus it is said.

In this regard, because the bound souls (paśus) lack autonomy and the fetters (pāśas) are insentient, the Lord (pati) is mentioned first; immediately after him, the bound souls, due to their commonality of being sentient; and following that, the remaining category, the fetters. Now, one might object:
Seven categories are taught in the Svāyaṃbhuvatantra; six in the Pauṣkara and Mataṅga;
five are stated in the venerable Parākhyatantra; and three in the Rauravatantra.

If it is asked, "Since we observe that categories (padārtha) possess various kinds of enumerations, how can it be that there are only three categories?", the answer is true: because those [categories] distinct from Pati and Paśu are included within the category of Pāśa,
and because our sage, Vāmadeva of the Santāna lineage, primarily follows the Raurava Āgama, it is according to that [tradition].

There is no contradiction, as it has been stated that there are three categories (*padārtha*). In this context, by the word "Lord" (*pati*), Hara is meant; just as saying "Indra" implies "Devendra," or as saying "Bhāma" implies "Satyabhāmā," the whole name is understood through the mention of a part of the name, thus "Paśupati" refers to Hara. Now, [one might ask] regarding the threefold activity consisting of creation, maintenance, and dissolution...
