If it is asked: "Since it is heard many times in the Vedas, Āgamas, and Purāṇas that [the world] has Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra as its agents, how can it be determined here that Hara alone is the Lord?"—[we reply: if it is stated that among the three forms presiding over the three qualities (guṇas), who are the agents of the primary creation and so forth, Rudra alone is the agent.

There is room for doubt here. To this I have replied: that which transcends the three qualities (*guṇas*), which is the causal essence of the three forms (*trimūrtis*), which is devoid of gross, subtle, and void forms, and whose sole nature is consciousness and bliss—that is, even though it is devoid of qualities, names, and actions, by way of metaphorical application (*yogavṛtti*), it is denoted by all such words as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and so forth.
That the supreme reality (paratattva) is what is to be expressed—of this there is no room for doubt.
2) As it is said in the Devīkālottara:
"Neither gross nor subtle, nor of the nature of emptiness, he is of the singular form of knowledge, the sole kinsman of the world."
In the Parākhyatantra it is said: "Indeed, that Supreme Lord exists as a single entity, though differentiated by names;
because of his vastness and because of his power of expansion, he is Brahma through his union with Śiva."
"Viṣṇu is the source and the Lord of the worlds because his nature is that of the originator;
he is called Rudra because he causes the destruction of suffering (ruj), and thus [he is so named] from the destruction of pain. Thus it is said.
In the Sūta-saṃhitā of the Skanda Purāṇa:
"The reality is free from conceptual construction, knowledge, bliss, and imperishable;
nor do names and forms belong to Śiva, the Supreme Self."
Nevertheless, through his illusory power (māyā), name and form are fashioned for him:
Śiva, Rudra, Mahādeva, Śaṅkara, Brahmā, and the supreme reality (sat-param).
"Names such as Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, and others apply to the Supreme Lord only through some figurative application (yoga-vṛtti), but not in their primary sense."

3) The essential definition (*svarūpalakṣaṇa*) of that reality is as follows: it is beyond the reach of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) pertaining to bound souls (*paśu*) and their fetters (*pāśa*);
it consists of pure, unsurpassed, self-luminous knowledge and bliss; it is all-pervading (*vibhu*), eternal, independent, and auspicious (*śiva*).
Thus it has been stated in the venerable *Svāyambhuva*:
"Immeasurable, indescribable, incomparable, and free from disease;
subtle, omnipresent, eternal, constant, imperishable, and the Lord. Thus [it is said].

And that this characteristic was stated solely by way of excluding what is not that has been explained right there: "It is immeasurable because it is infinite; it is indefinable because it lacks defining characteristics;
it is incomparable because it has no likeness; it is free from affliction because it is stainless."
It is subtle because it is unperceivable and all-pervading because it is omnipresent;
it is eternal because it is devoid of a cause and it is constant because it is immovable;
it is imperishable because it is perfectly complete and it is the Lord because it possesses the nature of a master. Thus [it is said].
And in the venerable Parākhyatantra it is said: "The essential nature of this Śiva, the Supreme Self, is the form of consciousness, which is characterized by the powers of knowledge and action."
In the Devīkālottara it is said: "O Dear One, seeing everything— both external and internal— as being like space, formless, and supreme bliss, one becomes a partaker of bliss."
"In the glorious *Acintya*: 'That supreme bliss of Śaṅkara is to be known as neither perceptual, nor inferential, nor even verbal.'"
"The supreme light is self-cognizable... and so forth.

4) Its definition as a bystander (*taṭasthalakṣaṇa*) is its performance of the fivefold activity (*pañcavidhakṛtya*). Nor is there an over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to [deities] such as Ananteśa and others, because even for them, it is through the manifestation of that [supreme light].

Because it is characterized by the performance of fivefold functions; those fivefold functions are creation, maintenance, withdrawal, concealment, and grace. As it is said in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
"The birth, maintenance, destruction, concealment, and liberation of the world..."
"For this very thing is to be known as its function, along with its factors of action and its fruit. Thus [it is said].
(Pratyabhijñā-hṛdaya 2.3) 5) Regarding the existence of this Lord, the Vedas, the Āgamas, and inference are the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
The Vedas and Āgamas are well-known. As for inference, however: [it is established] by way of the states of female, male, neuter, and so forth.
"The world, consisting of various kinds of bodies, instruments, and so forth, possesses a creator, because it is an effect, like a pot.
Or alternatively: "The world under dispute is preceded by a creator who knows its own material cause, because it is an effect, like a pot. And thus it has been stated in the *Śrīmacchivajñānabodha*:

"Because the world consists of female, male, neuter, and so forth, and because its effects are observed, there exists a creator; that Lord Hara, having withdrawn this [world], creates us. Thus [it is said].
In the venerable Pauṣkara:
"The universe, which is the subject of dispute, is preceded by a creator who knows the universe."
"Just as a product such as a jar is established for both of us by virtue of its being an effect. Thus [it is said].
In the *Śrīmṛgendra* (Pauṣpa-paṭala, verse 92):
"Now, having perceived that the body and so forth are entities characterized by the property of being effects..."
"We know its creator to be distinguished by means of inference. Thus [it is said].
And in the venerable Parākhyatantra:
"Therefore, action, being devoid of consciousness, requires that which joins it [to the soul]."
"He is the Uniter, the Great Lord, because he is powerful by his own will. Thus [it is said].
It is also stated elsewhere:
"The Lord is established as the impeller of insentient things such as Māyā;
he is the knower of all objects, the agent, the all-pervasive, and eternally manifest."
In the venerable *Mataṅga*:
"The possessor of a property is established by means of that property, and the cause by means of the effect;
in some cases the effect [is established] by means of the cause, according to what is observed in the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*)."
"Agency, as a property [derived] from [the property of] jars and so forth, resides in the substratum, the potter. Thus [it is said].
The meaning is: from the property (dharma) which consists of the power of action directed toward objects such as a jar.
6) Nor is there a lack of pervasion (ananugama) regarding the delimiting factor of the subject (pakṣatāvacchedaka) in the aforementioned inferences;
for it is intended that "being earth" and so forth (*kṣityāditva*) alone shall serve as the delimiting factor of the subject. Nor is there a lack of logical necessity (*aprayojakatva*).

Because, in the absence of such an agent, the non-perception of the effect itself constitutes a sublation [of the thesis]. Nor is "being an effect" unestablished in its own nature, since "being an effect" is established by virtue of having constituent parts (*sāvayavatva*). Nor is "being produced by a body" a limiting condition (*upādhi*), because, by the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*), "being produced" alone is the necessary factor for having an agent.

Precisely because the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) has been refuted, there is also no "unestablishedness due to lack of pervasion" (*vyāpyatvāsiddhi*) based upon it. Nor is this reason (*hetu*) contradictory (*viruddha*), because it is not pervaded by the opposite of the probandum (*sādhya*). Nor is it inconclusive (*anaikāntika*);
for in cases such as the self (*ātman*) and so forth, which are determined to be non-agents, the property of being an effect (*kāryatva*) is absent. And furthermore...

It should not be argued that there is "inconclusiveness due to doubt" (*saṃdigdhānaikāntikatva*) because of the doubt regarding the absence of an agent in things such as sprouts— which possess the property of being effects— since there is no inconclusiveness due to doubt when there is doubt regarding the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*). Otherwise,
even smoke and the like would be inconclusive due to the doubt regarding the absence of fire on a mountain and so forth.

Because this would entail the fallacy of being doubtful and inconclusive (*sandigdhānaikāntikatva*). Nor can it be countered by the opposing argument that "the subject of dispute is not without an author because it is not produced by a body," for that too is refuted by the very same method used to eliminate the limiting condition (*upādhi*).

7) Furthermore, this agent is threefold according to the distinction of states: capable (*śakta*), prepared (*udyukta*), and active (*pravṛtta*). When all effects are dissolved within the material cause (*upādāna*), it is "capable" because it possesses only the potential power to produce them. But when that power is directed toward the production of the effect, it is "prepared. And when...
That [agent] is "active" (pravṛtta) at that time because it is endowed with a power that has already begun its operation. As it is stated in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
"The agent is held to be of three kinds: capable, ready, and active;
the distinction among them is merely figurative, based on the different states of the capacity's operation."
And in the venerable Pauṣkara:
"This distinction, beginning with dissolution (laya) and so forth, exists by virtue of Śakti;
for the agitation of the Bindu proceeds from the Śakti of Śambhu alone."
She, whose nature is knowledge and action, is eternal and possesses ever-arisen radiance;
she is oriented toward the Supreme and is entirely devoid of even a trace of bondage.
The sovereign Goddess is, in reality, non-different from Śiva; her very self is his form. When she attains the state of dissolution, she then assumes the nature of the indifferent one.
Indeed, that state of equilibrium is indifferent because of the absence of any effect;
for there is an equality of cognition and action only among agents who are actively engaged.

"For at that time, there is equality between these two regarding the activity [with the thought] 'I shall do this,' because she who is engaged in the action is authorized in the tasks as one who has received the mandate. Thus it is said.

(Pau Pati Pa Ślo 38–42) 8) Now, what is the proof for the power (*śakti*) being inherent in Śiva? If it is argued that there is the inference: "The subject under dispute is produced by an instrument (*karaṇa*), because it is an effect," we say no; for [the reason] could apply to knowledge, will, and so forth, which can themselves function as instruments.

"Because it is impossible to establish *śakti* as something distinct from this [consciousness] since it would be a different entity (*arthāntara*),"—do not say so; for since cognition, will, and so forth are themselves *śakti*, there is no separate entity apart from them. If it is argued that "in that case, because they are diverse, *śakti* would also be manifold, and thus the doctrine of unity (*aikya*) would be contradicted," we reply: no, because even cognition, will, and the rest [are not ultimately distinct].

Because there is no difference [between them] in themselves. When that very same power (*śakti*) has the nature of reflecting upon unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) and so forth conducive to an effect, it is "cognition" (*jñāna*);
when its form is "let this be so," it is "volition" (*icchā*); and when it is the producer of various specific effects, then...
The state of being an agent (*kartṛtva*) is established through the differentiation of knowledge and the other [powers]. Thus, this one and only agent is divided into nine forms.

Among these, there are four parts devoid of form (*niṣkala*), known as Śiva, Śakti, Nāda, and Bindu; one part both with and without form (*sakala-niṣkala*), known as Sadāśiva; and four parts consisting of Maheśvara, Rudra, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā.
These are all the divisions. Among them, there are two divisions of Śakti; the others are the seven divisions of Śiva.
Thus, that single Śakti is divided into seven ways by way of the distinctions of Bindu-śakti, Manonmanī, Maheśvarī, Umā, Lakṣmī, and Vāṇī.

9) [Objection: But surely, by means of the different states of the *bindu*, a difference in the agent Śiva has been stated; that would not be consistent, because it is impossible for the insentient *bindu* to act spontaneously. If, on the other hand, it is the Lord (*īśvara*) himself who causes its activity, then he would be subject to modification (*vikāritva*). To this, it is said: In that case, agency...

It is twofold: by means of mere volition (*saṅkalpa*) and by means of an instrument (*karaṇa*). Among these, the agency of potters and others depends upon an instrument. Volition, too, is twofold: consisting of mental activity and consisting of mere proximity (*sannidhi*). Among these, the agency of Brahmā and others is through mental activity; however, that of Śiva is—

[It acts] by mere proximity, and not by dependence on external instruments that cause modification; for, due to its purity, it is devoid of limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as the instruments of action. In the world, it is observed that only those possessing limiting adjuncts are subject to modification.
Therefore, its immutability despite being an agent is not contradictory. Nor [is there a contradiction] if it were to possess limiting adjuncts such as a body...
It should not be argued that [agency belongs only to those with bodies] because agency is observed in the case of potters and the like;
for agency is observed even in the absence of an external adjunct (upādhi) in such acts as the movement of one's own body.
If another adjunct were to be postulated even in that case, it would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress (anavasthā). Therefore, in the first creation...

Śiva alone, devoid of all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) and possessing all powers in operation, must be accepted as the agent. And in regard to his fivefold acts, he acts by mere proximity (*sannidhimātra*), just as the sun acts toward the opening, closing, melting, and drying of lotuses, water-lilies, butter, and mud respectively.
The state of being an agent.
10) And thus it is said in the venerable Pauṣkara: The sages—
You have stated that there is a division of Śiva based on the specific state of the *bindu*;
however, because the *bindu* is insentient, its activity does not proceed by itself.
If Śiva were an agent for the sake of engaging in that [activity], he would then be subject to modification; since such a contradiction has thus arisen, O Lord, please state the resolution.
Īśvara said:
"O Brahmins, agency is of two kinds: through volition and through the instrument. For a pot is not made by potters through volition alone."
Śiva always effects the agitation of the *bindu* by mere volition;
it is not through any specific activity, whereby he might become subject to transformation.
O twice-born ones, because it is devoid of all limiting adjuncts (upādhi) and because it is stainless,
that which possesses limiting adjuncts undergoes modification at the time of the birth of effects.
Consequently, immutability is contradicted by agency;
since it is devoid of all limiting adjuncts (upādhi), how can agency not be denied?
O lords of sages, because the limiting adjunct (upādhi) is an obstacle to agency, through its separation from that adjunct, agency would instead arise for the sake of abundance.
Just as the agency of one who is bodiless is admitted in the case of impelling one's own body, so too,
if the agency of one who possesses a body is likewise admitted everywhere.
Since that body is also an effect, it too must be pervaded by another agent;
and since his body and so forth would likewise require further agents, there would be no finality anywhere.
Therefore, at the time of the first creation, the Great Lord alone is accepted as the agent, free from all limiting adjuncts (upādhi) and possessing all powers in operation.
"Just as the sun is the benefactor of all daily activities through its mere presence,
so too does Śiva accomplish everything by his mere presence."

(From Pauṣkarapañcārthapaddhati, verses 27–37) 11) If it is objected: "But since it is heard [in scripture] that Śiva has a body of mantras—beginning with the words 'That body [consists] of five mantras, which are employed for the fivefold acts'—how can he be bodiless? [The response is: True.

In this scripture, because it possesses the functions of reflecting (*manana*) and protecting (*trāṇa*), it is by means of the word "mantra" that *śakti* itself is designated; therefore, its body is *śākta*. Now, is this *śāktatva* (the state of being *śākta*) the fact of being originated by *śakti*, or the fact of being a transformation (*pariṇāma*) of *śakti*?
If that were the case, there would be a contradiction with the scriptures and other authorities which establish its changelessness, eternity, and so forth. Furthermore—

And it is precisely the Power (śakti), which is differentiated by its various effects, that is metaphorically accepted as the body through the conceptualization of it having a head and so forth; and since that [body] is non-different from her, its status as a body is not real. Thus it is said in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
In the world, a physical body is seen to perform actions, just like those of us and others;
however, because impurities and the like are impossible [in his case], the Lord’s body is not of such a nature, but is composed of power (*śākta*).
That body [of the deity] consists of five mantras suitable for the fivefold activity— Īśa, Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāma, and Jyeṣṭha— [which form] the head and so forth.

That quality by which he rules over the entire world while abiding above it is his "head" (mūrdhā), because of its being at the highest point; it is not a "non-head" (amūrdhā) in the sense of being a mere limb of the body.
Whichever body of his was worshipped, he steals [the merit] by means of that;
because of protecting that and because of manifesting it, he has the face of that person.
The heart is a synonym for awakening; since that [heart] is non-terrible (aghora) Śiva, the term "terrible" (ghora) is applied to the body only figuratively, because of its terrible nature.
The left is the triad [of virtue, wealth, and pleasure], and it is secret by its very nature because it is "left" (vāma). He whose supreme abode is the secret left is Devaguhyaka.
Because the forms of atoms arise immediately from His will, He is designated as "Sadyojāta" (the Immediately Born).
Or rather, He is Sadyomūrti because He bestows the state of being immediately manifest upon yogis; it is not on account of the speed with which a physical form is produced.
Thus, while performing the functions of the body, Śakti is designated by the words "body" due to the absence of a [separate] body.
Even those divisions of hers, such as Vāmā and the rest, are likewise designated by the Siddhas according to the differentiation of their functions.
"Thus, with his body [endowed] by this [deity] whose vigor is unassailable, he always performs whatever task is assigned to him whenever it is undertaken. (Mṛtyuñjaya-prayoga, Chapter 3, Verses 7–14)

(12) Nor should it be argued that because Ananteśvara, Śrīkaṇṭha, and other such divisions of Śiva possess bodies, Śiva himself must also possess a body; for even in their case, they remain divisions of Śiva.

This is because they are dependent upon the power (śakti) of Śiva, who is their presiding lord and is manifested therein. For this very reason, even these—the Mantreśvaras, Aṇus, and Sadāśivas—are included within the category of the Lord (pati).
Furthermore, the category of the causal agent (kāraka) is also included therein, as it consists of the power of Śiva in the form of initiation (dīkṣā).

13) And this [consciousness] alone is the efficient cause (*nimitta*) of the world; by virtue of its being conditioned by *māyā*, it is also the material cause (*upādāna*) through its inherent power of consciousness (*samavāyi-cicchakti*). It is neither atoms, nor primordial matter (*prakṛti*), nor is it mere *māyā* alone. For instance, first of all, it is not atoms.

The world has no material cause (*upādāna*), because those very causes are unestablished due to the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). [Objection: But inference (*anumāna*) is indeed a means of valid cognition.

For instance: "The subtle particle (*rajas*) situated in the rays of the sun through a lattice is composed of a substance possessing a dimension smaller than its own, because it is an effect-substance (*kāryadravya*), like a jar."

When the cause of the subtle dust that is being perceived is inferred, and its status as an effect— by virtue of its initiating a gross substance— is also inferred, then by that very same reason, it too is inferred to have been produced from a substance of that same nature. And thus, regarding that which is visible...

That which is the ultimate producer of subtle substance through a continuous series is itself the atom (*paramāṇu*). This is also established by the following inference: the gradation of atomic dimension (*aṇuparimāṇa*) must terminate somewhere, because it is a gradation of dimensions, just like the gradation of large dimensions (*mahatparimāṇa*).

Regarding the claim that "the atom is established," it is not so; for the first reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to curds and the like—which are produced from milk of equal dimension—and ghee and the like—which are produced from butter of greater dimension.
In those cases, there is no evidence for their being composed of the same constituent parts. And as for the second [reason], regarding what is actually perceived...
Because rest is possible only in [the concept of] magnitude itself, it does not establish the desired object.

Therefore, since atoms themselves do not exist, they cannot be the material cause (*upādāna*). Nor can *prakṛti* be so, for we accept that its status as a material cause is relative to the intellect (*mahat*) and the other evolutes.

However, it does not possess the status of being the ultimate material cause (*paramopādānatva*), because its being an effect will be established later, and thus it is itself something to be derived (*upādeya*). Nor is it *māyā*;
rather, if one merely accepts that it falls within the category of material causes, there is the consequence of proving what is already accepted (*iṣṭāpatti*). Of that...

However, the position that [Śiva alone] possesses the status of material cause (*upādānatva*) is sublated by the evidence establishing that Śiva qualified by *māyā* is the material cause; and that evidence consists of scriptural passages such as the use of the fifth case-ending (*pañcamī-śruti*).
14) For it is said in the Skānda:
"All this, consisting of the sentient and the insentient, has manifested from Śiva, whose sole defining characteristic is the light of supreme bliss and truth."

Thus, the ablative case in the sense of the *apādāna* (point of departure) is heard [in the rule]. And that [ablative] is prescribed for what denotes the material cause (*upādāna*) by means of the technical designation *apādāna*, according to the rule *janikartuḥ prakṛtiḥ* (Pāṇini Sūtra 1.4.30). Therefore, that very ablative is the authority in that context.
Likewise, in that same [work]:
The wise and powerful one gazed upon creation, thinking, "May I become many."
Thus, the resolve for manifold becoming is heard [in scripture]. And that [resolve] is possible only if [the cause] is the material cause (*upādāna*).
For a potter, who is merely an instrumental cause (*nimitta*), does not have the resolve, "May I become a jar. Likewise, in the *Devikālottara*:
"And I am the elements, both stationary and moving."
And however many others there may be, I alone am they.

Thus, there exists a designation by way of grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya). And this is observed only in cases such as "the clay pot" between the material cause (upādāna) and its effect (upādeya), but not in the case of two absolutely distinct things like a staff and a pot; therefore, that too is a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). As it has been said:
In the *Śivajñānabodha*:
"Though being distinct [from the body], he is not other [than it] due to his pervasive nature.
|| Thus [it is said].

(Śiva Sūtra 2) 15) If it is argued that, in this case, the scriptural statements establishing [the Lord's] changelessness would be contradicted, we say no; for [this is resolved] in accordance with such statements as "From Śiva, the Lord who possesses power... and so forth.

Even though Śiva, characterized by the power of grasping the two-fold *māyā*, is the material cause (*upādāna*), it is *māyā* alone—which serves as his limiting adjunct—that undergoes modification. For even when there is modification [in the adjunct], there is no contradiction in the fact that the pure [Śiva] remains changeless. Now, one might object: Śiva cannot be the material cause, because he is conscious (*cetana*).

If it is argued that there is either a sublation (*bādha*) or a counter-argument (*pratirodha*) by the inference "like a beast" against the scripture (*āgama*) which teaches that Śiva is the material cause (*upādāna*), we say no; for since scripture is more powerful than inference, it is scripture alone that sublates the inference.
Otherwise, [one could likewise argue] that ritual acts such as sacrifice are not means to heaven, because they are actions (*kriyā*).

For, by the inference that [the world] is like a futile effort, there would arise the undesirable consequence of subverting or obstructing even those scriptures that teach that sacrifices and the like are the means for attaining heaven.
Now, [it may be argued that this applies only] when there is a plurality of inherent causes.

If it is argued that "the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) consisting of their conjunction is obtained [in the case of the effect], whereas if Śiva were the material cause (*upādāna*), no non-inherent cause could be obtained; therefore, his status as the material cause is not tenable"—we say no; for there is no evidence for a rule that an existent effect must necessarily be produced by a non-inherent cause. On the contrary, [The text continues: ...pratyuta... (but rather...)

This is because it is ascertained by scripture that the absence of those [qualities] themselves serves as the material cause (*upādāna*), and because there would be a logical inconsistency (*vyabhicāra*) due to the absence of a non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) in the case of effects such as sound. Nor is the conjunction of the drum and space, etc., the non-inherent cause even in that case; for [the effect] is not necessitated by the absence of that [conjunction].
Because there is no evidence for its being a cause, as its absence is not observed in the absence of the effect;

otherwise, one would have to postulate that even the dimension of space (*ākāśaparimāṇa*) is an non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) in that case, and because there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of a thread produced from a single yarn. Nor is it the case that [the same applies] there either.

It is logical that only the constituent parts of the threads possess the capacity for origination, and that their conjunction is possible; for it is impossible for a thread to be produced in the same location as the threads themselves, given the contradiction of corporeal entities occupying the same space. Furthermore, since the existence of the thread is perceived, one cannot assume its destruction.

Because it is sublated. Thus, the inference that "Śiva is not the material cause because he is an agent, like a potter" is refuted; for that [inference] does not even arise, being sublated by scripture (*āgama*). Now, one might object: even by scripture, the status of being the direct material cause is not taught, but rather the state of being pervaded by it.

[The two reasons are] non-difference from the effect and being the substratum of its dissolution and so forth. Thus, these two would indeed constitute a case of counter-balanced opposition (*satpratipakṣa*), and therefore a definitive determination of [Brahman's] status as material cause (*upādānatva*) is not tenable. Nor is it correct to argue that being the substratum of dissolution and so forth is stronger because it is taught by scripture (*āgama*); for agency (*kartṛtva*) is likewise [taught by scripture].

Because it is understood by that very [means]. And if, through the cognition of the property-of-the-subject (*pakṣadharmatva*)—which is connected with agency and is itself understood through scripture—the pervasion (*vyāpti*) belonging to it is also cognized, then let that pervasion be sublated either by the state of being the locus of dissolution (*laya*) and so forth, or by [the absence of] agency; for there is no distinction between the two cases.
Therefore, it is precisely the state of having a counter-argument.

16) "Therefore, there is no certainty regarding [Śiva's] being the material cause (*upādāna*). Do not say this; for, in the present context, the ablative case (*pañcamī*) directly communicates the status of being a material cause by signifying the nature of being a source (*prakṛtitva*), since the scripture itself conveys his status as the material cause. [Objection: But in that case, Śiva would not be the efficient cause (*nimitta*), because [the category of] cause is restricted to that which is distinct from the material and the non-inherent causes (*asamavāyin*).
If it is argued that [Brahman] cannot be the material cause because the word "cause" (nimitta) signifies an instrumental cause, we say no;

for just as [Brahman] is the material cause by virtue of being the substrate (*prakṛti*), it is equally logical that it is the instrumental cause by virtue of possessing a desire to act (*cikīrṣā*) and other such qualities conducive to creation.
Furthermore, the definition of an instrumental cause is simply the possession of a function different from that of being the substrate; and this [function]...

Since this [agency] remains unimpaired even in the case of Śiva, who possesses utility through the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*) and so forth, it is established that Śiva alone is both the material cause (*upādāna*) and the efficient cause (*nimitta*).
17) But if this is so, then God is their efficient cause (nimitta), while that Sovereign Bindu is the material cause (upādāna).
Śiva is the efficient cause; Prakṛti, both supreme and non-supreme,
being insentient, attains the state of being his effect.
If it is argued that this contradicts such scriptural statements, we say no;

for such statements are intended to show that [the Self], being subject to modification through *māyā*, does not possess the status of a material cause (*upādānatva*). Furthermore, as for the collection of statements such as "May I be many" and "Whatever else exists, I alone am all that," [these too refer to the same].

This refers solely to the state of being the exclusive material cause; furthermore, since that [cause], while being distinct, is non-distinct through its pervasion, it refers to the manifestation of the continuous thread characterized by the existence of pervasion within the effect—thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever.

18) Thus, both Śiva—the one whose nature is the auspiciousness of the path—and Māyā presided over by him, function as the material cause (*upādāna*) of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), which is their effect. This is because [Śiva] exists in the form of the manifestation of his own attributes, such as existence and consciousness, while [Māyā] exists in the form of insentient modifications and the like. However, for Śiva, [the relationship with] Māyā...

The distinction is that [the latter] possesses a superior status as a cause by virtue of being the presiding agent (*adhiṣṭhātṛ*). Just as in the case of smoke, which is the effect characterized [by its nature], although both moist fuel and fire serve as the material causes (*upādāna*), the color of the effect—smoke—is only the black color belonging to the wood, and not the luminous color belonging to the fire; so it is here.
Even though the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) has both Śiva and Māyā as its material causes (*upādāna*), it does not possess the nature of consciousness and bliss;

rather, its nature consists in being illuminated by the attributes of inert Māyā and being subject to modification. In that regard, Śiva’s role is merely instrumental (*nimitta-kāraṇa*), like fire [is to smoke], and thus he does not possess those superior attributes [of consciousness and bliss]. Nor does fire [possess the nature of smoke] in the smoke.

It must be said that [fire] is merely a causal sign (*nimitta*), not the material cause (*upādāna*); for, since no other material cause exists and the theory of atoms (*paramāṇu*) will be refuted later, fire and fuel alone constitute the material cause. Nor is it the case that wood alone is the material cause while fire is...
It can be said that [the Lord] is merely the efficient cause (*nimitta-mātra*).
Since qualities belonging to fire, such as heat, are also perceived, they would be equivalent to the perceiver.
Therefore, it is established that the Lord, qualified by *māyā*, is both the efficient cause and the material cause (*upādāna*).
19) Regarding the statements that establish this, it is said in the Vātula:
"Everything has arisen within the *liṅga*, and its dissolution is said to be in that very place.
The *liṅga* should be known as Śambhu, and the *pīṭha* is declared to be Śakti."
By way of the female organ and the male organ, it is the cause for the purpose of creating the universe;
because its state is one of constant union, it is declared to be capable of assuming any form at will.
Within that *liṅga*, the entire world—both stationary and moving—is born;
therefore, the *liṅga* is specifically declared to be the form of karma.
Upon the arising of karma there is creation, and at the end of karma there is dissolution.
This form of Karmeśa brings about creation, maintenance, and withdrawal.
Brahmā is born from the right limb, and Hari is born from the front limb.
From the heart comes Nīlarudra, and from the head comes the one known as Śiva.
From a thousandth part of Maheśa, the god Rudra was born;
from ten millionth part of this Maheśa, Brahmā and Viṣṇu were born.
From his right, left, and upper eyes, the Sun, Moon, and Fire respectively originated.
In the vital breath (prāṇa), the wind arises; in the ear, the origin of the kīla and so forth occurs.
Knowledge arose in his mouth; Gaṇeśa was born from his throat;
Ṣaṇmukha was born in his heart; and the gods were born from his navel.
"And fifty crores of gods born from a portion of Maheśa, as well as crores of sages born from the pores of his skin. Thus it is said.
"Knowledge" refers to the sciences such as the Vedas.
(20) But even so, how can it be that Śiva alone is the creator of the world? For you yourself have admitted that Ananteśvara and others are also creators.
Sometimes they belong to Śiva, sometimes they originate from the Lotus-born Brahmā;
sometimes they are Vaiṣṇava, and sometimes they are composed by sages.

If it be argued that this is because the world is heard to have an indefinite creator, it is not so; for [the Lord], presiding over Brahmā in that very creation from primordial nature (prakṛti) or māyā, and presiding over Viṣṇu in that same māyā during its preservation, and again [presiding] over that same [māyā] during its creation, maintenance, and dissolution.

Presiding over Rudra in the impure māyā during creation, maintenance, withdrawal, and concealment; and presiding over Īśvara in the pure māyā as the cause during creation, maintenance, withdrawal, concealment, and grace.
The agency belongs directly to Sadāśiva alone.

21) If it is argued that elsewhere it is stated that the triad of Brahmā and the others are the causes of only the three effects beginning with creation, and not that the five Lords are the causes of the five effects,
[we reply that] there are [scriptural passages] establishing that the five effects have the five Lords as their agents.
There are indeed many scriptural statements from the *Kāmika* and other Āgamas, as well as statements from the Purāṇas which supplement the Vedas. In the *Kāśī-khaṇḍa*, it is said:
"The common refuge of all five gods, beginning with Brahmā..."
"The Liṅga awakened by the syllable Oṃ is the supreme Pañcāyatana. Thus it is said.
And in the *Narasimha Purāṇa*: "From the navel upwards is the form of Brahmā; from the throat upwards is the body of Viṣṇu;
from the head upwards is Rudra-Īśāna; and beyond that, it is entirely Śiva."
And by the venerable Śaṅkarācārya in the *Saundaryalaharī*:
"The Creator (Brahmā) procreates the world, Hari protects it, and Rudra destroys it; yet the Lord (Īśvara), casting this aside, conceals even his own form."
Śiva, who is ever-present, favors all this by relying upon your command— the movement of your two creeper-like eyebrows in a mere moment.
Because it has been stated thus, it is established that the five Lords perform the fivefold functions.
And so, the conscious power (*cicchakti*) of the Supreme Lord, the Creator, exists as a subtle body.

Just as the power of *parigrahabindu* functions as the initiator of one's own body by way of being the gross body, it should be understood that it likewise initiates creation and the other cosmic processes. Thus, whether through mediation or without mediation, Śiva alone is the agent of all effects in the phenomenal world (*prapañca*). And that effect—

[The world] is fivefold by way of the distinctions of transformation (*pariṇāma*), commencement (*ārambha*), collection (*samūha*), manifestation (*vivarta*), and function (*vṛtti*). Among these, the world is only function (*vṛtti*), not transformation and the rest. For instance, the world is certainly not a transformation (*pariṇāma*), since transformation is the attainment of another state through the abandonment of a previous state, as in the case of milk.

The transformation of milk consists in its abandoning its previous state and attaining the form of curds and so forth. However, in this case (the Self), there is no abandonment of a previous state, nor is there origination; for "origination" refers only to that where a single effect is produced through the mutual conjunction of various constituent causes, as in the case of a jar or similar objects.

In this case, however, because Māyā alone is the cause, the theory of "origination" (ārambha) cannot withstand scrutiny. Nor is it correct to argue that origination occurs here as well through the conjunction of Māyā and Śiva;
for there is no equal utility for both of them. For it is Māyā that is utilized by virtue of its capacity for transformation.

But it is called *Śiva* because He is their presiding controller (*adhiṣṭhātṛ*). Furthermore, since conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is a non-final cause (*acaramakāraṇa*), there would otherwise be the consequence of the effect being produced at all times. For this very reason, it is not even a "collection" (*samūha*); for while we observe collections of many hairs in the form of chowries and the like, such a collection is impossible in the present case. Nor is it an "illusory manifestation" (*vivarta*).
Because that [transformation] consists in the world’s becoming otherwise than it truly is, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the world being absolutely non-existent.
Therefore, just as the state of a wall for a cloth or the state of a coil for a snake is an attainment of another state by that which has not lost its prior form, so too is the world.
The activity of both the pure and impure māyās is indeed presided over by Śiva.

23) And this [Self] is the object of the cognition of its own nature; it is not absolutely non-manifest, nor is it an object of [ordinary] means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), for if that were the case, the consequences of insubstantiality (*tucchatva*) and insentience (*jaḍatva*) would follow.
Furthermore, since the individual self (*jīvātman*)—as the object of knowledge produced by the means of valid cognition in the form of the mind—is devoid of insentience...

There is an inconsistency. Since that [self] would be the object of a cognition produced by a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), it would follow that, in its absence, there could be no manifestation; consequently, there would arise the possibility of doubt—such as "Am I or am I not?"—and the error of "I am not," which necessitates accepting its self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) alone.

Because it is impossible for [Śiva] to be the object of knowledge produced by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Nor is it correct to argue that if Śiva were inaccessible to the means of valid cognition, the previously stated fact that he is known through inference and scripture would be contradicted; for even though the substratum (*dharmin*) is self-luminous, its attributes—such as agency and material causality—are nonetheless accessible through that [self-luminosity].
This is because the previously mentioned fact that Śiva is accessible through means of knowledge such as inference is established; thus, it is proven that Śiva is self-luminous.

Thus ends the exposition of the category of the Lord (*pati*) in the *Śaivaparibhāṣā*, composed by the venerable Jñānaśivācārya, the foremost among the lords of yoga, a protector of the Śaiva faith, and a preeminent teacher who transcends the [conventional] castes and stages of life (*ativarṇāśrama*).
The second chapter, titled "Names."
The Third Chapter:
1) Now, the category of the bound soul (*paśu*), which is non-different from the Lord (*pati*) by virtue of its nature as consciousness, is defined.
In this regard, the "bound soul" is that which is distinct from the body, senses, and so forth, eternal, consisting of consciousness, and manifold.

The [Self] is all-pervading, covered by beginningless impurity, and an independent agent. Here, by the phrase "distinct from the body, senses, and so forth," the doctrines that identify the Self with the body, the senses, the vital breath (*prāṇa*), or the intellect (*buddhi*) are refuted.

By the word "eternal" (*nitya*), the doctrine of a momentary Self is refuted; by the term "consisting of consciousness" (*cidātmaka*), the doctrine of an insentient Self is refuted; and by the word "manifold" (*aneka*),...
By the phrase "the pervasiveness of the doctrine of a single self," there is the exclusion of the doctrines of a self that is either atomic in dimension or of intermediate dimension;
by the two phrases "covered by beginningless impurities" and "not independent," there is the exclusion of the doctrine of a self that is the Lord (Īśvara);
and by the word "agent," there is the refutation of the Sāṅkhya doctrine of the self. And so it has been said:

Therefore, because it has the nature of cognition, the term *gati* is derived in the sense of continuous movement; since movement arises from a cause consisting of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), the word *gati* has the meaning of "knowledge."
"Selves are all-pervasive, infinite, and of the nature of consciousness; the bound souls (paśus) are of three kinds. Thus [it is said].
And in the *Śrīmanmṛgendra*:
"He is not non-pervasive, not momentary, not unitary, nor is he insentient;
he is not a non-agent, because he is joined with non-differentiated consciousness and attains the state of Śiva at the end of the bonds."
And in the venerable Parākhyatantra:
"The Self is distinct from the body, imperishable, all-pervasive, separate [from matter], possessed of consciousness, and non-inert."
"The agent who experiences the fruit of his own karma, possessing limited knowledge, is a bound soul (paśu) under the governance of a Lord. Thus [it is said].
(Regarding the section called *parākhya*, verse 15):
2) Now, how can the self be distinct from the body? For the body itself is the self. To explain:
whatever is observed only when something else exists is seen to have that as its cause. And so it is here.

Consciousness arises spontaneously from the body itself through the transformation of the four elements, just as the diverse effect of intoxication arises from the subtle power of yeast and other ingredients.
Therefore, consciousness originates solely from the body, which is composed of the elements.

Furthermore, neither the self (ātman) nor God (īśvara) need be postulated as the substratum for that consciousness; for this very reason, the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in cognitions such as "I am fat" or "I am thin" is logically established. On the other hand, cognitions such as "this is my body" are merely figurative (*aupacārika*), like the expression "Rāhu’s head."

If it is argued that, therefore, there is no self distinct from the body, we say: not so. We do not claim that the diversity of effects does not arise from the potencies of their causes; rather, we maintain that an effect contrary [in nature] cannot be produced from a cause that is contrary [to it]. And thus, how could [consciousness] arise from the insentient body?

The emergence of consciousness consists in its nature as luminosity. Furthermore, the destruction of a quality occurs either through the destruction of the substratum or through the appearance of a contradictory quality. But here, when the body has died, since neither of these two conditions exists, how could there be a destruction of the consciousness that is a quality of that [body]?

If it is argued that [consciousness does not manifest] because the vital air (*prāṇavāyu*) has departed from a portion of the elements that constitute the body, we say no; for even when that [vital air] is present during deep sleep, consciousness is not perceived. Nor should it be said that the non-perception of consciousness at that time is due to the cessation of the instruments [of perception], since in your own view there is an absence of karma as a cause for the cessation of the instruments.

Furthermore, because consciousness would have to arise even while one is asleep [if it were identical with the body]. Therefore, that in whose presence there is movement of the body, and in whose absence there is its cessation—that consciousness, distinct from the body, must be accepted as the Self. Moreover, since the body differs across childhood, youth, and old age, how could [an action] performed in childhood [bear fruit] in old age?
Reconnection [of the self with the body]: Therefore, the doctrine that the body is the self is refuted by perception itself; for this very reason, we observe such cognitions as "this is my body.
As for the cognition "I am fat" and so forth, it is merely figurative (aupacārika). Furthermore:
Even when there is contact between a faultless sense organ and its object, the apprehension of that object is not observed. For what reason?
If you say it is because of being distracted (*vyāsaktatva*), then alas! in that case, a subtle self (*ātman*) must be admitted as the cause of the mind’s distraction.
3) And this has been established in the illustrious Pauṣkara and Parākhyatantras:
"Because consciousness is observed in the body, the self cannot be identical with consciousness.
For that which is seen when something else exists is accepted as the effect of that [other thing]."
In this case, the body, being no different from [other] causes, is the prover of consciousness;
for there is a connection between the body and a jar, just as there is between the effects known as liquor and a cake.
A cause, such as molasses or flour, is seen to be indistinguishable [from other substances];
yet, prior to the cake, the power of intoxication was non-existent within it.
Therefore, since consciousness arises from the body itself which is composed of the elements,
what need is there for another self or a lord to preside over that consciousness?
Īśvara says: Who has said that there is no diversity among distinct effects?
An effect contrary [to its nature] does not arise from a cause that is contrary [to it].

Moreover, how could consciousness, which is diametrically opposed [to it], arise from the inert body? Furthermore, when a property belongs to something, the destruction of that thing entails the destruction of the property.
Or if, O twice-born ones, it were otherwise due to the presence of a contrary quality,
then why is consciousness not admitted to exist even when the body is present in a dead person?
That by whose presence or absence the body experiences activity or inactivity is called consciousness, and it is distinct from the body.
Furthermore, how can there be a continuity of the body through the distinctions of childhood, youth, and old age,
such that [the self] remembers what was done in childhood?
He first reflects, "This woman is the very same one I enjoyed previously";
therefore, the doctrine that the body is the self is refuted by direct perception.
Therefore, [the notion] "I am fat" and so forth should be understood as being like "the head of Rāhu.
Furthermore, the cognition "the body is mine" and so forth certainly exists in its full abundance. Thus it is said.
Even when the body is a mere collection of elements, due to the mental determination [of it as a self],
one who is intent on grasping at a real entity [remains so] even when the eyes are perfectly pure.

For since there is no apprehension of an object by this [person] whose mind is directed elsewhere— just as there is none for another person who has arisen with an empty mind— therefore, there exists yet another person.
The fourfold states, beginning with childhood, are observed in the body;
they are each distinct and differentiated by specific transformations.

"Whichever other [object] one contemplates, even when that state has passed away, he is the rememberer of it in this [present state]; memory is knowledge distinct from that which issues from the senses of the elements. Thus [it is said].
(Regarding the section called *parā*, concerning the bound soul [paśu], verses 19–20; 22; 24):

4) Now, it is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that the sense organs are the causes of cognition. Therefore, let the status of being the knower (*jñātṛtva*) belong to them alone, since postulating another knower would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Is this not so?
It should not be argued that, due to the diversity of the sense organs and the absence of a relationship of primary and subordinate status among them,

simultaneous contradictory operations would result; for even in the absence of such a relationship of primary and subordinate status *per se*, [this is possible] for those existing within a single body.
For them, like inhabitants of a single village, the relationship of primary and subordinate status is established by necessity;
or, let there be no such relationship of primary and subordinate among the sense organs, even so,
the absence of simultaneous contradictory operations is still established through the accompaniment of the mind as a cooperative cause.
For the operation of that which is powerful is logically established. Nor should it be argued that they do not possess agency because they are causes;

for since we do not accept their status as instruments (*karaṇa*), this reason is unestablished for one of the two parties (*anyatarāsiddha*). Nor is it correct to say that there is no lack of proof because they are established precisely as the instruments for the perception of color and so forth.

This is because their existence is established through inference based on the fact that they possess causes. Therefore, [the claim] that the senses themselves are the self—on the basis of experiences such as "I am mute" or "I am deaf"—is not correct.
For even in the absence of the senses, as in dreams and similar states, cognition is perceived; thus, it is impossible for the senses to be the knower. Why?

Furthermore, it is established by experience that the sense organs, such as the ear and so forth, have specific, restricted objects, whereas the self is the grasper of all; therefore, a self distinct from them must be admitted as the grasper of all objects, such as sound and the rest. Moreover, the sense organs themselves are experienced as being impelled [into action]. And yet—

An independent self possesses the quality of being an impeller; therefore, it is impossible for those [faculties] to be the self. Furthermore, the auditory organ and the others do not know their own nature, whereas the self knows the nature of the auditory organ and the others.
Thus, because they possess contradictory attributes, the auditory organ and the others are not the self. Moreover, "I who [perceived] with the eye..."

The recognition "I who saw the jar now touch that very same [jar] with my skin" is experienced; this is not possible if the sense organs were the self, because there is no recognition by one person of what was perceived by another. Why?

If the sense-faculties were the self, there would follow the consequence of simultaneous engagement in contradictory activities. Nor is it tenable to argue—as was previously stated—that their relationship of subordinate and principal is determined by their respective functions, like villagers living in the same village; for even they [the faculties] possess their own uncommon functions.

Because there is an absence of the relationship of subordinate and principal [between them]. Nor can the relationship of subordinate and principal be established according to the maxim of a bridegroom’s assembly (*varagoṣṭhīnyāya*), for that maxim applies only when multiple suitors are simultaneously devoid of proximity to their own respective objects of enjoyment;
for it is only among suitors that one [is distinguished] by the presence of his own object of enjoyment.

For others who are devoid of that [primary status], it is logical to accept the state of being subordinate (*guṇabhāva*). When the sense-faculties are simultaneously in contact with their respective objects, it is not possible for even a single one among them to be accepted as having the status of primary (*pradhāna*) and subordinate (*guṇa*). Therefore, it is not [the case].
The relationship of primary and secondary status [between the senses] is also like the maxim of the "assembly of suitors.

Nor is the engagement in activity produced by the predominance of association with the mind (*manas*), because in your own view, it is precisely the association with the mind in a single instance that is untenable. For in my view, the self (*ātman*) is independent; when an organ perceives what is desired by itself, [it functions].

It is logical that there should be a conjunction of only one [factor], namely that "the mind applies itself. However, in your view, the sense organs themselves are independent, while the mind is dependent upon them. Furthermore, it is not logical for a subordinate factor to converge in one place when its primary factors are in disagreement. Nor does the mind itself draw the sense organ toward itself.

Because there is no means of determination [to the contrary], it follows that if the sense organs were the self, there would be the consequence of simultaneous, contradictory activities. Therefore, the sense organs are not the self.

5) Let it be, then, that the vital air (*prāṇavāyu*) is the self (*ātman*), because of the experience "I live. Nor is it correct to argue that if a plurality of selves were to follow from the distinction between inhalation (*prāṇa*), exhalation (*apāna*), and so forth within a single location, there would consequently be the simultaneous occurrence of contradictory activities due to differences in desire; for [this is not the case] since it is a single [self] that possesses different activities.

This is because there is no evidence for a distinction between the vital breaths (prāṇa), apāna, and so forth, based on the occurrence of distinct designations such as "prāṇa" and the like. Nor is it correct to argue that since the prāṇas and others exist even during deep sleep (suṣupti) and similar states, the status of being a knower (jñātṛtva) would persist;
for the absence [of knowing] in those states is logically accounted for by the cessation of the activity of the sense organs. Therefore, the vital air (prāṇavāyu) alone is the Self (ātman).

Not so; for since even the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*) is experienced as being subject to control just like the body, one must necessarily admit the existence of some other superior being who controls it. Nor is the body and so forth themselves the controller of their own effects, because that which is accepted as the self cannot be subject to the control of the body when it is the body’s controller.

Furthermore, since it is impossible for the specific quality of air (sound) to perish while that [air] exists, it would follow that even during deep sleep, one would still possess the status of a knower. Nor can the group of internal organs (antaḥkaraṇa) be the Self, because they are insentient and thus subject to its control.

6) Now, let it be that the continuum of cognitions (*jñāna-santati*) is the self (*ātman*). Nor is there an impossibility of a continuum due to the lack of difference among cognitions, because the distinction between cognitions of a jar, a cloth, and so forth is established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). If it is argued that since a continuum does not exist apart from the members of the continuum (*santānin*), the nature of the self must be ascribed to those members of the continuum, that too is not [the case].

It is possible [to maintain this], because otherwise, due to the absence of any connection by one person with what has been experienced by another, there would follow the undesirable consequence that recognition and so forth could not exist. Now, as for how momentary consciousness can be the self—it is not so; rather, it is by virtue of the unity of the continuum (*santāna*).

Because recognition and other such phenomena are logically established. For that which is the experiencer of a cognition entering into a particular continuum is the recognizer of that same cognition when it falls within that very same continuum. Nor is it correct to ask how there can be identity given the absence of any [entity] distinct from the continuum; for even though there is no "forest" apart from the trees, the nature of being a forest [still exists].

Since the state of being a continuum (*santānatva*) also exists as a distributed occurrence (*vyāsajyavṛttitva*), just as "one forest" is a distributed occurrence, the unity of the continuum is logically established. Therefore, momentary consciousness alone is the self. To this, we reply:
you yourself agree that the stream of consciousness is interrupted during deep sleep; otherwise, [the following would occur]...

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of recollection and other such cognitions arising at that very same time. Furthermore, how could there be recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) in the form "this is the very same thing that was seen by me yesterday," given that the continuum (*saṃtāna*) of the previous cognition is interrupted during deep sleep, and thus the identity of the continuum is also absent? Now, one might object: let the identity of the continuum not be the determining factor (*prayojaka*).

If it is argued that there will be identity of the body—since the rule holds that whatever cognition is associated with a body is the cognizer, and that very same cognition is the recognizer—this is not so; for in your view, since the body is also momentary, its identity is likewise non-existent. Or, [if you argue] that there is identity of the continuum of the body...

If you consider [the body] to be the instigator (*prayojaka*), even so, it is untenable for an infant to have the recollection of experiences from a previous life that served as the immediate cause for their initial activity, because in that case there is no identity of the continuum of the body. For this very reason,
one would also not be the enjoyer of the fruits of actions performed in another birth, since the action was performed by one [body] and the result would accrue to another.

Because the enjoyment of the fruit is impossible; for there is an absence of either the unity of the stream of consciousness or the unity of the stream of the body, which would serve as the requisite condition for being that enjoyer.

7) But where has it been observed that the one who experiences is the one who recognizes, and the one who acts is the one who enjoys the fruit—such that the self would have to be accepted as permanent? Furthermore, prior to the establishment of its permanence, you cannot know that identity is the determining factor. Therefore:
If it is argued that there is mutual dependence here, we say no; for since we do not observe anyone other than Devadatta—
such as Yajñadatta— to be the rememberer of what he experienced or the enjoyer of the fruits of the actions he performed,
it is logical to establish the persistence [of the self] by postulating identity as the necessary condition.

8) But surely, since everything is momentary, the persistence of a self is impossible. For instance: persistence consists in a single entity’s connection with two points in time, and that is not possible;
because connection with one time is pervaded by the absence of connection with another time, as in the case of blue.
Because there exists the apprehension of concomitance (*sahacāra*) and so forth, which grasps the pervasion (*vyāpti*) by means of the absence of yellowness;

and because it is impossible for a permanent entity to possess existence in the form of causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), and because for that which exists, momentariness is necessarily entailed. To explain: the causal efficiency of a permanent entity—

Is it successively or simultaneously? Not the first [alternative], because if that [cause] possesses the capacity to produce an efficient action (*arthakriyā*), a succession is impossible since there can be no delay for what is capable; and if it lacks such capacity, a succession is even more impossible. Nor is it the case that even a capable [cause] fails to produce that effect at another time.

It is logical that the production of an effect occurs sequentially according to the proximity of auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*). For if the auxiliaries do not impart any excellence (*atiśaya*) [to the cause], then—given the absence of any distinction from non-auxiliaries—the cause would lack productive power. If, however, one accepts the imparting of excellence, [then the question arises] regarding that excellence...

If [the seed] were distinct from the seed and so forth, it would follow that there is an infinite regress. If it were not distinct, then by admitting that the seed which produces the sprout arises at that very same time, it would follow that one accepts its momentariness.

Nor is the second alternative possible; for if that which is capable of producing those many effects simultaneously were to exist in a subsequent moment as well, [it would contradict the nature of causal efficiency].

Even then, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the effect arising at that very moment; however, if it were non-existent in the subsequent moment, one would be entering our own position. Therefore, everything indeed possesses momentariness. Nor does this render the recognition "this is that same jar" untenable; for that [recognition]...

If it is argued that because [the cognition] is conceived as having similarity as its object—since we observe such cases as "this is that same lamp"—therefore the permanence of the self is not established, this is not so. For since it is possible for recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) to have identity as its object, it is improper to conceive of it as having similarity as its object. It is not [so].

By the reasoning already stated, it is impossible for [the cognition] to have identity as its object; for even a single tree can be related to multiple times, just as it is related to various things such as monkeys and men, and because it is possible for a stable entity to produce effects sequentially in accordance with the proximity of auxiliary causes. Not so.
If [the self] does not impart any excellence [to the cognition], its status as a cooperative cause (sahakāritva) is untenable;

yet even if that were the case, its status as a cooperative cause is established through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) and so forth. Therefore, the self is not of the nature of momentary cognition.
9) This has been stated in the venerable Pauṣkara:
The sages asked:
"Whatever knowledge there may be, none of it arises from the power of consciousness (cicchakti)."
All that must be accepted as being of the nature of the Buddha, by reason of its perishability.
Īśvara: That is not so; since the intellect (*buddhi*) is insentient (*jaḍa*), how could it be the producer of knowledge?
[Rather,] consciousness (*cita*) appears only occasionally due to its connection with a manifesting agent (*abhivyañjaka*).
Momentariness is indeed experienced even in the case of what is considered eternal;
for as long as a lamp remains, it continues to illuminate objects.
Because manifesting causes proceed only as a continuous stream.
Even a continuous stream of cognition is experienced as being momentary;
for this very reason, cognitions [are established] by virtue of the momentariness of all entities.
The torment of hope for those who assert momentariness has been warded off.
The sages asked: "O Lord, why is it that the non-existence of momentariness is not accepted through the principle of existence?"
For existence consists in the capacity for causal efficiency, and that [capacity] resides in momentary things;
it is not possible in permanent things because of the impossibility of [causal efficiency occurring] through either successive or simultaneous action.
Because delay is impossible and because stability would be destroyed,
that which is inherently incapable cannot achieve its purpose even with hundreds of auxiliary causes.
Momentariness is established by the capacity for causal efficiency;
[the opponent objects: "If things were momentary, the relationship between cause and effect would be destroyed."
By way of the nature of cause and effect, the cause attains the state of being an effect;
just as a lump of clay becomes a jar through its present state as a jar.
Therefore, that which persists for two moments is the cause for the production of an effect;
however, when those two [moments] are distinct entities, it is the latter that is the cause for its production.
Otherwise, why would an entity existing at the same time not also be a cause? Since both are distinct entities, how could there be a difference in their timing?
O twice-born ones, from where could there be any distinction in the cause due to auxiliary factors? Or why would the production of a jar not occur from threads?
Therefore, the relationship of cause and effect is established only among stable entities;
and the capacity for purposeful action (arthakriyā) is likewise established as occurring sequentially for those that endure.
Furthermore, because that which is capable is necessarily restricted to performing its function at all times,
fire— even though it is capable of burning— requires a finger for the act of bursting [the blister].
The notion of momentariness is a false hope, based on the distinction between succession and non-succession;
moreover, this cognition that arises is the very same cognition experienced previously.
If all things are momentary, how can recognition of them arise? Or rather, let momentariness belong only to those things that are insentient in nature.
Only three causes are required for all effects;
even those entities such as the *bindu* and others undergo an identical transformation.
"Knowledge alone is stable and eternal, the illuminator of the mass of insentient things;
its momentariness should be understood from the momentariness of objects. Thus [it is said].
(From the *Pauṃsya-patala*, verses 214–232) 10) And in the venerable *Parākhyatantra*:
"If knowledge were subject to momentary destruction, whose acquisition of karma could there be?"
That fruit of karma is not to be experienced when knowledge has been destroyed without remainder.
Is that latent impression (*vāsanā*) which was described by you not characterized by continuity?
For if it were of a different nature [from the moment], it would not be contained within that same moment;
and since that moment has perished, the impression would consequently have perished as well.
It is uninterrupted, stable, unitary, and the substratum for various cognitions.
When investigated through scripture and reasoning, [the body] is not distinct from the self;
for [if it were], there would be grief, joy, and the like upon union with the limbs of another birth.
Likewise, even in the case of the recollection of past births, the stability of that memory is understood from prior experience; for there is no memory without experience.
"The intelligent experiencer, because of its stability, is known by that [consciousness] as the stable, all-pervading Lord. Thus it is said.

(Parā-prapañca-śloka 30–35) 11) Furthermore, the self (*ātman*) is not conjoined with momentary consciousness (*kṣaṇika-vijñāna*), because the quality of being a knower (*jñātṛtva*) is an attribute of the eternal self. Indeed, in the world, it is never observed that something eternal possesses non-eternal attributes. Moreover, that [consciousness]...

The nature of being a knower (*jñātṛtva*) is all-pervasive (*vibhu*), because it is an attribute of the essence of the reflection (*bimbātmadharmatvāt*), and not merely localized. For this very reason, the Self possesses the capacity for seeing and acting upon all objects. If its nature as a knower were merely localized, the omnipresence of that Self would be compromised; for in the world, the extent of the pervasion of an attribute is exactly equal to the extent of the pervasion of its substratum.

Pervasion is observed; just as the whiteness residing in a cloth remains pervading the entire cloth, so too does the state of being a knower remain pervading the self. Nor should it be said that knowledge does not arise in the absence of an object, for the very nature [of the self] is itself the object. As it has been said:
In the venerable Pauṣkara:
"The state of being a knower is also eternal for that [Self], because it is a property of an eternal entity;
O lords of sages, a substratum cannot possess non-eternal properties; the Self is eternal."
And because it is here [in this system] the nature of the all-pervading, it is not held to be localized;
therefore, like eternity, the Self remains possessed of the capacity for seeing and acting with respect to all objects.
If its nature as a knower were also merely occasional, how could it possess omnipresence? For a property exists only to the extent that its substratum pervades.
Just as whiteness residing in a cloth remains pervading the entire cloth,
so too does the state of being a knower always remain pervading the self.
And cognition is not devoid of an object, nor does it depend on another by its own nature. Thus [it is said].

(Pau Paśu Pa, verses 100–104) 12) [Objection: Granted that the all-pervasiveness of the self (*ātman*) were established, its attribute would thereby be established as all-pervasive. However, that is not possible; for since the self is not perceived elsewhere than in the body, its all-pervasiveness is untenable.
Regarding this, the Pāñcarātras describe the self as having an atomic dimension (*aṇu-parimāṇa*):
"The individual soul (*jīva*) should be known as a part of a hundredth part of the tip of a hair, further divided into a hundred parts; yet it is capable of infinity."
(Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad, Chapter 5,

Verse 9) 13) The Jainas, however, describe the self as possessing contraction and expansion like the light of a lamp, having a dimension corresponding to that of the body. Neither of these two positions is tenable.

The self is all-pervasive, because it perceives objects situated elsewhere than its own body; for that which is not so is not thus, like a jar. Furthermore, the self is all-pervasive because its effects are perceived everywhere; thus, its omnipresence is established. Moreover, if the self were of intermediate dimension, it would lack permanence.
Whatever has a medium dimension is impermanent, as in the case of a pot; this is the inference [applied here].

Therefore, like space (*ākāśa*), the self (*ātman*) is all-pervading, and even knowledge (*jñāna*), which is its attribute, is likewise all-pervading. Consequently, the Vaiśeṣika doctrine of the self is refuted by direct perception itself.
14) And so it is said in the venerable Pauṣkara:
The Sages asked:
"If the all-pervasiveness of the atom is established, then there would be the pervasiveness of its qualities."
How can there be pervasiveness for that which is not perceived elsewhere than in the body?
Īśvara says:
It is not logical that atoms possess the same dimensions as the body;
therefore, because they perceive objects situated elsewhere than the body, [the soul must be omnipresent].
Furthermore, wherever the body, sense organs, and so forth— which are its manifestors— are present,
the Self is omnipresent there, because its effects are observed everywhere.
This [self] is all-pervasive because it is formless, just like space;
therefore, the knowledge that constitutes its attribute is likewise pervasive and directed toward objects.
The thesis that consciousness is eternal in nature and devoid of objects is refuted by direct perception,
because [consciousness] apprehends both itself and others.
Because the atom is established through individual self-awareness (pratyātmasiddha), neither inference nor perception can subvert it;
furthermore, the status of being a grasper does not belong here to the intellect, because its insentience (jaḍatva) has already been proven.
Furthermore, this state of being a grasper does not reside in the selves due to any difference [between them],
for their very nature is established as being constituted by the state of being a grasper.
Indeed, an analysis of things by means of their parts is never appropriate;
for no one ever wonders, "What is fire like without its power?"
Therefore, the self is established as always being the grasper of both self and other. Thus [it is said].
Elsewhere it is said:
"Wherever there may be a manifesting agent, there indeed is a body."
"The manifestation of qualities would be for the sake of experience; by that, its all-pervasiveness is understood. Thus it is said.

15) Furthermore, it is not the case that the selves (ātman) are non-knowers according to the system propounded by the Sāṅkhyas, because they are observed to be apprehenders of objects. Nor should it be argued that even if the self consists of mere consciousness (jñapti), the principle of intellect (buddhitattva)—which is synonymous with the principle of the Great (mahattattva)—is the knower; for that [intellect] is insentient (jaḍa).
Because it is that which manifests knowledge. Furthermore, the self is experienced as illuminating both itself and others.

And this quality of illuminating others is the very attribute of the self known as "knowership" (*jñātṛtva*). It must be stated that knowership belongs to the self when it has attained identity with the intellect (*buddhi*).

Because superimposition (*adhyāsa*), which would establish the identity with the intellect, is itself unestablished. Furthermore, since superimposition consists in the appearance of something previously perceived elsewhere, one must assert that the status of being a knower belongs to something distinct from the Self; yet that is not possible, because it has been stated that the intellect, being insentient (*jaḍa*), lacks the capacity for knowing. Now, if...

If the status of being a knower belongs to the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth by virtue of being a reflection of consciousness, then the intellect itself would have to be conscious. Furthermore, the reflection of that which has the nature of consciousness is simply not possible; for it is the transformation of the insentient intellect that constitutes reflection. Therefore, it is not tenable to assert that the Self is reflected in the intellect.
Thus, through superimposition, the agency of the Self is a construction of the intellect.
16) And so it is said in the venerable Pauṣkara:
"And this [Self] is a knower, not merely consciousness, because it is the grasper of objects.
The Sages:
This very [Self] is designated as having the nature of cognition; its state of being a knower is considered to belong to the Great One (Mahat).
O Maheśvara, even in this Tantra, the Lord is one whose nature is free from great attachment: "All living beings here are always seen to be indeed knowers."
This agency of knowing is not tenable for that [intellect], because it is insentient;
rather, in this case, cognition is always manifested by means of the intellect and other factors.
Furthermore, the self is indeed experienced as that which illuminates both itself and others;
and its capacity to illuminate others is eternal, because it is an eternal quality.
This state of being a knower cannot be something produced anew today;
for the superimposition of what has been perceived elsewhere is desired [only] upon another [object].
Since the status of being a knower cannot be established for anything other than the Self, superimposition (adhyāsa) is not accepted [as the cause of its appearance].
Now, it might be argued that the intellect and so forth possess the status of a knower through the reflection of consciousness (cit).
In that case, even the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth would become consciousness (*cit*) by means of the reflection of consciousness;
however, they are not conscious, because it is consciousness itself that is reflected in the form of consciousness within the intellect.
Nor is this reflection considered to belong to the Self, whose nature is consciousness;
for the transfer of the insentient into the insentient is logical only for that which is subject to transformation.
"Even the reflection of the intellect and so forth could not exist in the Self, because it is impossible;
this doctrine of mutual superimposition is a fabrication of false views."
(Pau Paśu Pa, verses 91–99) 17) Now, what is the proof for the plurality of selves? If it is argued that perception (*pratyakṣa*) is the proof, we say no;
for since the self is an incorporeal substance, it is not an object of the external sense organs. Nor [is it perceived] as "I am happy," "I..."

The distinction between selves is established through mental perception such as "I am suffering" and so forth; for that cognition does not lack the capacity to serve as a determinant of difference.
