Nor is it the case that the inference—"selves are distinct from one another because they are substrata of mutually contradictory properties, like fire and snow"—is the means of valid knowledge.

This must be stated: because mutually contradictory attributes, being merely conceptualized by their respective limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), do not reside in the Self, the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*). For when the space within a jar is joined with dust, smoke, and so forth, the spaces within a monastery or other locations are not likewise joined.
Therefore, if it is asked how there can be a plurality of selves when the observed difference is merely adventitious (*aupādhika*), it is said:

Selves are distinct, because they possess mutually contradictory attributes such as birth and death; for whatever possesses such attributes is distinct, just like a jar, a cloth, and so forth. Nor [can this be denied] because of the absence of birth and other such states in the case of selves.
The reason is unestablished (*asiddhi*). For when the body and so forth alone are absent from birth onwards, consciousness itself is not observed therein.
Therefore, it is the body and so forth that are produced as already endowed with consciousness.

18) But how can there be the production of eternal consciousness? Just as for you the production of the body, senses, and so forth—which are [otherwise] eternal—is possible, so too it is possible for the Self. Or, if you say that the body, senses, and so forth are not eternal in this form, but rather exist in the nature of their causes; then—

For me as well, it is established that the selves possess the properties of origination and dissolution in their limited (avacchinna) forms, whereas in their unlimited (anavacchinna) state they are eternal;

thus, the selves have the nature of arising and merging. Now, an objection is raised: just as the properties of origination and so forth belong to jars, pots, buckets, and the like, but not to the space delimited by them (tad-avacchinna), [so too should these properties not belong to the self].

If it is argued that properties such as birth and so forth belong only to the body and the like, and not to the Self as delimited by them, we say no; for the distinction between Selves is established precisely through the difference in the desires and other qualities belonging to the Self itself, which have objects such as eating and walking. Nor can these qualities be considered merely adventitious (aupādhika), because they constitute the very nature of the Self.

This is because its characteristic has been stated as "having infinity of vision and action" (*dṛkkriyānantyalakṣaṇam*). Nor should it be argued that the status of being a knower (*mātṛtva*) would not be established for selves if they were objects of knowledge (*meyatva*) due to their distinctness; for there is no contradiction between being an object of knowledge and being a knower. Otherwise, it would follow that it is impossible for selves to be objects of knowledge.

Śiva’s omniscience would be undermined; furthermore, upon the liberation of one, the liberation of all would follow as a logical consequence. This is not an acceptable conclusion, because it would entail the simultaneous destruction of the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*). Consequently, even the effort toward liberation would be fruitless. Therefore, the selves (*ātman*) are indeed distinct.
19) And so it is said in the venerable Pauṣkara:
The sages asked, "The selves are said to be many; by what means is this plurality understood?"
That reality is not accessible to direct perception, nor is it an object of inference.
Since difference is a property of the object of cognition, how could the cognizer become the object?
Furthermore, the absence of a cause or a means of proof does not establish a difference in the self.
Due to the distinction of one conditioned attribute of the Self from another conditioned one,
it is as when a single space within a jar is joined with dust, smoke, and so forth.
Just as not all [mental factors] are associated with one another, so it is with living beings and pleasure and the like;
therefore, let a solution be provided for this [alleged] identity of self.
Īśvara:
There are many selves, due to the distinctions of birth, death, and so forth;
for qualities such as birth and destruction are observed in distinct entities.
Therefore, birth, destruction, and so forth, which are established as the differentiators of the self, do not belong to the body alone;
rather, they pertain to the selves together with the bodies and other such adjuncts.
If consciousness were not observed to arise from the body and so forth,
then consciousness would have to be admitted even for infants born from a body.
Being inseparable from consciousness, the body and so forth arise;
therefore, bodies characterized by distinctions such as birth and the like serve as proof for the distinction of consciousness.
If you think, "How can there be birth for consciousness, which is eternal here?", this is a very small objection; for these things—the body, the senses, and so forth—are also eternal.
The non-existent has no being, and the existent has no non-being;
therefore, this doctrine of a single self is imagined by those of deluded intellect.
The Sages said: Just as space remains one and the same within jars, pots, buckets, and the like, even so the Self is established within all bodies.
Īśvara:
Furthermore, that space is of a single uniform nature, whereas consciousness is not held to be so;
for while one [self] has the desire to enjoy, another may have the desire to move away.
Thus, the consciousness of the self appears as if existing in distinct forms;
however, if it were non-different [from all], then the desire to experience would arise for everyone simultaneously.
The Sages:
But was it not stated that this is due to the difference in the attributes of the Self when possessed of limiting adjuncts?
Īśvara: [Yes,] it was.
O elder brothers, since the non-difference of the atom has been established, it must be stated accordingly.
When difference has been established through logical arguments, it is not auspicious to accept its non-establishment;
for this very reason, when the space within a jar is joined with dust, smoke, and so forth—
It is not a fault that all [cognitions] do not associate [with their objects] as others do;
for the distinction [between them] was previously stated to be a property of the object of cognition (*meyadharma*).
And that reason adduced here regarding the cognized and the non-cognized objects is unestablished;
for while difference would reside in both [the object and the subject], there is no lack of cognizability on the part of the knower.
"For the selves are indeed the objects of measurement for Śiva; otherwise, his omniscience would be impaired. Thus [it is said].
Elsewhere it is said:
"If liberation were situated elsewhere [than within oneself], the consequence would follow that worldly existence must be severed [from without]."
And yet that cessation of existence does not exist; therefore, those [cessations] are considered by you to be many. Thus it is said.

20) Thus, the self's distinctness from the body and other such things, its eternity, its nature as consciousness, its agency, and its manifoldness are established. Omniscience, moreover, is established by itself; however, limited knowledge arises from the cause that is impurity (*mala*). As it is said in that very same [text]:
Since the atom is established by direct perception, inference cannot subvert that perception;
nor is there here any grasping agency on the part of consciousness, because its insentience has already been proven.
Furthermore, this state of being a grasper does not exist for selves due to any difference [between them];
rather, their very nature is established as being constituted by that state of being a grasper.
"Furthermore, an analysis of entities based on their parts is never appropriate.
Likewise, these [souls] are omniscient by nature; however, limited knowledge arises from a cause.
That which obstructs omniscience is taught to be impurity (mala). Thus it is said.

(From Pauṣpaśukla, verses 110–112, 114) 21) Now, is this [consciousness] with form (*sākāra*) or without form (*nirākāra*)? If it is the former, is it of the nature of the perceptible (*dṛśya*) or of the nature of both the perceptible and the imperceptible (*dṛśyādṛśya*)? It cannot be the first, because nothing else is perceived within the body; nor can it be the second.

Because visibility and invisibility are contradictory in a single entity. If it is argued that both can exist through a difference in time—just as wood and fire, or a branch and the moon—it is not so; for in that case, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of its never being seen at all, just as in those examples.
Nor is the third [alternative] possible; for it would entail the non-distinction of the subtle body [from the self]. Nor is it formless; [for that would contradict perception].

Because, through connection with that [Self], movement and so forth would not be possible in the body; for movement never occurs anywhere merely through conjunction with space, since it is observed that only conjunction with something possessing movement—such as a bellows and the like—produces movement. Furthermore, if the Self were of the nature of consciousness (cid-rūpa), [the senses...]
Otherwise, it would result in futility; for it is not logical that consciousness, in its capacity as a knower, should require association with the non-conscious (the body).
Moreover, if the self were all-pervasive, it could not reside in specific locations such as the forehead, which would lead to the impossibility of the five states of existence.

Thus, the nature of the self is refuted by this lack of logical consistency; to this it is replied: this self is indeed formless. Nor does this entail the impossibility of movement in the body, for that is possible through the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*).
Nor should it be argued that because that power exists at all times, movement would also occur at all times; for [the manifestation of] that...

Because the effect is occasional— given that it is as if non-existent due to being veiled by *āṇava* [impurity] and because it depends upon the intensity (*saṃrambha*) in the form of a mental modification (*buddhivṛtti*) which acts as its manifestor— it is logically established. Nor should it be argued that "let this intensity alone be the cause of activity, so what is the use of a power of action (*kriyāśakti*)," for [it is not so], because intensity alone...
Because it is impossible for an insentient nature to be the motivator of activity, the power of consciousness (cetanā-śakti) is necessary;
and because the power of action (kriyā-śakti) is necessary to produce impetus (saṃrambha),
[the Lord] also possesses form through the metaphorical attribution of form to knowledge and action.
Thus, even though the Self is of the nature of consciousness (*cid-rūpa*), there is no logical inconsistency in its dependence on the senses.

Since the power of consciousness is veiled by impurity (*mala*), such dependence is justified for the purpose of producing the awakening in the form of the intellect (*buddhi*) so that that [power] may be manifested. For it is only the power of consciousness manifested through the modification of the intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti*)—which is itself insentient—that [perceives].
Because it is illuminating. Thus, even regarding its all-pervasiveness (*vyāpakatva*), there is no inconsistency whatsoever.

Since the adjuncts of the waking and other states reside in the forehead and other locations, it is logical that what is delimited by them is also restricted to specific places such as the forehead. This is because the subtle body (*sūkṣmadeha*) possesses mobility.
And because the transition to the next world and so forth is logically established for that [self] as delimited by [the body], even in all its states.

22) For instance: there are three states of the Self—the state of isolation (*kevalāvasthā*), the state of totality (*sakalāvasthā*), and the state of purity (*śuddhāvasthā*). Among these, when [the Self] is deprived of the two kinds of bodies, as well as the vital breaths, the senses, and the internal organs—and consequently, due to the absence of any manifesting medium, [its] *āṇava* limitation, volition, knowledge, and action—
When one remains without perceiving anything at all, that is the state of isolation (kevalāvasthā).

When one is delimited by the subtle body and the sheaths consisting of food, vital breath, mind, intellect, and bliss, that is the state of totality (sakalāvasthā). This occurs when there is equilibrium of karma.

And when that [seed] has fallen with its power determined, through the manifestation of the bliss of Śiva by virtue of the Guru’s grace, there occurs the manifestation of identity with Śiva via the cessation of the three impurities (*malas*);
that is the pure state (*śuddhāvasthā*). In that regard, compared to the state of being *sakala* (with parts/limitations):

At the time of attaining the state of Kevala, there is a fivefold distinction of states. When [the Self], residing in the forehead, experiences all objects together with the thirty-six principles beginning with Nāda and ending with Earth, that is the waking state accompanied by creative intuition (sapratibhā jāgrad-avasthā); this itself is the Sakala state.
The five pure principles (tattvas) are the impellers, being devoid of the unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) that experiences objects;
the seven principles are the experiencers; and there are the five great elements.
When these seventeen have ceased, [there remain] the five beginning with hearing and the five beginning with speech.

The four— mind (manas), intellect (buddhi), ego (ahaṅkāra), and consciousness (citta)— the five [objects] beginning with sound, the five [faculties] beginning with speech which are real, and the ten [winds] beginning with prāṇa; together with these, the Self named Kṣetrajña,
when it stands within the mouth as the thirty-fifth...

When one does not properly perceive objects even while awake due to the absence of activity in the *preraka* (the impeller) and *bhojayitr* (the enjoyer) sections, resulting from the predominance of the *āṇava* [impurity], that is "non-appearance while awake" (*apratibhā jāgrat*). The causes for the experience of the subtle body are the five [objects] beginning with sound, the five [faculties] beginning with speech, and the ten [vital functions] beginning with breath.
The four— mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and consciousness (*citta*)— together with these constitute the twenty-five-fold group.

When the self, known as the *kṣetrajña*, is situated in the throat and, having abandoned empirical objects, experiences objects that are merely momentary appearances, that is the state of dream (*svapna*).

When one has abandoned the enjoyments of the gross and subtle bodies and the third self remains in the heart together with the mind and the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*), that is the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*). When the second self remains in the region of the navel together with the vital breath, that is the fourth state (*turīya*). But when [the self] is in the *mūlādhāra*...

When one has abandoned all things—such as reality (tattva), unreality (atattvika), and so forth—and only the Self alone remains, veiled by the atomic impurity (āṇavamala), that is the state beyond the fourth (turyātītāvasthā). That very state is the eternally isolated state (nityakevalāvasthā); thus, the isolated state (kevalāvasthā) is fourfold.

23) [Objection: Granted that during the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), since all principles (*tattva*)—whether real or unreal and so forth—are dissolved, it may be possible for the Self (*ātman*) to abide in a state of absolute isolation (*kaivalya*); however, how is this possible now, when the principles persist until the dissolution and the omnipresent Self continues to exist?

If it is argued that this is due to the absence of their respective activities, that is true; for just as iron lacks the power to burn even when fire and iron are present due to the absence of the activity of a person who joins them, so too,
although the principles (tattvas) exist, [their lack of function] is caused by the absence of the impelling unseen merit (bhojakādṛṣṭa).
Due to the absence of the impulsion of Śiva’s power (śakti), there is no enjoyment of objects. As it has been said:

"Just as there is a union of iron with fire and a separation of fire from iron, so too the union and separation of the principles (tattvas) and the self occur through power (śakti) under the influence of karma."

24) Now, the stainless state of waking (*nirmalajāgrat*) is described: through the union of Śiva and Śakti, who preside over the syllables *a*, *u*, *m*, the point (*bindu*), and the resonance (*nāda*), the self (*ātman*)— possessing a stainless internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—
abiding in the heart perceives the entire manifest world (*prapañca*) as having the form of Śiva.
And one experiences sensory pleasure as the bliss of one's own essential nature; that is the stainless waking state (*nirmalajāgrat*).

When the form that is the cause of the waking state dissolves into the vowel *u*, and the mind that grasps external objects dissolves into the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), then the fourfold group beginning with the ego-sense [dissolves] by means of the fourfold group beginning with the vowel *u*.
The state of abiding with the contemplation of "I am" (so'ham) in the throat is the stainless dream;

this occurs when the *ukāra*, which is the cause of the dream state, dissolves into the *makāra*, and when the ego (*ahaṅkāra*), which is the cause of the conceit "I am," dissolves into the intellect (*buddhi*).

At the root of the palate, which is the locus of deep sleep, there exists the triad of the intellect and the other two [the ego and mind], along with their impellers— the three beginning with the letter *a*— abiding in the form of the triad of the known, the knower, and the knowledge, which is beyond the reach of speech and devoid of the functions of the body and the senses.

Aṃ is stainless deep sleep (*nirmala-suṣupti*). When the instrument that produces the state of deep sleep— the letter *a*— and the discerning intellect (*nirṇāyaka-buddhi*) have dissolved into the *bindu* within the mind, the Self, together with the mind, along with the *bindu* and *nāda*,
[resides] in the space between the eyebrows, which is the locus of the fourth state (*turyāvasthā*), being devoid of the activity of both external and internal organs.
Abiding in mere consciousness is the stainless fourth state (*nirmala-turīya*).

When the *bindu* and *nāda*, which are the causes of the fourth state, as well as the mind and its inherent nature (*prakṛti*), have dissolved into the *kuṭilā*, then in the *brahmarandhra*— the locus of the state beyond the fourth— the Self alone, pervading both internally and externally, [remains].

While remaining [in this state], there is the manifestation of Śiva—who is indivisible in form, existence-consciousness-bliss (saccidānanda), non-dual, and perfectly full—as non-different from oneself;
that alone is the stainless state beyond the fourth (turyātīta). That indeed is the pure state.
As it has been said in the *Siddhāntasārāvalī*:
The waking state (*jāgrat*) is the individual soul’s cognition of its own objects by means of both external and internal organs;

from that [comes] dreaming (*svapna*), which is the cognition of objects consisting of the modifications (*vṛtti*) residing in the internal organ; deep sleep (*suṣupti*) is the supreme [state]. However, when the intellect (*mati*) is devoid of the activity of the senses within the body and is perceivable only by the self, it is the fourth state (*turyam*).
"When the body and senses have ceased [their activity], the mind is absorbed in one's own consciousness; thereafter, there is the arising of the state of Śiva. Thus [it is said].
And in the *Siddhāntabodha* (Yogapāda, verse 8):
"The cause of the waking state itself is the experience of the conjunction of the letters within the heart."
Then, through the functioning of both sense-faculties, there is the perception of a form that was previously latent.

When there is a perception by means of the internal organs alone, from the region of the throat, through the connection with subtle particles known as the objects of a previous experience, that is dream.
The dissolution of the functioning of the internal organs at the region of the palate is deep sleep;
the emergence of the *bindu* at the midpoint between the eyebrows is the fourth state (*turya*) through its transcendence.
In this context, there is a synthesis of cause and effect, as well as of the object and its designation;
it is the perception of sound (*nāda*), which is the cause for the manifestation of all objects through the functions of vision and action.
"The state beyond the fourth (turyātītā) and the aperture (randhra) are included here, along with the end of the staff (daṇḍānta) and so forth. Thus [it is said].

26) Thus, it is established that the bound soul (*paśu*) is all-pervasive, possessing a nature of consciousness connected with impurity (*mala*), and endowed with various states. Furthermore, this bound soul is threefold according to the distinction of its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*): the *sakala*, the *pralayākala*, and the *vijñānākala*. Among these, the one called *sakala* is characterized by having the power of vision obstructed by impurity.

For the sake of its expansion, [the soul] is bound by karma for the purpose of experience when it possesses the *kalās* and so forth. That which is called *pralayākala* is one who, having abandoned the *kalās* during the dissolution (*pralaya*), possesses the complete exhaustion of karma pertaining to the impure path (*aśuddhādhvan*)— whether through initiation (*dīkṣā*), expiation (*prāyaścitta*), or through [the end of] experience.
One who possesses a connection to the *kalās* brought under his own control through the karma of the mixed path that is about to be experienced is called a *vijñānākala*.
One who, by means of *vijñāna* and so forth, has abandoned all karmas and *kalās*, yet remains possessed of only the *kaṇva-mala* which obscures vision and action, is a *vijñānakevala*.
And so it is said in the venerable Pauṣkara:
"The bound souls (paśus) are to be known as threefold: the sakala, the pralayākala, and the vijñānākala. Listen now to their characteristics in due order."
One whose power of vision is obstructed by impurity (mala) possesses the limited powers (kalā) and so forth for the sake of their manifestation;
such a one, bound by karma for the sake of experience, is taught as the "sakala" (the conditioned).
One whose power of sight has been suppressed as before, who is devoid of *kalā* due to the ripening of karma,
yet is fit for a future *kalā* by means of that very karma— he is the *pralayākala*.
"Because his power is obstructed by impurity, his own vision and action are as if void;
he is recited in the Tantra as the third, known by the name Vijñānakevala. Thus [it is said].
(Pau Paśu Ślo 2–5) 28) Therein,
the abode of the *sakala* [souls] is in the lower part of impure *māyā*, on the path of impurity (*aśuddhādhvan*).
But for the *pralayākalas*, [their location] is on the path mixed with the midst of impure *māyā*;
for the *vijñānakevalas*, it is above impure *māyā* and below pure *vidyā*.
This state of abiding, even though they possess omnipresence (*vibhutva*), is perceived due to the influence of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). As it has been said in that very same work:
"Their sequential arrangement is [as follows]: at the beginning is Māyā, in the middle is Āṇava, and at the end is Kārmika.
Furthermore, the persistence of the individual soul (aṇu) is observed through its bondage, owing to its pervasive nature. Thus [it is said].

(Pau Paśu Pa, Śloka 6) 29) Now, since those who are isolated in consciousness (*vijñānakevala*) are veiled by *mala* alone, and since *mala* is all-pervasive, how can it reside in only one part, namely, within the sphere of *māyā*? It is said in reply:

Because impure *māyā* has already been experienced, there is no desire for it; and although the pure *māyā* yet to be experienced is characterized by a desire to consume it, there is currently an absence of Śiva’s will to bring that about. Therefore, it is said that they remain in between those two. And those two...
By the will of Śiva, they come to abide on the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*). Even for those who abide there, they do not possess the state of being "with parts" (*sakala*);
rather, by the will of Śiva, because they are accompanied by the impurity of office (*adhikāra-mala*), they possess only the state of being "parts of knowledge" (*vijñānakala*).
They are called *vijñānakalās* because their "part" (*kalā*) consists of the nature of knowledge (*vijñāna*).
And so it is said in the venerable Pauṣkara:
The Sages:
"For the bondage of the individual souls who are isolated through pure knowledge (vijñānakevala) is indeed only impurity (mala)."
Since impurity is all-pervasive, how could there be a state of existence at the end of Māyā?
Īśvara said:
"O auspicious ones, O highly wise brahmins, regarding that Pure Path (śuddhādhvan) previously mentioned,
it is [distinguished] by its state of being about to be experienced and by the state of having been experienced as the other."
By implication alone, they are said to abide in the middle as those who are liberated through pure consciousness (vijñānakevalas);
indeed, those eminent sages are themselves directly the vijñānakevalas.
Subsequently, by the will of Śiva, they shall abide on the pure path;
for Māyā acts as the regulator of the individual soul (aṇu) with respect to the pure path.
"Those residing therein are not all [souls], but rather the *vijñānakevalas*,
who are forever freed from the impurity of *adhikāra* (office/authority) and permitted by the will of Śiva."

(Chapter on Pau, Paśu, and Pa; verses 7–11) 31) Furthermore, the reason for their being devoid of *māyā* and *karman* is stated in that very same place: "But here, the method (*yukti*) for the attainment of the *vijñānakevalas* is now declared."
Either by initiation that pierces through the intermediate levels of the principles (tattvas) of Kalā, or even through knowledge.
When karma is exhausted either through yoga, through enjoyment, or through renunciation, then,
because of that exhaustion, there is also the exhaustion of māyā which depends upon it.
Only the impurity (mala) remains; therefore, they are known as *vijñānakevalas*.
Even liberation (*kaivalya*) is not accepted for those who are freed from the views of the Buddhists and others.
Because their karma pertaining to the levels above the *buddhitattva* has not been fully exhausted,
they are to be known as *sakala* (with parts), since their connection with *kalā* remains established.
In this very way, the atoms (aṇu), established by reasoning,
remain as isolated souls (pralayakevala) either through the dissolution of the principles (tattva) or through the dissolution of karma.
Let the *pralayākalas* be understood as those who have abandoned the subtle and gross external bodies, yet remain joined with unripened karmas that serve as the basis for future experience.
"Because of its connection with all the *kalās*, it is twofold—subtle and gross.
This principle (*tattva*), beginning with *kalā* and ending with the earth (*avanī*), is determined for each individual soul. Thus [it is said].

(Chapter on Paśu, verses 12–18) 32) The *vijñānakevalas* are of two kinds: those whose impurities have been stilled and those whose impurities have not been stilled. Among them, Śiva, having observed the ripening of the impurity (*mala*) in certain individuals, [bestows grace].

He joins some to the office within the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*); he joins others to the principle (*tattva*) called experience (*bhoga*). Having been joined there, they enjoy various desired experiences and proceed to offices by the will of the Lord (*pati*).
However, those who have reached the principle of Īśvara are endowed with the qualities of office.
The great universal monarchs (*cakravartins*) are eight, beginning with Ananta, who possess progressively superior qualities as previously described;

furthermore, there are some who have attained the principle known as *vidyā*, namely the seventy million great mantras (*mahāmantras*). Among these, whoever develops detachment regarding their own specific domain—

In accordance with the ripening of their impurities alone, the Lord, having bestowed his grace and led them to supreme liberation, unites those situated in the *sādākhya* principle with the station of the *īśvara* principle; those situated in the *īśvara* principle with the station of the *vidyā* principle; and those situated therein with the station at the summit of *māyā*.
33) This has been stated in the venerable Pauṣkara: "In the beginning, Śiva, having favored by His mere will those who are *vijñānakevalas*,
leads some into the realm of the pure path, depending solely upon the ripening of their impurity (*mala*)."
Having made them intense through vision and action, he appoints some to offices;
others he appoints to the principle called enjoyment, and still others to that called Īśvara.
I invoke others who are all-knowing and powerful in the reality called Vidyā.
Endowed with the qualities of Sadāśiva and resting upon the principle known as Bhoga,
they enjoy various objects of enjoyment desired by their minds.
Those who, engaged in the offices of remedial rites by the will of their husband,
have attained the reality of Īśāna, are especially qualified for ritual action.
Endowed with the qualities of their respective offices, these eight great universal monarchs— beginning with Ananta and Sūkṣma— are superior in qualities in successive order as previously described.
Possessing extreme beauty and charm, with minds never diminished, they have always attained both knowledge and ignorance; in number, they are seventy million.
All these great-souled ones of immeasurable splendor have their impurities completely stilled;
yet among them, in whichever great-souled one dispassion has arisen—
"What is the use of this authority, which is an obstacle to the highest good?"—
thus the Supreme Lord, having regard for the ripening of that impurity, [withdrew it].
By His own will, He bestows grace through a vision intended for the manifestation of liberation;
therefore, the omnipresent Lord places that person who is near to liberation in His own state as the youngest [disciple].
"Having favored another, he also appoints him to that very position. Thus [it is said].
(Chapter on *paśu*, verse 49–58) 34) Likewise, the *pralayākala*s are also of two kinds: those whose impurities are matured (*pakvamala*) and those whose impurities are immature (*apakvamala*).
Among them, Śiva, having favored those with matured impurities, bestows upon them the status of lords of the worlds (*bhuvanapati*) during the periods of dissolution (*pralayakāla*).
Those whose impurities are unripened, being under the influence of their natural karma for enjoyment, become *sakala* (conditioned) souls, endowed with the body of the *puryaṣṭaka*.
As it is said in that very same work:
"The Lord, by His own will, bestows grace even upon the atoms [souls] at the time of dissolution."
And elsewhere [it is said]:
"In the case of those among the *pralayākala*s whose impurity (*mala*) and karma have ripened, others proceed [to higher states]."
Endowed with a body consisting of the eightfold city (puryaṣṭaka), [the soul] dwells in all wombs by the power of subtle karma.
Having favored some, Maheśvara bestows upon them the status of lords of the world. Thus it is said.

35) All [these types] are also threefold, according to the distinction between those who are spontaneously perfected (*sāṃsiddhika*), those who are disciplined (*vainayika*), and those who are ordinary (*prākṛta*). Among these, one who is "spontaneously perfected" is someone who, in a previous birth, performed hearing, reflection, and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*), yet has not yet achieved the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of Śiva; for that purpose—
Like Śuka, Vāmadeva, Jaḍabharata, and others, he has assumed a body through the power of uninterrupted *nididhyāsana* (meditative contemplation) and,

by the grace of Śiva, possesses the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of Śiva. The one called *vainayika* is one who, being disciplined in humility toward the Guru, receives initiation and becomes purified by the Śaiva duties of mind, speech, and body.

One who possesses thorough knowledge of both the worldly and Śaiva scriptures will explain the manner of that [scriptural] grace in the section on initiation (*dīkṣā*). The so-called "natural" (*prākṛta*) person is one whose cognition consists of both the known and the unknown—like the cognition in a dream—and who possesses the conceit of self (*ātmābhimāna*) regarding the body, senses, and so forth, which are produced by primordial nature (*prakṛti*). As it is said in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
For those whose minds are illuminated by the impressions of distinguished dharmas,
their innate quality shines forth even after the departure of the body, just as before.
The quality of discipline shines forth from the world, the intellect, and the scriptures;
the disciplined person is polished by the conduct of mind, speech, and body.
"In its natural state, when conjoined with the body, it becomes manifest and possesses the cognition of dreams and so forth. Thus [it is said].
(Pratyaṅgirā 10, verses 26–28) 36) Furthermore, the modes of bondage and liberation for this entire [system], as well as the distinctions between its states,
have been expounded in the venerable *Kiraṇatantra*.
Garuḍa said: "If this is so, then what kind of animal is it that is bound, and how is it bound?
How is it released? Tell me this for the sake of dispelling my doubt."
The Blessed One said:
"The individual soul (paśu) is eternal, indeed formless, ignorant, inactive, devoid of qualities, and not a master;
it is all-pervasive, situated within the belly of Māyā, and does not contemplate the means for its own enjoyment."
From Śiva, *kalā* comes into connection with that impure [soul];
its capacity being empowered by that [kalā], it perceives the objects presented by *avidyā*.
Furthermore, colored by passion— which is itself composed of the qualities (guṇas) of primordial matter (pradhāna)—
the bound soul (paśu) is fettered through its connection with the host of instruments beginning with the intellect (buddhi).
Then, due to the connection with destiny (niyati), one is constrained by time within that which has been earned by oneself,
being deluded by the enjoyment of the effects to be experienced according to the reckoning of time.
Thus, bound by the digits of reality (tattva-kalā), possessing limited knowledge and joined with a body,
embraced by the enjoyment of Māyā, absorbed in that, and veiled by the innate nature (sahaja).
Then, by virtue of his own karma, he enjoys the entirety of pleasure and other such enjoyments; subsequently, when his karma becomes equalized, this occurs through the power of the passage of time.
When one is initiated by a Guru through the descent of intense power (tīvra-śakti-nipāta),
he becomes omniscient like Śiva himself, entirely devoid of limited knowledge.
At that time, the transmigrating soul is no longer a bound being, for it is fully manifest in its state of Śiva-nature;
thus, through this gradual process, the one who was bound is liberated by means of sequential yoga.
The Puruṣa is traditionally taught to exist in three states: as Kevala (the solitary), Sakala (the conditioned), and Śuddha (the pure).
Liberation from the impurity of consciousness is attained through the stainless Śiva.
"One who is such as this is declared to be a mere beast; what else do you ask? Thus [it is said].

(From Kiraṇa Paśupata, verses 14–24) 37) The definition of the impurities (*mala*), *māyā*, and *karman*, which constitute the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) for these [three powers], will be stated in the *Pāśapaṭala*. Now, if the Self (*ātman*) is established, its differentiation is logical; but what is the proof for its existence?
It is said: the body and so forth, while in motion, must be presided over by a conscious being, because they are insentient, like a jar;

and thus the Self is established as the initiator of the insentient. Or, for example, the body, the instruments, the worlds, and so forth, which have God as their agent, must exist for the enjoyment of someone, because they are insentient; [it is] not [otherwise].

Īśvara alone is the enjoyer of that [world], because all his desires have been attained. Nor is the world and so forth the enjoyer of it, because it is impossible for something to be both the object of enjoyment and the enjoyer of itself. And this is not purposeless, because it is the work of an intelligent agent. Therefore, by the method of elimination, there must be another enjoyer of it besides the insentient world and Īśvara.
It must exist; and thus it is established that this is the Self.
38) This has been stated in the venerable Pauṣkara:
The Sages said—

And when a self truly established is proven, then that which was previously stated shall become fruitful. Therefore, O Śambhu, let the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for its existence be declared.
The Lord [states]: "The body and so forth, when functioning, are always presided over by a conscious being,
because, being insentient, they lack inherent activity, like a jar and other such objects."
"But that which is the initiator [of action] is what is proclaimed by others as the Self. Thus [it is said].

And in the venerable *Mṛgendra*: "The effects are earth and so forth; the Lord is the agent. There is no need for another agent to create that [Lord]. (Śloka 59–61). 39) Śrīmanmṛgendre ca: kāryaṃ kṣityādi karteśastatkarturnopayujyate |
It does not act for its own sake because it is insentient, nor is it purposeless because the agent is authoritative.
By process of elimination, that [body] is for the sake of another; he is the *kṣetrajña* (knower of the field), distinct from those two.
The body is "other" because it exists for his sake; indeed, the earth and other elements are for the sake of another.
The body, too, because it lacks consciousness, more easily serves the purposes of another;
for if it were conscious, it would never be fit to be enjoyed by another due to its own subjectivity and its state of constant transformation.
"Objects of experience, such as cloth and the like, are seen to be subject to change when devoid of consciousness. Thus [it is said].

Thus ends [the section] from the *Śaivaparibhāṣā* composed by the venerable Jñānaśivācārya, the foremost among the lords of yogins devoted to Śiva, the preeminent teacher of the conduct beyond the castes and stages of life (*ativarṇāśrama*), and the protector of the Śaiva tradition. (Mṛgendrapaddhati 6, verses 2–5).
The third chapter, titled "The Definition of the Category of Paśu."
The Fourth Chapter:

1) Now, the category of *pāśa* (the bond) is investigated. In this context, *pāśatva* (the state of being a bond) is defined as that which opposes the manifestation of the bliss of Śiva. And this [bond] exists in the form of the *āṇavamala* (the impurity of limited individuality), by virtue of its nature as a veil.

It should be understood that this [pāśa] functions as the impeller of the concealing power (*tirodhāyaka-śakti*), and likewise, through the production of objects of enjoyment and the means of enjoyment, it generates worldly pleasure and the like by means of *bindu*, *māyā*, and *karman*. Furthermore, this *pāśa* is fivefold: *āṇava*, the concealing power, *bindu*, *māyā*, and *karman*.

In this context, four categories are insentient in nature. The power of concealment (*tirodhāyaka-śakti*), however, although its essence is consciousness (*cid-rūpa*), is metaphorically designated as a "bond" (*pāśa*) because it favors the bonds. Among these, what is called "atomicity" (*aṇutva*) is the obstruction of the self's powers of vision and action. This is termed "atomicity" because it produces a state of limitation (*aṇutva*) for the all-pervading (*vibhu*) self.

2) Now, what is the proof for its existence? It is certainly not perception, because it is admitted to be beyond the reach of the senses. Nor is it inference; since it is never observed anywhere, there is an absence of the apprehension of concomitance (*sahacāra*), and thus an affirmative (*anvayin*) inference is impossible. As for a negative (*vyatirekin*) inference, by the reasoning already stated...

Since it is understood through perception and inference, in the absence of that [inference], the negative concomitance (*vyatireka-vyāpti*) cannot be grasped, and consequently, even the *vyatirekin* [type of inference] has no application. Therefore, we see no evidence whatsoever for the existence of *mala*. To this, it is replied: The Self has its omniscience partially veiled, because it is a possessor of limited knowledge (*kiñcijjña*). That which...

He who is not partially obscured in his omniscience is not even a knower of a few things, just as Śiva [is not]; thus, the existence of *mala* (impurity) is established through negative inference (*vyatirekyanumāna*). Nor should it be said that there is no proof for the omniscience of souls; for their power of cognition has all things as its object.

Because it possesses the power of knowledge, like the power of the Lord (Īśvara); for this [reason] serves as the proof in that case. Nor is this [argument] unestablished (aprayojaka); for, in the absence of being produced by an instrument connected to each respective object—which is the factor determining the restriction of objects—it would be impossible for it to have a restricted object-domain.
Alternatively, if their state of limited knowledge were innate, it would contradict the scriptural teaching that they possess omniscience in liberation.
Thus, the capacity for knowledge does not inherently have all things as its object; rather, this must be admitted as being dependent solely upon concealment (*āvaraṇa*).
And since that [limited cognition] is produced by a concealer, the existence of impurity (*mala*) is established by its nature as a concealer. And it is said in the venerable *Pauṣkara*:
"The Self is veiled by impurity, because there is limited knowledge (*kiñcijjñatā*) despite [its] omniscience."
But he who knows nothing at all is not even covered by impurity.
"Just as Śiva is, so is this [Self]; it is not at all enveloped by impurity. Thus [it is said].
(From *Pau*, *Paśu*, verses 124–126) 3) Nor can there be a difference in meaning [between the two] due to ignorance (*ajñāna*), because it cannot withstand logical analysis. To explain:
is that ignorance the absence of knowledge (*jñānābhāva*) or a misapprehension (*anyathājñāna*)? It cannot be the first.
Because non-existence is incapable of producing anything; for the non-existences of jars and the like do not perform any causal function.
Furthermore, is that absence of cognition a prior absence (*prāgabhāva*), an absence through destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*), or an absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*)?
Not the first, because it would entail the arising of cognition only at a later time. Not the second, because [at a later time]...

Because it would follow that knowledge could never arise. Nor is the third [alternative] possible, because it is contradicted by evidence. Nor is it "knowledge otherwise" (*anyathājñāna*), because such a thing does not arise without a defect (*doṣa*). Furthermore, is this "knowledge otherwise" adventitious or inherent? If it were adventitious, it could not sublate the eternal power of consciousness (*nityacicchakti*). Nor...
The second [alternative]; for if that were inherent, change would be impossible.
And so it is stated in the venerable Pauṣkara:
"In this context, if consciousness were merely knowledge, how could the absence of knowledge be ignorance?"
Or else, there is no other way [of understanding] than as an appearance otherwise.
Ignorance is not the mere absence of knowledge, because such an absence is incapable of producing any effect;
nor indeed does the absence of a jar ever fetch water here.
If it were the prior non-existence of knowledge, then the arising of knowledge would necessarily follow;
nor is this [non-existence] something other than knowledge, since that too does not arise by itself.
The cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell would not occur without a film [on the eye];
moreover, is this erroneous cognition adventitious or otherwise?
If it were adventitious, it could never obstruct the power of consciousness;
if, on the other hand, it were non-adventitious, then that very thing would not be false cognition.
O twice-born ones, that object of knowledge is indeed impermanent, like the cognition of silver;
moreover, this erroneous cognition does not sublate right knowledge.
It has not been observed that the cognition of mother-of-pearl is sublated by the cognition of silver. Thus [it is said].
(Pau Paśu Pa, verses 115–121) 5) Furthermore, this impurity must be of the nature of a substance (dravya-rūpa), because it possesses manifold powers, like fire.
And it is said in the venerable Pauṣkara:
Furthermore: "Moreover, impurity (mala) is a substance because it possesses multiple powers, just like fire."

For this very reason, this [ignorance] is not a quality (*guṇa*) of the Self; for if it were a quality, the relationship between quality and qualificand would be eternal, which would entail the impossibility of its cessation, contradicting the scriptural declarations regarding its cessation in liberation. It is not.

For the inference of the Cārvāka proponent, passion constitutes a "different subject" (*arthāntara*), because it is ineffective with respect to that which is stainless. If it were present even in the stainless, it would also exist in liberated souls. Furthermore, since passion is a property of the intellect (*buddhi*) and is thus material (*prākṛta*), it is non-eternal.
It is not possible for the eternal power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) to be obstructed.
And it is stated in the *Pauṣkara*:
"If it is argued that passion (*rāga*) is the cause of the power [of action], then what is the use of impurity (*mala*)?"
It is true that passion exists as its cause, yet it effects nothing in that which is stainless.
If that [attachment] were to exist even in Amala for the sake of power, it would follow without distinction even in the case of the liberated one;
for neither the liberated one nor Śiva is ever attached to enjoyment.
Furthermore, since this passion is said by the Buddhists to be of the nature of a mental state (*pratyaya*),
and since consciousness (*buddhi*) is established as being derived from primordial matter (*prakṛti*), therefore it is perishable.
"How can a sublater be admitted for the power of consciousness (cicchakti), which is eternally established? Thus [it is said].

(From Pauṣpaśukla, verses 127–130) 7) Nor can there be a difference in entity [between the Self] and action (*karman*); for since that [action] is to be accomplished by the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) and is the cause of experience consisting of cognition, it is incapable of being an obscuration [of the Self]. Or, if it were an obscuration, then...

Furthermore, because [the intellect] consists of cognition, merit, and demerit, it is impossible for it to be a binder above the level of the *buddhi*-tattva. Moreover, how could those two [merit and demerit], whose sole function is experience (*bhoga*), have any operation in the act of veiling?

8) If it is argued: "In that case, let that very [knowledge] alone be the accomplisher of both effects; what is the point of the trouble of postulating a separate category?"—alas, then, since all effects would be fully accomplished by a single knowledge, the postulation of a distinct reality would be useless, as no difference between the effects would be observed.

Therefore, it is established that [ignorance] is not an obscuration of the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*). And it has been stated in that very same place: "O twice-born ones, even by means of action (*karman*), no sublation of knowledge is possible, because action is something to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and exists as a means for the person (*pums*)."
Furthermore, since that [knowledge] is the sole cause of enjoyment, how could it be an obstacle to enjoyment?
For enjoyment consists of knowledge; indeed, there is no obscuration of that [knowledge] by itself.
Action consists of merit and demerit, and these two are established as being mental (buddhi-born);
since they lack pervasiveness, how could they bind [the soul] everywhere above them?
Furthermore, how do those two function in the engagement with enjoyment?
Even though they are engaged elsewhere, they may still serve as causes for this [engagement].
The postulation of multiple principles is refuted by the diversity of effects;
therefore, established as it is, karma does not sublate the power of consciousness.
Furthermore, how can an action that merely manifests [consciousness] be an obstacle to the power of consciousness? Thus [it is asked].

(From Pau Paśu Pa, verses 130–135) 9) Nor can there be a difference in object by means of *māyā*; for since *māyā* is established as that which produces a different kind of effect, it is incapable of producing another effect in the form of an obscuration (*āvaraṇa*). Furthermore:

Furthermore, because [Māyā] acts as the cause for the manifestation of the powers of sight and so forth by means of producing the kalās and other categories, it is impossible for it to be the cause of obscuration, which is the opposite of that. And it has been said therein:
"Nor is Māyā the impurity (mala), because it is the illuminator of the effects."
That which is illuminating by virtue of its effect is not, in itself, an obscuring agent.
Just as both fire and a lamp are seen to be illuminators,
fire is never a cause of illumination that is itself non-illuminating.
Furthermore, illusion does not exist as something that performs a function for persons by way of its own intrinsic nature;
because it does not provide even the slightest assistance through its effects, it is not so [effective] in its own essence either.
Just as a thread [is perceived] only through its own effect, the cloth, and not by itself. Thus it is said.

(pau māyā pa ślo 51–54) 10) For this very reason, even the body does not possess the quality of being a concealer; for that too, by means of generating mental modifications (*buddhi-vṛtti*) and so forth, serves as a manifestor of that [Self]. Therefore, of the selves...

It is established that the *āṇava* [impurity] is one, beginningless, pervasive, and consists of a collection of powers that obscure vision and action, which reside within each individual and persist until the end of time. And this is logical, as stated in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
"That is one, beginningless, dense, and great for all living beings."
"Abiding within each individual, perishing at its own time, and possessing a collection of powers. Thus [it is said].
This is the obstructive power (*rodha-śakti*) of Śiva that acts as its favorer. As it has been said:
"Among those [powers], the auspicious power of Maheśvara is the favorer of all."
It is precisely because of following after phenomena that it is metaphorically designated as a "fetter. Thus [it is said].
Likewise, elsewhere—in the *Siddhāntasārāvalī*—it is said:

"Ignorance (*nīhāra*) is one and beginningless, co-existent with the individual soul, like the blackness of copper; it possesses manifold powers that obscure the vision of each person and are destroyed only at the end of its own jurisdiction."

"He is one who is to be bound, purified, and awakened, because he possesses the state of being an enjoyer, dependence on karma and the like, and union [with them]; the power of the Lord (Īśa-śakti), which restrains these [states] by means of its own activity, [is the means]. Thus [it is said].

(If she [is so], verse 6) 12) Furthermore, this impurity (*mala*) is sevenfold due to the distinctions among its effects, namely: delusion (*moha*), pride (*mada*), attachment (*rāga*), dejection (*viṣāda*), fever (*tāpa*), and desiccation (*śoṣa*). Among these, "delusion" refers to the beginningless, innate state of the selves (*ātman*) that gives rise to pride and the other afflictions.

The cause of these six is the impurity (*mala*) which produces delusion even in those who possess knowledge regarding women and other objects. *Mada* (pride) is the excessive conceit felt toward women and others whom one has acquired as one's own. *Rāga* (attachment) is the longing for sense-objects. *Viṣāda* (despair) is the state of dejection when those objects are not obtained. From that arises *tāpa* (torment), which takes the form of lamentation.

The variety of thoughts regarding sense objects consists of [the notion] "There is no one equal to me in terms of sons, friends, wife, wealth, and so forth. Upon their destruction, there is a state of being paralyzed and withered;
as it is said in the Pauṣkara:
Impurity is also to be known as sevenfold: delusion, intoxication, passion, and another called despondency, along with fever and the seventh, emaciation.
The variety of all impurities is also proclaimed here;
among them, the impurity called delusion (*moha*) is innate to men and beginningless.
O best of the twice-born, she is the source of the six [afflictions] beginning with pride, because of her primacy;
for as long as she exists, delusion arises in the self even toward women and the like, despite one's knowledge.
That is known as delusion (moha), due to the failure to distinguish between what is to be avoided and what is not;
for by means of it, one praises even a woman who has been obtained [as a wife], thinking, "She is not another's wife."
"This woman alone is a celestial nymph"—such is that intoxication which is abandoned;
for when she is not obtained, there arises despondency and tears in the eyes.
That dejection is called the stain, which brings extreme suffering to living beings;
from that arises internal torment, consisting of extensive lamentation.
From that, the impurity known as *tāpa* (fever) becomes *śoṣa* (wasting);
for when the self is paralyzed, the impurity becomes exceedingly difficult to overcome.
This is my kinsman, this is my wife, and this earth with its refined wealth is mine;
I have achieved my purpose, or rather, who is there to protect me?
That thought which arises in men regarding their family and such matters,
producing various mental states, is this impurity known as "variety" (vaicitrya).
"These seven are declared to be the innate impurities of men who are possessed of impurity. Thus [it is said].

(Pau Paśu Pa, verses 137–146) 14) What, then, is the relationship between the Self and impurity? If it is argued that it is inherence (*samavāya*), it would follow that impurity is a quality (*guṇa*). This is not an acceptable consequence; for if a quality were insentient (*jaḍa*), the possessor of that quality (*guṇin*) would also [be insentient].
Because it would follow that [the soul] is insentient; furthermore, because since inherence (samavāya) is eternal, it would follow that liberation is impossible.

Therefore, the impurity (mala) is indeed a substance (dravya) that appears as if it were a quality (guṇa) through the state of being inseparably established (ayutasiddha). Consequently, the relationship between the two is merely conjunction (saṃyoga).

15) [Objection: But surely conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is the relation between two things established separately (*yutasiddha*); thus, even conjunction does not hold, because of the definition of conjunction. [Reply: True; for that [definition] is the characteristic of produced conjunction (*janyasaṃyoga*).
However, conjunction in general is the relation between two substances devoid of the relationship of material cause and its effect (*upādānopādeyabhāva*).

The characteristic [of bondage] is to be understood as follows: thus, that which pertains to the individual (āṇava) and its obstructing power (rodhaśakti), which is its grasper, is established as being called "bondage" (pāśa).

16) Now, *bindu* is defined: *Bindu* is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the pure principles (*tattva*) and those [impure] principles of a similar nature. It is insentient in form and is the Lord’s power of appropriation (*parigraha-śakti*), synonymous with *kuṇḍalinī*. Within this very [power], there occurs the differentiation of states, such as the dissolution (*laya*) of Śiva and so forth, as well as that of the individual souls (*rudrāṇu*).
Awakening and liberation [are attained]. And it is stated in the venerable Pauṣkara:
"The distinctions such as absorption (laya) previously mentioned belong to Śiva with respect to his limiting adjuncts (upādhi)."
That should be understood as the Bindu; it is considered to be Kuṇḍalinī itself.
Moreover, it is that by which the Rudrāṇavas are bound, or wherein they abide.
"From which this [world] is liberated, let that be understood as the Bindu. Thus it is said.
(Pau Bindu Pa, verses 1–3) 17) The proof for its existence is as follows: the bodies of Ananteśvara and others,
along with the principles (*tattva*), worlds (*bhuvana*), and so forth that serve as their substrata, possess a material cause (*sopādāna*), because they are effects, like a jar.

Nor is there the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*). For the entire range of effects, from the *kalā* down to the earth, is produced by a body-possessing agent, because it is an effect associated with suffering, like [any] agreed-upon example; thus, by this inference, the existence of the body of Ananteśa is established as the instrument for all effects belonging to Māyā. Likewise—

That body has the world as its locus because it is a body; and that world is produced from the *tattvas* because it is a world, just like [the worlds] commonly accepted [as such]. Thus, since the establishment of both the *tattvas* and the worlds is possible, there is no possibility of a different meaning [for the reason] due to *māyā*, because the infinite bodies and so forth are produced solely by the totality of the effects of *māyā*.

Because [an accomplishment] would be impossible as an effect of *māyā* due to its being established [as something else]. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of having to postulate yet another body even in that case. Likewise, Ananteśa performs his work only while possessing conceptual knowledge (*savikalpaka-jñāna*), because he is an agent who employs others to act.

When the pure *śabda* is established through the inference "like a potter" by virtue of being the object of a conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka-jñāna*), the *bindu* is also established as its cause. Nor can it be argued that the state of being the object of that conceptual cognition belongs only to the impure *śabda*.

This is logical, because prior to the creation of the *kalās* and other categories, impure sound is impossible. Furthermore, its existence is established by its role as the provider of space for those residing on the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*), since the ether belonging to *māyā* cannot provide space there.
And it is said in the venerable Pauṣkara:
"Furthermore, what is the material cause (upādāna) consisting of Māyā and the rest that produces the bodies and senses of men?
It is the agitated [power] of that Agent which produces his own body, senses, and so forth."
One should understand that the drop (bindu) is that which is born from grasping;
moreover, the cognitions of human beings arise permeated by sound.
"For sounds can never arise without a cause;
that which is their cause, O Brahmins, is the Bindu, which possesses many functions."
Even *māyā* is not the material cause here, because it causes delusion by its own power; for that reason,
it is not the cause of the awakened body, soul, and instruments.
All those who abide in the pure path are awakened by the splendor of Śiva;
even though they possess bodies, senses, and so forth, they are not unawakened among them.
Furthermore, since all individuals are devoid of karma on the pure path,
how can illusion, having undergone transformation, follow the course of karma?
O twice-born ones, there must be a material cause for those bodies, senses, and so forth;
therefore, the cause of this pure path is indeed its own conforming reflection.
O best of the twice-born, let this pure [element] called Kuṇḍalinī be accepted;
and that Kuṇḍalinī is the power (śakti) of Śambhu, pure yet insentient in nature.
She does not abide through identity, but rather exists within the embrace [of Śiva];
for this Kuṇḍalinī does not abide in identity with Śiva, the agent.
Because it is the material cause, just as clay is in the case of a potter. Thus [it is said].

(Pau Bindu Pa Ślo 6–12) 19) Nor is Śiva’s power alone the material cause here, because [the world] has consciousness as its nature (*cidrūpa*). Indeed, transformation (*pariṇāma*) belongs to that which is insentient (*acit*). [Objection: Let it then be a mere illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) of consciousness; and thus, Śiva’s power alone [would appear] in those various forms.

If it is argued that [the world] is an illusory manifestation (*vivarta*), that cannot be so; for if that were the case, it would follow that the entire collection of effects is false. Nor is this a desirable consequence, because it is untenable for the world—established by all means of valid cognition—to be of such a nature. And it has been stated in that very same place:
In this case, power is not the material cause because it is of the nature of consciousness, just like Śiva;
transformation is said to belong to that which is non-conscious, and it is not possible for that which is of the nature of consciousness.
"If consciousness alone were intended as the transformation, then there would be an absence of effects;
how then could the world, which is established by all means of valid cognition, be a transformation of consciousness?"
(Pau-bindu-pa, verses 4–5) 20) Here, the function of sound (*śabdavṛtti*) is fourfold: *sūkṣmā*, *paśyantī*, *madhyamā*, and *vaikharī*.
Among these, *sūkṣmā* is speech that has knowledge alone as its locus and which illuminates the general nature of objects.

Speech that is incapable of conveying specific distinctions of phonemes and meanings, like the undifferentiated color within the yolk of a peacock's egg, is *paśyantī*. That same speech, when the phonemes have ascended into the intellect (*buddhi*), endowed with their specific sequence, and not yet come within the range of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), is *madhyamā*. It becomes manifest through the activity of the vital breath (*prāṇavṛtti*).

That very [speech] which is capable of making known the specific objects perceivable by the ear is *vaikharī*. In this context, *sūkṣmā* should be seen as the cause of *paśyantī*, *paśyantī* of *madhyamā*, and *madhyamā* of *vaikharī*. These modes of activity (*vṛttayaḥ*) consist of the cognitions (*pratyayātmikāḥ*) of the individual souls (*aṇūnām*). Among these, three exist only within.

[Some] are situated [within]; another is situated outside. And these sounds are subtle in the pure path (śuddhādhvan), gross in the mixed path (miśrādhvan), and grosser still in the impure path (aśuddhādhvan).
21) It is stated in that very same work:
"Those sounds are also fourfold, according to the divisions beginning with Vaikharī:
Vaikharī, that which is called Madhyamā, Paśyantī, and the one designated as Sūkṣmā."
Vaikharī is the object of the sense of hearing; it consists of the apprehension of gross phonemes and, when the breath is directed toward the points of articulation, it is beneficial to the speaker.

This speech, called Madhyamā, is the verbal expression of an object preceded by the mental synthesis of phonemes; it transcends the activity of the vital breath (prāṇavṛtti) and is intensely radiant within,
being devoid of the synthesis of the forms of phonemes.
Just as the fluid within a peacock’s egg contains all colors without distinction,
this Paśyantī speech should be known as the third [level] in the teaching of Śiva;
it is subtle, finds refuge solely in consciousness, and has all its powers withdrawn.
Madhyamā is the cause of Vaikharī, and Paśyantī is the cause with respect to Madhyamā;
the subtle [state], whose nature is free from conceptual construction (nirvikalpa), is the cause of Paśyantī.
These four modes of activity of the atoms consist of cognition;
three remain within, while the other is situated outside.
From cowherds, women, and children, down to the barbarians who speak vernacular tongues,
and even to the beings dwelling within the water, they constantly utter those words.
There is no bondage greater than these, nor any liberation other than freedom from them;
for that [bondage] is inseparable from their cessation, as it obstructs both perception and action.
Those persons do not consider themselves as distinct from those [aggregates] anywhere;
rather, the notion that "I am suffering" or "I am happy" is merely struck by words.
"The words on the path of purity are subtle; those situated on the mixed path are gross;
and those words on the impure path are always exceedingly gross."
(Pau bindu pa ślo 20–30) 22) Furthermore, the establishment of the *bindu* is also due to its being the cause of the *kalās*, such as *nivṛtti* and the rest. And it is said therein:
"And there are other functions of the *bindu*, consisting of the *kalās* beginning with *nivṛtti*."
Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and likewise Śānti.
These five, beginning with Śāntyātītā, reside previously on the pure path;
they are mixed in the impure path, established as the supports for the principles (tattva) and so forth.
"The *kalās* should be known as having the nature of objects (*vastu*), while those proclaimed by others [the *tattvas*] have the nature of sound (*śabda*).
This *bindu*, however, consists of both sound and object; it does not consist of either one alone. Thus it is said.
(Pau bindu, verses 30–32) 23) Here, the five principles (*tattva*) known as Śiva, Śakti, Sadāśiva, Īśvara, and Śuddhavidyā are originated from the *bindu*. And it is said in that very same [text]:
"And its function, which consists of the principles (tattvas), is established as fourfold:
the Śiva-principle, that called Sadeśa, the Īśa-principle, and likewise that named Vidyā."

(Pau bindu pa ślo 33) 24) Therein, within the Śiva-tattva, is the function of speech known as *sūkṣmā*. It is precisely here that the worlds (*bhuvana*) of the *śāntyatīta* [state] are situated. And it has been said:
For the awakening of the atoms [of consciousness] through conceptualization and for the establishment of the principles,
Śiva created the five kalās, the five principles, the worlds, and the mantras and so forth.
"Beyond Śānti, the Śiva-tattva formerly became the support of the worlds. Thus [it is said].

25) And because this [tattva] is presided over by Śiva, it is designated as the Śiva-tattva. The Śakti-tattva is a modification (vikāra) of the Śiva-tattva. It is precisely here that the function of speech known as Paśyantī and the kalās, beginning with Nivṛtti, reside. And because this [tattva] is the locus of Śiva and Śakti, it is denoted by the term Śakti-tattva.

The Sadāśiva-tattva is a modification of the Śakti-tattva. This very [tattva] is the substratum of the speech designated as Madhyamā. Likewise, it is the cause of the bodies, worlds, and so forth, for those who possess the liberation of Sāmīpya (proximity) and others, as well as for the Praṇavas and other causes of the various divisions of the Kāmika and other Tantras. It is a modification of the Īśvara-tattva.

The reality of Vidyā (vidyā-tattva). This alone is the substratum for the function of speech known as Vaikharī. Likewise, it is the producer of the bodies, worlds, and so forth, of the seventy million mantras and the queens of Vidyā that serve as instruments.
And it is said in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
"Bhṛguṇī, Brahmavetālī, Sthāṇumatī, Ambikā, Parā,
Rūpiṇī, Nandinī, and Jvālā— these seven are the lords of the seven arbudas."
The Vidyārājñīs are fully described as those praised by Rudra within the Vidyā;
above them stands the radiant and glorious Lord, the Sovereign of Vidyās.
Followed by the eightfold assembly of Rudras permeated by the consciousness of the Lord of Mantras,
they are Ucchuṣmas, Ambaras, Caṇḍas, and those who go to the station of Great Prowess.
The Rudras, the Gaṇas, the guardians of the quarters, and the masters of the scriptures are established there;
they, beginning with Ananta, have indeed been mentioned by name.

And in their own form, O Brahmins, they previously [appeared] in connection with the questions; [they were] Sadāśiva, whose limbs are pure and who is equipped with the entire array of ornaments and attributes.

Lord Sadāśiva resides in the Bindu; the lords of the Kalās, beginning with Nivṛtti, reside in the Nāda; Dhvani resides in the Pati within Śakti; and he who is the best among all possessors of power resides in Śakti.
"The womb of the universe is Vāgīśā; beyond her are the Lords, and beyond them is Śiva. Thus [it is said].
(From Mṛgendra-prabhṛti, Chapter 13, Verses 157–162) 27) Others, however, state that the defining characteristic of all five [tattvas] is their being mediated by Śiva.
The *tattva* presided over by the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) who is endowed with pure knowledge is the *śivatattva*.
The principle of Śakti is presided over by that which is endowed with mere action.
The principle of Sadāśiva is presided over by that which possesses both [action and knowledge] in equal measure.
The principle of Īśvara is presided over by that which possesses predominant action. [The principle of Śuddhavidyā is presided over by that which possesses predominant knowledge.]

Regarding the phrase "the reality of knowledge" (*vidyā-tattva*): some, however, assert that even the pentad of principles beginning with Śiva is directly the effect of the *bindu*. Furthermore, this [set of principles] beginning with the principle of Śiva is an effect in the form of a function (*vṛtti*) of Śiva as qualified by the *bindu* and so forth; it is not a transformation (*pariṇāma*), because [the cause] is interwoven throughout everything.
Because there is no abandonment of the prior state, neither the theory of origination (*ārambhavāda*) nor the theory of aggregation (*puñjavāda*) is applicable here.

For it is determined that Śiva alone is the cause; and this effect, which consists of functional manifestation (*vṛtti*), exists as nothing other than the nature of the cause. Even if it were to exist as an effect, [it would still be the cause].
This is because it is impossible for there to be a dissolution (*pralaya*) consisting in the destruction or departure of the states (*avasthā*) of the *tattvas*.

However, the designation "tattva" is not contradicted, as they persist until the end of the kalpa (*ākalpāvasthāyitayā*). Furthermore, this pure path (*śuddhādhvan*) is not a cause of bondage, due to the absence of any connection with karma (*karmānvayābhāvāt*).

28) But surely, how can there be manifold enjoyment for those who abide in the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*), given the absence of karma as its cause? Or how can there be the arising of knowledge, given the absence of *kalā* as its cause?
Or how can there be orientation toward objects, given the absence of *vidyā* as its cause? And how...

Why is there attachment to sense objects? Because of the absence of passion (*rāga*). Or how is there a limitation on the quantity of enjoyments? Because of the absence of time (*kāla*). And how is there a fixed determination of the specific enjoyer? Because of the absence of necessity (*niyati*). It is replied:
first of all, there exist in the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*) the principles (*tattva*) beginning with *kalā* and ending with *bindu*.

[These include] the body, the instruments [of perception], the worlds, and enjoyments. In that regard, although there is no karma—which is the cause for the variety of enjoyments—nevertheless, a diverse enjoyment is possible by virtue of the ripening of impurity (*mala*). To illustrate:
he whose ripening of impurity is most intense experiences enjoyment in the state called *sādhākhya*; whereas he whose...

However, that [agency] is even more predominant in the principle of Īśvara and the principle of Vidyā. Therefore, in this context, karma is not the cause of experience; rather, it is solely the will of Īśvara. Nor is there partiality or cruelty on the part of Śiva here, because there is an absence of experience consisting of suffering. Consequently, on the Pure Path (śuddhādhvan), [liberation] depends upon the ripening of impurity (mala).
Enjoyment is indeed of the nature of bliss.
And it is said in the venerable Pauṣkara:
"Furthermore, because they lack connection with karma, the pure paths are not causes of bondage."
Likewise:
"This path is designated as the object of enjoyment; enjoyment consists in that which is established through passion and the other [afflictions]."
In this regard, O Maheśvara, how can there be enjoyment in the absence of those [objects]?
Īśvara said:
"O best of the twice-born, here too there exist principles (tattvas) headed by Kalā, just as they do below; however, in this case, O excellent brahmins, they are pure and belong to the Bindu."
Likewise: "These principles are pure for the great-souled individual souls of Rudra. (Pauṣkarabindu, verse 56–57)
And they were large, inlaid with various garlands of cities.

"With divine splendors, great wonders, and enjoyments free from suffering, as well as with bodies, objects of enjoyment, sense faculties, and so forth; yet [others] are devoid of these and are lowly. Thus it is said.
Likewise: "On the path of purity, there is great enjoyment; it is taught that karma does not exist. (Pau Paśupata Śloka 34–35)
O Lord, how is it that the experience of those who abide within that [universe] is likewise diverse?
Īśvara says:
"In the pure path, karma is not the cause of the variety of experiences;
rather, it is the diverse ripening of impurity that is the cause here."
He whose [karma] is most intense has its fruition in the principle of experience (bhogatattva) and is thus an enjoyer of experiences;
the other, however, becomes an enjoyer of experiences within the principles known as Īśvara and Vidyā.
"O best of Brahmins, what is the use of ritual action here, where enjoyment according to one's desire is sought? Thus [it is said].
And likewise:
"In this world, there is never any cruelty on the part of Śambhu."
"For one who yokes [beings] to sufferings is merciless both here and in the next world;
however, on the pure path, he is essentially blissful, and such is remembered as true enjoyment."
And this collection of pure principles is designated as the "impelling section" (*preraka-kāṇḍa*) for the *pralayākalas* and *sakalas*.

30) Now *māyā* is defined. It is etymologically derived as follows: it is called *māyā* because it "measures" (*mayati*) or "gives" (*dadāti*) the universe, or because the universe "measures itself" (*māti*) or "comes" (*āyāti*) into it. As it is stated in the *Pauṣkara*:
"The entire universe is measured (*mayati*) from this; therefore it is designated as *māyā*."
Elsewhere [it is said]: "That in which the world is contained during sleep, or from which it departs after being created, is therefore [Māyā]. (Pau Mā Pa Ślo 1)
"Therefore, it is called 'māyā' (illusion); the reality has been thus declared by the most excellent gurus. Thus [it is said].

This [māyā] is also the insentient power of the Lord that serves as the material cause (*upādāna*) for the entire range of effects beginning with the subtle elements (*kalā*) and ending with the earth; it is one, because there is no evidence for its multiplicity; it is eternal, because it is the root cause; and it is not non-eternal, because if it were non-eternal, it would follow that at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*), actions (*karman*) would be left without a substratum. Nor is it...

The *bindu* is its substratum, because action belongs to it. Nor is it the selves (*ātman*), for that would entail the consequence of their being insentient. And it is all-pervasive, because effects are perceived everywhere.
As it is said in the *Pauṣkara*:
"Perpetual, unitary, all-pervasive, having the nature of a real entity, the substratum of action, and inauspicious. Thus [it is said].
And in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
"That one, non-auspicious seed of the world possesses manifold powers."
It is co-operative, persists until the end of the term of authority, is all-pervasive, and is imperishable.
By whatever causal property of the world a creator is inferred, by that same [property] there must also be a material cause; for a cloth does not exist without threads.
That [cause] must indeed be insentient, because its effects are observed to be insentient.
During the state of dissolution, the effects, which exist in the form of potencies, reside within that [insentient cause].
"In the modification, the forms of the individual entities operate for the sake of accomplishing the purpose. Thus [it is said].
Likewise, in the Pauṣkara:
"This [nature] is eternal because it is the cause of all effects; otherwise, [it would not be so]."
That [illusion] is not eternal, unlike a thread; therefore, even māyā is imperishable.
If this were considered impermanent, where would there be a stable foundation for karmas?
A single *bindu* is not the locus of karmas, because a *bindu* is preceded by karma.
"And they have no stability in the self, because the self would [otherwise] be insentient. Thus [it is said].

(From the *Pauṣkarāgama*, verses 27–29) 32) Furthermore, this [māyā] possesses manifold powers (*vicitraśaktitva*) by virtue of producing diverse effects; it is also delusive (*mohinī*) because it is the cause of the delusion of selfhood (*ātmabhrama*) with respect to what is not the self, such as the body and so forth. And she is [the source] of all the *sakala* [souls].
It is common, being the cause of the subtle and gross bodies and so forth of those whose bodies have dissolved during the cosmic dissolution (*pralaya*). And it is said in the *Pauṣkara*:
"O lords of sages, it is common to all the *sakala* [souls]."
At the dawn of the day, for the transmigrating atom whose body was dissolved during the dissolution, [the following occurs].
"Māyā is the cause of the body and so forth, which consist of both subtle and gross aspects. Thus [it is said].
(From *Pau mā pa*, verses 2–3) And this [consciousness] is of the nature of a real entity (*vasturūpā*), because it is the cause of the world which is itself of the nature of a real entity.
(Verse 33) Now, it may be objected that the world’s being of the nature of a real entity is unestablished.

Because the relationship between the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the objects of knowledge (*prameya*), and [the knower] is difficult to establish.
