To explain: it cannot first be perception (*pratyakṣa*); for the negation of other things, which consists of the distinction between the knower and so forth, lacks the status of being an object of perception that has a positive entity as its domain, such as in the case of "I know the jar. Therefore...

If there were an object of cognition existing as distinct from the cognizer, perception would not be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Since inference is also rooted in that [perception], it too is not a valid means of knowledge in this case.
Furthermore, scripture whose subject matter contradicts perception and the other means of knowledge has no authority regarding its own meaning, just like statements such as "rocks float."

Validity. Therefore, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) whatsoever for the existence of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*). Or, even if the existence of the means and objects of cognition were granted, what would be the relationship between the two? It cannot be a relationship characterized by identity (*tādātmya*); for if that were the case, [the same would apply] to that which produces dream-cognition.

It would follow that dream-objects are real; therefore, if the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is false, its underlying cause, *māyā*, must also be false. To this it is replied: There indeed exists perception whose object is a real cognizable entity. For instance:

In the doubt, "Is this a post or a person?", how could the perception arising after the negation of the alternative—"This is not a person; it is indeed a post"—not have that difference as its object? Nor is this [perception] erroneous due to being conceptual (*savikalpaka*), because there is no sublation (*bādha*). For indeed...

When a post is determined to be such by virtue of its crookedness, hollow interior, and other characteristics, its [status as a post] may at some time be sublated; however, there is no such absence of sublation in the case of a rope-snake and the like, because that [sublation] is established for all people. Furthermore, an error is possible there due to the similarity between the rope and the snake; but [such an error] is not possible for consciousness in the form of a jar and so forth.

In cognition, we do not perceive any similarity whatsoever. Furthermore, even if the object of knowledge (*prameya*) were the domain of non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka*), the establishment of the perception of difference remains intact; otherwise, for a person who has not grasped a difference, there could not arise the subsequent conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*) with a differentiated object, such as "This Devadatta is a Brahmin."

How could it arise? Furthermore, is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that has the falsity of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) as its object itself false or not? In the first case, the reality of the phenomenal world is established. In the second case, however, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of the reason for falsity [since the cognition itself would be real]. Therefore, the reality of the phenomenal world is established. Nor [is there a problem] regarding the knowledge and the object of knowledge...
There is no impossibility of a relationship, because the relationship consisting of the state of being the object and the subject exists.
Therefore, since the entire world is real, it is established that the *māyā* which is its root is also real.
35) This has been stated in the venerable Pauṣkara:
"The phenomenal world (prapañca) is certainly not of the nature of a real entity (vastu), because of the absence of means of valid cognition (pramāṇa),
likewise because of the absence of objects of cognition (prameya), and also because of the absence of their relationship."
This phenomenal world (prapañca), consisting of the distinctions between the knower and so forth, is not within the range of the senses;
for perception is the establisher of objects, not their negator.
Without negation, difference never exists;
therefore, perception is not a means of establishing the reality of the phenomenal world.
Since pervasion is preceded by that [perception], even inference is not a valid means of knowledge;
nor is scripture a valid means of knowledge regarding an object contradicted by perception and the like.
Therefore, the non-existence of the object of cognition is also established from the non-existence of the means of cognition;
let there be the means of cognition and the object of cognition, but the relationship between the two is difficult to establish.
First of all, the connection between cognition and the jar cannot be characterized as identity;
for if it were, the jar would become internal because cognition is internal.
If an object were real even in a dream, it would possess the nature of both the produced and the producer;
likewise, if the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) were unreal, how could *māyā* be a real entity?
There exists an ancient means of valid cognition for the existence of the manifold world;
first of all, perception is the means of valid cognition regarding objects that have differentiation as their domain.
In the doubt, "Is it a post or a person?", the cognition "It is indeed a post,
not a person"— which is of a discriminative nature— is seen to arise directly from the senses.
"One might argue that this [perception] is erroneous because it involves conceptual construction, like the [misapprehension of a] rope;
however, for everyone and at all times, the jar is accepted as being simply the jar, unimpaired."
The rope is never actually such that it appears as a snake to some men while appearing as a garland to others; yet this is not the case with jars, pots, and the like.
Furthermore, how can an error arise here through the similarity between a snake and a rope?
What commonality exists between consciousness and the perception of objects such as jars?
Even when there is non-conceptual sensory cognition, a cognition characterized by differentiation persists;
otherwise, a subsequent consciousness distinct [from it] would not arise.
For one who has not grasped the distinction between objects, it is like [the cognition] of specific features such as their names;
furthermore, by whatever means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) the non-existence of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is asserted, [that same means would apply].
Consider whether that [scripture] is a valid means of knowledge or not;
for if it is a valid means of knowledge, the phenomenal world exists, since it is contained within it.
If it were invalid, then the world would all the more be of a positive nature;
for there exists a relationship between knowledge and the jar, characterized by that of the knower and the known.
Thus, how could the universe, which consists of real entities, be born from that which is unreal?
Therefore, Māyā, whose nature is substantial, exists as the cause of the universe.

(From the Pauṣkarāgama, Mālinīvijayottara, verses 10–26) 36) As for the proof of its existence: the collection of principles beginning with *kalā* and ending with the earth must have dissolved without distinction into some cause, since it is a single effect.

The following inferences [are established]: because they are differentiated, [the elements] are like the sprouts and leaves from a seed; the primordial matter (kalā) and so forth possess a material cause (upādāna), because they are effects, like a jar; and the karma existing at the time of dissolution rests upon something, because it is a latent impression (saṃskāra), like that which is commonly accepted. Nor is there the fallacy of proving what is already established (arthāntaratva) by means of "time" (kāla), because...
Because, according to the method to be explained, it is subject to destruction and therefore cannot serve as a substratum at that time.

(37) Now, one might object: "If karma is established, then Māyā is established by virtue of being its substratum; but what is the proof for the existence of that [karma]? It is said in reply: The experience of pleasure and pain by living beings must depend upon something.
Because this [destruction] is non-inherent, like color produced by baking;

[and] rites such as *iṣṭāpūrta* possess an operation existing at the moment immediately preceding the production of the fruit, because—while having perished prior to that production—they are its generator, like agriculture, medicine, and so forth. Nor can it be argued that the grace of God alone is the operation.
This is logical; for since that [agency] is unimpeded and productive of results, it would follow that the result must arise immediately. And it is said in the Pauṣkara:
"While the state of being an enjoyer is indistinguishable [for all], some enjoy [the fruits] in heaven."
For some, this [suffering] in the Avīci hell and similar realms would not be without cause.
O best of sages, it should be understood that karma is the cause in this matter;
for while both are equal in their cultivation, one person bestows the grain.
"O twice-born ones, there is nothing else that serves as the cause for his action. Thus [it is said].

(From *Pau mā pa*, verses 31–33) 38) Nor can it be said that [bondage] is produced by *prakṛti*; for since *prakṛti* is that which is to be experienced (*bhogya*), it is incapable of being the experiencer (*bhojaka*). Now, one might object: "But action (*karman*) is indeed of the nature of the qualities of the intellect (*buddhi-dharma*), which is itself derived from *prakṛti*."

If it is argued that [the self] is the object of enjoyment by virtue of being the nature of existence (*bhāva*), and the enjoyer by virtue of being the nature of action (*karman*), [we reply that this is not so], because that which consists of the attributes of the intellect (*buddhi*) is merely of the nature of existence. Furthermore, since there is no equilibrium among those [attributes], there must be some impelling agent; yet, [the self] cannot be its own [impeller].
It must be stated that [the self] is the instigator; for there is a contradiction in an action being directed toward oneself. Thus it is said in the Pauṣkara:

"And here, primordial nature (prakṛti) is not the cause, because of the contradiction in its being the object of enjoyment. That which is the object of enjoyment and that which is the enjoyer cannot be one; therefore, another factor, namely karma, should be accepted."

If it is your view that the transformation of primordial nature (prakṛti) which consists of the eight categories belonging to the intellect (bauddha) is of the nature of karma, while the other [transformation] is that which is to be experienced (bhogya).
That too is essence-less, because things consist of conditions;
and those various conditions are always observed within atoms.
"O elder brothers, there can be no equality there for any reason whatsoever;
nor can things themselves be the causes for their own diversity, because that would lead to an infinite regress. Thus it is said.

(pau mā pa ślo 33–37) 39) And this action (*karman*) is threefold, due to the distinction between the causes consisting of mind, speech, and body. Among these, that produced by the mind takes the form of meditating upon a desired deity, the desire to seize another's wife, and so forth. That which is vocal (*vācika*)...

[The cause] consists of forms such as the recitation of mantras and the disparagement of others; the bodily [cause] consists of forms such as the worship of deities and approaching those who should not be approached. Likewise, because of that threefold causality, the effect of the threefold karma—happiness, suffering, and so forth—is also threefold, distinguished as internal and so on. Among these, there is the clarity or agitation of the mind and so forth.
Internal [suffering]; that produced by sandalwood ointment, sword-strokes, and so forth is external (ādhibhautika);

that produced by desired or undesired rain, heat, and so forth is celestial (ādhidaivika). Likewise, action (karman) is fivefold, according to the division into worldly, Vedic, internal, pertaining to the path, and pertaining to mantras. Among these:

The worldly [karma] is that which, produced by the construction of ponds, wells, and the like, or by the eating of forbidden food and so forth, generates experience within the limits of the path pervaded by the *nivṛtti-kalā* (the power of cessation), as well as the body and other factors that serve as its causes.
[The trans-worldly karma] is that produced by the performance of sacrifices such as the *jyotiṣṭoma*.

The Vaidika [experience] arises from ritual action (*pratiṣṭhā*) and generates enjoyment extending up to the path pervaded by the *kalā* of ritual action (*pratiṣṭhā-kalā*). The Ādhyātmika [experience] arises from dispassion (*vairāgya*) and so forth, and generates enjoyment extending up to the path pervaded by the *kalā* of knowledge (*vidyā-kalā*).

The Ādhimārgika [experience] arises from yoga and generates enjoyment extending up to the path pervaded by the *kalā* of peace (*śānti-kalā*). The [experience] arising from higher consciousness (*vijñāna*)...
The mantra-karma generates experience up to the limit of the path pervaded by the kalā beyond peace (śāntyatīta).
This fivefold karma is a bond (pāśa) because it is the cause of worldly pleasure, pain, and so forth.
The various [entities] that have arisen, both directly and indirectly, from Māyā—which is established as having this karma as its substratum—[are the objects of bondage].

The thirty-one principles (tattvas) begin with *kala*. Among them, *kāla* (time) is the cause of *kalana*, which consists of the delimitation of the extent of experience; it is the first modification of *māyā*, characterized as the specific perception of units such as *lava* and *truṭi*.
Some, however, say that *kala* itself is the first modification. This [time] is both the time of creation (*sṛṣṭikāla*) and the time of maintenance (*sthitikāla*).
And the time of withdrawal; thus it is threefold.

40) [Objection: But how can this [Time] be an effect? [Response: Because, while being one, it is beginningless due to its producing an endless stream of effects. Nor is the qualification unestablished; for when Time is established by a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) aided by parsimony (*lāghava*), since there is no evidence for its plurality, its unity is also established. For this very reason, [even if] it were insentient (*jaḍatva*),...
Nor is it correct to argue that its status as an effect is inferred from its plurality; for the subject of the inference is unestablished.

Furthermore, one must not claim that distinctions such as "prior" and "subsequent" are experienced in time itself; since that which was prior at one time is the very same thing that is subsequent at another, such distinctions necessarily depend upon external conditions (*upādhi*).

"Therefore, time is indeed beginningless"—do not say so; for if the distinctions of time were merely adventitious (*aupādhika*), then since all those respective effects could be accounted for by the adventitious factors alone, it would follow that time itself is unestablished. Furthermore, if time were a single entity, it would serve as the substratum and thus be the cause of all effects; consequently, [the distinction between effects] would have to be attributed to the exclusion of specific times.

Furthermore, it would follow that the distinction between specific effects could not be accounted for; and because there is no limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) to account for the divisions of moments, instants, and so forth. Therefore, the distinction of time is indeed intrinsic. For this very reason, since it is insentient and manifold, it is subject to both arising and destruction.

41) [Objection: But in that case, how can there be permanence (*nityatva*) for the selves? If it is argued that this is because the meaning of the word "permanent" is simply existing at all times, we say no; for permanence is possible for the selves because the meaning of that term is precisely the absence of limitation by time (*kālāvaccheda*). As it is stated in the *Pauṣkara*:
Then, time impels the person who has been set in motion by the three principles beginning with *kalā*,
measuring him by means of its own functions such as *lava* and *truṭi*.
And since those very actions of the body belonging to the world of Bhuvana are then the cause of the past,
present, and future functions, [they are the means].
That should be understood as Time, which produces for men the objects of enjoyment. Thus [it is said].
Likewise: "Some maintain that Time is the one, all-pervading, eternal Lord. (Pauṣkarapañcārthapāśupataśāstra, verses 47–49)
O Blessed One, you should explain why it is not accepted here in that manner.
The Lord [says]:
"If time were held to be one, it would not be distinct from action;
for action, by its very nature, possesses no such form as 'past' and so forth."
If that very [past time] were admitted as the time for that [present action], then it would follow,
O Lords of Munis, that the present and other categories of objects [would be past].
"The establishment [of time] occurs through distinct divisions such as the present and so forth;
therefore, this time is not one, but rather possesses the activity of infinite selves. Thus it is said.
Likewise:
"Because it is insentient and manifold, this [self] is not eternal, just like a jar."
"The omnipresence of that which is impermanent is refuted. Thus [it is said].
The Sages said:
Time has been declared to be impermanent; how then can there be permanence for the selves?
O Lord, eternity consists in the state of persisting at all times; it is just like that.
Īśvara says:
"Because it is devoid of limitation by time, its eternity exists like that of time itself;
for there is no eternity of time, since a temporal entity cannot be established [without itself being limited by time]."

(From Pauṣkarapañcārthabhāṣya, verses 64–65) 42) Nor should it be argued that because time itself is withdrawn during the reabsorption of the Great Object (*mahārthasaṃhāra*), there must be a dependence on another period of time even then; for that is established by the will of the Lord (*īśvara*) alone. As it is said in that very [text]:
The Sages said:
Since time is established as perishable by virtue of its arising from *māyā*,
how can there be a restriction by time regarding the withdrawal of the Great Object (*mahārtha*)?
The Lord establishes a rule for the withdrawal [of the universe] solely by His own will;
therefore, dependence upon time is not accepted regarding the withdrawal of activity.
"Even during the dissolution, the Blessed One constantly bestows grace, creates, protects, destroys, and conceals, without depending on time."

(From Pauṣkarapañcārthabhāṣya, verses 68, 70–71) 43) Space (*dik*) cannot be a separate reality (*tattvāntara*); for there is no necessity for it within the categories of the impeller (*preraka*), the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*), and the object of enjoyment (*bhogya*). Now, does this mean that space does not exist at all? No; rather, those [spaces]...

Determined by limiting adjuncts such as the sun and so forth, these are accepted as both common with respect to each individual object and uncommon for the sake of establishing the order of merit and demerit.

44) *Niyati* (destiny) is the reality that is the cause of restriction (*niyamana*). This is the second transformation of *māyā*. Restriction, moreover, consists of the connection of the doer of evil deeds with their fruit, the exclusion of the fruit of good deeds from one who did not perform them, and [the determination] of that body and so forth.
And it is the non-production of experiences associated with another person. This very effect is the proof for the principle of necessity (*niyatitattva*).

For in the absence of the principle of necessity, no one would experience the fruit of their own misdeeds, and another might experience the fruit of the merit performed by someone else; [this would apply even to] the body of Yajñadatta.
It would produce the experience of Devadatta.

(45) But surely, since there is a rule that an evil deed must produce its fruit, its non-experience is indeed impossible; for one does not postulate a separate entity [to prevent the fruit] merely to avoid the contingency that an effect might fail to arise when the causal totality (*sāmagrī*) is present. Nor...

The rule that an evil deed necessarily produces its fruit is unproven, for the very scripture that prohibits it serves as the authority in this regard. Likewise, since even a good deed possesses the inherent capacity to yield a fruit only for the agent, the experience of that fruit by one who did not perform the act is not a possibility. Therefore, there is no other distinct principle [involved].

To prevent that [undesirable consequence], it must be accepted [that the action belongs to the agent]. For one does not accept a distinct ontological principle (*tattvāntara*) merely to prevent water from being a burner. Nor is it unestablished that its status as a producer (*janakatva*) pertains only to the fruit residing in the agent;

for this is established by the middle-voice (*ātmanepada*) affix prescribed for actions whose fruits accrue to the agent, according to the principle: "The agent [is the locus of the fruit] because the scripture would otherwise be purposeless" (*kartā śāstrārthavattvāt*).

This is established by such reasoning as found in *Brahma-sūtra* 2.3.33, and because otherwise there would follow the consequence that ritual performance (*anuṣṭhāna*) is fruitless. Likewise, the rule that even the body produces its respective experiences only by virtue of being acquired through specific karmas is thus logically consistent; therefore, the principle of necessity (*niyatitattva*) is not established even on the basis of that [the body].
"Therefore, since the restriction is established otherwise, one should not accept that the restriction exists for the sake of that [the agent]," so it is argued.

This is not so; for even though there is a restriction that evil action produces a result, there is no restriction that the agent must experience that result, because that is possible even through the connection of the result with someone else. The same applies to good action as well.

The scripture has established merely that [an action] produces a result, but not that it brings about a connection between the agent and the result. If it is argued that the connection of the result with the agent is established by means of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) and so forth—this is true; for this very reason, [the scripture establishes] its causality.

The reality of necessity (*niyatitattva*) is that which is to be resorted to. Moreover, it is not karma alone that is the producer even in that case; for, just as in the case of agriculture and the like with respect to the harvest, karma’s function is fulfilled solely by the production of the nature of the fruit.
For the sake of bringing about a connection with a specific person, necessity (*niyati*) must also be relied upon, just as a royal decree or the like is required [to assign a specific outcome].
In this way, although the body is acquired through various specific karmas, a fixed rule does not hold in the absence of *niyati* (the principle of necessity).
This is because, in the absence of a king’s command, we observe that even crops and the like acquired through various acts of cultivation do not invariably produce their respective enjoyments.
If it is argued that all such regulation occurs solely through the power of Śiva, and thus *niyati* is redundant, we say no.

Since that [nature] produces those respective effects only through its association with their respective determined causes, it is impossible for it to produce them in isolation; therefore, the principle of necessity (*niyati-tattva*) must be admitted for the sake of this restriction.

46) [Objection: Granted that the principle of necessity (*niyatitattva*)—which is uncommon and has entered into the transportive body (*ātivāhika-śarīra*)—exists as a cause of regulation; however, since the common substratum of the worlds and so forth does not possess that causality, how can it be called the "principle of necessity"? Or, even if it exists, what is the proof for its existence? [Reply: This is not so.

Because, by virtue of belonging to that same class, it also produces restriction; however, for its actual existence, scripture alone is the authority. As it is said in the venerable Pauṣkara: "Now, O best of sages, hear about Niyati (the principle of necessity) in brief."
For one who is intent upon enjoyment through the functions of the arts, sciences, and so forth.
When there is the removal of the fruits of accumulated karmas,
this Niyati (the principle of necessity) proceeds toward their destruction, according to the teaching of Śiva.
O twice-born ones, it does not proceed according to such a fixed rule for the impurities known as *mala*, *māyā*, and *karman*; rather, it proceeds only for the person who is joined with them.
Even if he is unwilling, she forcibly compels him toward enjoyments;
yet she does so only with those acquired by himself, never with those acquired by others.
If she did not exist, others would enjoy what has been acquired by others;
just as bandits enjoy what has been acquired by others in defiance of the king's command,
so too does she [the *adṛṣṭa*] destroy such inconsistency.
By this [means], that which consists of the body, the senses, and so forth, is necessarily [transformed].
Now, if it is argued that the power which is Śāṅkarī herself must be the regulator, that is true;
however, she is not so by her own nature, but rather through the mediation of Niyati.
If that very destiny were the cause by which they would be liberated through that connection,
then karma would not be able to connect men with their own fruits.
"Because it is an action, like agriculture; therefore, in this case, action is not the determining factor."

(From Pauṣkarapañcārthapaddhati, verses 79–87) 47) *Kalā* is the principle (*tattva*) that manifests the consciousness whose nature consists of the powers of vision (*dṛk*) and action (*kriyā*) belonging to the Self (*ātman*).
Manifestation is the cessation of the veil that obscures [consciousness]. Furthermore, this [cessation] does not entail the destruction of the essential nature of the veiler.
But is it by the destruction of the power of concealment that the cessation of the power qualified by it occurs?
Or is it an incapacity for action, according to the analogy of water and *śaivāla* moss? As for the proof of its existence:
the cessation of that which conceals consciousness must depend on some uncommon factor, because it is an effect.
"Like the *saṃmata* [scripture]," such is the inference. Since the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) and so forth are common [to all], there is no deviation of the subject (*arthāntaratva*) by means of them.
And this [scripture] effects the partial removal of impurity in persons according to their karma. As it has been said:
Consciousness, consisting of the nature of knowing and acting, is the power of the Self;
it is manifested by a portion [of that power], for it is indeed obscured by that very same [power].

"The *kalā* does not manifest the consciousness of the individual soul (*aṇu*) in its entirety; rather, according to [the soul's] karma, it manifests it through a single portion of its function. Thus [it is said].
48) [Objection: Let it be that the manifestation of the powers of vision and action occurs through effort (*yatna*), which is a quality of the intellect (*buddhi*);

for even you must admit that effort possesses the capacity to manifest. Otherwise, there would be a manifestation of vision and action even by a mere fraction [of time], without any effort directed toward the lump of clay and so forth.
If it is argued that this would result in the potter and others being the creators of the jar and so forth, we say no;
for since [the activity] occurs only after the manifestation of the powers of knowledge and action, it cannot logically function as a manifestor. To explain:
the effort directed toward a lump of clay and the like is preceded by a cognition directed toward that same clay and the like. And that [cognition]...

By means of mental activity (*manovyāpāra*). That [activity] too depends upon a substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) within its sphere of operation. And this substratum consists in the form of the manifested powers of vision and action (*dṛkkriyāśakti*). Nor can that manifestation occur through effort (*yatna*), because effort itself is dependent upon mental activity, which in turn is dependent upon manifestation. Therefore, [effort must reside] elsewhere.

Even though the mind's initial activity and so forth also manifest the powers of vision and action, it must be admitted that the manifestation of the powers of vision and action belongs to *kalā* alone. Therefore,
the principle of *kalā-tattva* must be accepted for the manifestation of the powers of vision and action.
49) *Vidyā* is that principle which impels persons whose consciousness is intensified by *kalā* toward sense objects.

This is established by the inference: "Intellect (*buddhi*) is a cognition accompanied by an instrument, because it is an action, like [the cognition of] what is agreed upon. Thus it is stated in the venerable *Pauṣkara*:
In the teaching of Śiva, that which is the instrument for the observation of the action characterized by the intellect— the agent being *kalā*— is *vidyā*.
For the intellect (*buddhi*) is an object of action because it is graspable, like a pot or a wall;
just as form and other objects are seen to be graspable only in dependence upon their respective instruments, so too,
once an object has been determined in succession by the eyes and the other senses, [it is grasped by the intellect].
"A person perceives that [reality] through knowledge by means of cognitions whose objects have been ascertained. Thus [it is said].

(From Pauṣkarapañcāśikā, verses 9–11) 50) Nor is there a difference in object by means of the mind (*manas*), because [the mind's activity] is dependent upon the certainty that is itself dependent on the operation of that [intellect]. And because the operation of the intellect is dependent upon the self-awareness of the intellect. Therefore, of the self-awareness of the intellect...

Because it exists prior to the mental operation (*manovyāpāra*), the mind is not its producer therein; for the mind is established as having only volition (*saṅkalpa*) and so forth as its cause. Although the manifestation of the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) necessarily requires the illumination of the intellect (*buddhi*) as its cause, nevertheless—
In the manifestation of the power of consciousness (cit-śakti) within the scope of the senses and other factors conducive to the illumination of the intellect, knowledge alone is the cause.
51) *Rāga* (attachment) is the principle that colors the objects [of experience]. As it is stated in the venerable *Pauṣkara*:
"From *kalā* arises *rāga*, for the immediate engagement of persons;
for no individual soul (*aṇu*) is ever seen enjoying anything without desiring it."
"Because of passion, due to attachment to objects of enjoyment, one is therefore entitled to enjoy those objects of enjoyment. Thus [it is said].
And this [power] is established as that which manifests the power of will (*icchāśakti*) conducive to the initial operations of the senses and so forth.
Otherwise, although the property of the intellect (*buddhidharma*) manifests attachment, it is the principle of passion (*rāgatattva*) alone that is the manifestor therein;
likewise, its existence should be understood through its being the cause of attachment as a property of the intellect.

52) But surely, in that case, it is the very cognition of [the object] as a means to pleasure and so forth that is the producer [of attachment]. Nor is it correct to say that attachment is not observed even when such a cognition exists in one who is dispassionate; for you yourself must admit that its non-arising in that person occurs because of his perception of the defects of the object and so forth. Otherwise, [your position would fail].
For even in your own view, since attachment arises there through the state of passion (*rāgatattva*), it cannot be remedied; moreover,
because it is illogical for the state of passion to be the cause of a desire directed toward a specific object,
it is more appropriate that the cognition of something as a means to pleasure and so forth is itself the cause.

Therefore, [the opponent argues that] attachment (*abhiṣaṅga*), which is a property of the intellect (*buddhi*), depends upon the beauty of the object and is not governed by the nature of passion (*rāga*); [we reply:

it is not so. For even an attachment to a specific object, though dependent on the beauty of the object, is—like a madder-dye or similar color—dependent on a general capacity for desire (*icchāśakti*), just as [the redness of a cloth] is dependent on the decoction of *triphalā*.
Because it depends on the manifestation residing in the passion.

53) The *puruṣatattva* is the principle that serves as the cause for the soul's natural state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*). This [state] is brought about by ignorance (*avidyā*) and the fivefold sheath beginning with *kalā*. Furthermore, this [principle] is the impeller (*bhojaka*) only for the *sakala* individual;
it is not so for the *vijñānākala* and *pralayākala*, because those two lack contact with *kalā* and the other [sheaths]. Nor is it...

It must be said that in this case, let the *kalā* and so forth alone be the efficient cause; what is the use of an intermediate separate principle (*tattvāntara*)? For since that [principle] has already been established as the producer of other effects, if it were the efficient cause here as well, there would be the undesirable consequence of a confusion of principles (*tattvasāṅkarya*). Furthermore, just as in the case of the *vijñānākala*, it would be impossible for the *sakala* (the bound soul) to be an enjoyer.
Nor is ignorance (*avidyā*) and the rest the determinant of manhood (*puṃstva*); for in the absence of *kalā* and the other categories, the agency of the person (*puruṣa*) would be impossible.

Therefore, one must admit a principle of manhood (*puṃstattva*) that is initiated by *kalā* and the rest, accompanied by primordial ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth, and which serves as the cause for primordial experience (*bhoga*).

And it is said in the venerable Pauṣkara: "The Puruṣa is proclaimed as being joined with the five coverings (kañcukas), intent upon enjoying Prakṛti, and conjoined with [the afflictions] beginning with ignorance."
Therefore, neither the Vijñānākala nor the Pralayakevala receives the designation "Puruṣa," because [only the latter] is devoid of ignorance and the other [afflictions].
Therefore, the entire atom alone receives the name "puruṣa" (spirit),
provided that the pentad beginning with *kalā* is indeed the instrumental cause for its state as a spirit.
In that case, the primordial nature (prakṛti) would not possess the status of being an enjoyer, just as it does not in the case of the *jñānākala*;
likewise, the individual soul (*puruṣa*) cannot be the instrumental cause for the mere existence of ignorance and the rest.
In the absence of the *kalās* and other factors, there being an absence of agency, how could there be an enjoyer?
That which consists of the *prakṛti*, ignorance (*avidyā*), and so forth, is traditionally held to be the impurity of masculinity (*puṃstva-mala*) in men.
"Pervaded by that [Prakṛti], the Puruṣa, enriched by the Kalās and other [categories], is designated as such. Thus it is said.

And the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: "The experience of the substrate (*prakṛti*) by the individual soul (*aṇu*) is dependent on something specific and restricted, because it is an effect, like that which is commonly accepted. And this reality is indeed restricted to each individual soul.

55) [Objection: But surely, in the *Dīkṣā* [treatise], the worlds (*bhuvana*) are said to reside within the principle of the Person (*puruṣatattva*). If it is asked how they can be situated there, it is replied: just as in the expression "the hamlet on the Ganges," their location is possible precisely at the head of *prakṛti*, which is in close proximity to the Person because it is its object of experience (*bhogya*).
And it is said there:
"In the past, during initiation, the worlds were indeed described as residing within the person;
how then do they exist here? Cut through the darkness born of this doubt."
Īśvara:

Since the maintenance of the world has been described there by means of the function of secondary indication (lakṣaṇā), let it be conceived as occurring within Prakṛti itself, which exists at the limit of that [world].
Just as when it is said, "a village on the Gaṅgā," it is understood to be on its bank; so too [is this case].
These seven principles, beginning with Māyā and ending with Puruṣa, which possess both pure and impure forms,
are designated as the *bhojayitṛkāṇḍa* (the section concerning the enjoyer).

56) Primordial Matter (*prakṛti*) is the fundamental material cause consisting of the [three] qualities (*guṇa*) down to earth. This, moreover, is produced from *kalā* by the agitation of the power of Śrīkaṇṭha. Now, one might object: primordial matter is not the material cause of the qualities; rather, it is simply the qualities themselves when they have reached a state of equilibrium. And these [qualities] are the ultimate cause. If they were effects...

Because there is a lack of evidence for that. If it is argued that the Great Principle (mahat), ego (ahaṅkāra), and so forth arise as both primordial matter (prakṛti) and its modifications (vikṛti), we say no;
for since the guṇas are insentient and manifold, they are effects and thus cannot constitute the ultimate cause.
Nor can it be maintained that despite their plurality, the equilibrium of the guṇas is a single unity, and that this alone is primordial matter (prakṛti).

This is logical; for even though equilibrium (*sāmya*) is one, because it depends upon a material cause (*upādāna*) distinct from the manifoldness of the *guṇas*, another material cause would have to be postulated. Furthermore, when there is disequilibrium of the *guṇas*, the cessation of the equilibrium that serves as the material cause would entail the cessation of the effect as well. Since these [qualities] are *guṇas*, they are not included among the *tattvas*.
Enumeration: And it has been said—
since the collection of principles beginning with *guṇa* and ending with the earth arises from it,
that is declared to be the Unmanifest (*avyakta*), which is to be agitated by the strides of Śrīkaṇṭha.
The sages asked:
"The guṇas themselves, when they have reached a state of equilibrium, are called *prakṛti*.
How then is that *prakṛti* established as the material cause (*upādāna*) of that [world]?"
Īśvara said:
"O best of sages, in the teaching of Śiva, *prakṛti* is not an equilibrium of the *guṇas*,
because the *guṇas* are one due to their insentience."
"It is accepted that [the world] is preceded by a cause, and that [cause] is designated as *prakṛti*. Thus [it is said].
(pau puṃ pa ślo 18–21) 57) These seven principles, beginning with *kalā* and ending with *niyati*, are called the "section of the enjoyer" (*bhojayitṛkāṇḍa*).
From this very principle of *prakṛti*, [the world arises] in the form of the three *guṇas* oriented toward diversity (*vaiṣamya*).

A principle called *citta* arises, which produces merely the manifestation of cognition and is synonymous with *guṇa* and *avyakta*. *Citta*, *mahat*, *guṇa*, *avyakta*, *kārya*, *māyā*, *prakṛti*, and "the lower portion" (*adhobhāga*) are its alternative names. And this *guṇa*—
It is threefold, distinguished by *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. Among these, *sattva* has the function of illumination;
*rajas* has the functions of activity and so forth; *tamas* has the functions of restraint and so forth. And it has been said:
"The quality of *rajas* and the others is declared to have action as its essence, established in illumination."
Likewise: steadiness, fortitude, as well as dexterity, gentleness, and lightness;
contentment, straightforwardness, purity, perseverance, forbearance, and mindfulness.
Contentment, supreme eagerness, self-restraint, tranquility, and supreme compassion are declared to be the functions of *sattva*; now the functions of *rajas* are described.
Valor, cruelty, great energy, pride, deceitfulness,
firmness, ruthlessness, indulgence, hypocrisy— these are the qualities of rajas.
Discontent, dullness, dejection, malice, as well as heaviness,
excessive sleep, intoxication, laziness, obstruction, and delusion—
these are declared to be the various functions of *tamas* found in all living beings.
Thus, O Brahmins, the true nature of the qualities has been briefly illustrated. So it is said.
58) Even though the sense-faculties (*indriya*), the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), and so forth,
have as their material cause (*upādāna*) the single principle called *ahaṃkāra*, they do not possess the nature of being a single principle (*ekatattvatā*); likewise, [the following applies].

It is not logical that even the *guṇas* possess a single reality (*ekatattvatā*); nevertheless, their unity as a reality is logical because they act together to produce effects. Nor is it correct to ask how designations such as "this is *sāttvika*" or "this is *rājasa*" can apply if every *guṇa* is a producer of every effect; for [such designations refer to] the specific activities (*vṛtti*) of each.
This is because it is established through the predominance of luminosity (*prakāśa*) and the other qualities. As for the proof for the existence of the *guṇas*:

pleasure, pain, delusion, and so forth, must be produced by something [other than themselves], because they are effects, like [the potter, etc.,] which is commonly accepted. Nor can their production be accounted for solely by the cognition of specific objects; for even in the case of a single object, such as a woman, [multiple states arise].

Because they produce pleasure, pain, and so forth according to the distinction of persons. To illustrate: Caitra feels affection for Padmāvatī; Maitra, not obtaining her, feels pain; and her co-wives feel delusion due to jealousy. Furthermore, all such mental states regarding Padmāvatī have been explained. And it is not...

The distinction lies in whether [the object] belongs to oneself or to another; for even in the case of common objects such as music and the like, we observe differences in mental states—such as joy or dejection—depending on the particular person. Nor is it reasonable to ask how pleasure, pain, and so forth can arise differently according to the person in the case of an object composed of qualities and actions.

For the systematic arrangement is logically established such that whenever a particular quality arises with respect to a particular object, then its corresponding effect, such as pleasure and so forth, arises with respect to that object.
59) From this very essence of consciousness (*cittatattva*), [the mind] emerges with *sattva* predominant and *rajas* and *tamas* subordinate.
The principle of intellect (*buddhi-tattva*) arises. That intellect is of two kinds: determinative (*adhyavasāyinī*) and non-determinative (*anadhyavasāyinī*).
Among these, the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) resides in the determinative intellect. The proof for its existence is as follows:
merit (*apūrva*) produced by sacrifices, charitable works, and so forth, must have some substratum, because it is a latent impression.

Like the [accepted] consensus. Furthermore, the selves cannot be the substratum of that [consciousness], because it would follow that they are subject to modification. Likewise, certainty must depend on something else, because it is an effect, like the accepted consensus. Similarly, qualities such as the knowledge of dharma and so forth must reside in something else, because they are qualities, like the accepted consensus; likewise...
Its existence is also established by its being the substratum for the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) that produce memory.
And it has been said:
"O best of sages, the intellect (*buddhi*), which is subordinate to the principle of *guṇa*, came into being."
The mental modification (vṛtti) is suppressed by rajas and tamas, yet it is predominant through sattva.
That intellect (buddhi) described in the Tantra is that which determines objects;
here, cognition (bodha) is said to be of two kinds, [the first] being that which determines the object.
That which is of the nature of non-determination is one thing, while that which is of the nature of determination is the intellect (*buddhi*);
the other, however, is the essential nature of the self as the subject who perceives.
Moreover, actions such as constructing water-booths and tanks, performed by those seeking rewards,
do not indeed bestow their fruits here immediately thereafter.

However, because they pertain to the future life, those actions, even after having perished, persist until the time of the fruit; therefore, there is a latent impression (saṃskāra) designated as "the unprecedented" (apūrva).
That [impression] cannot be attributed to the person, because of the reason that [the person] is subject to modification;
furthermore, the refinement resulting from agriculture and other such acts is not observed to reside in the person.
"In that [rite] where they perform the consecration (saṃskāra), that ritual action is considered to possess eight qualities.
O best of sages, in the same way, the consecration of knowledge and so forth should also be inferred. Thus [it is said].
(Pau Puṃ Pa Ślo 42–49) 61) And those eight qualities are: dharma, jñāna, vairāgya, aiśvarya, adharma, ajñāna, avairāgya, and anaiśvarya. Among these:

Knowledge of the Dharma, dispassion, and sovereignty are sattvic modifications; lack of dispassion is rajasic; and non-dharma, ignorance, and lack of sovereignty are tamasic. Here, dharma is of two kinds: yama and niyama. Among these, yama is fivefold:
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and freedom from guile. Thus [it is said].
The discipline (niyama) is also fivefold:
freedom from anger, service to the teacher, purity, contentment, and straightforwardness. Thus it is said.
62) In this context, non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) means the non-production of suffering even toward those who are hostile toward one.

Scriptural violence (*śāstrīyahiṃsā*) is also considered non-violence. Truth (*satya*), however, is the non-utterance of untruth even when one has fallen into danger or fear; furthermore, the utterance of untruth for the sake of one’s teacher, deity, or Brahmin is also truth. Non-stealing (*asteya*) means [not taking] by unjust means...

The non-appropriation of another's wealth; even regarding with the same indifference as a blade of grass any distinguished object heard of or seen; celibacy (*brahmacarya*), which consists of perceiving a woman—even when she solicits one—as one's mother and remaining free from sexual transformation; and freedom from malice (*akalkatā*), which is the absence of turbidity even when harmed—these are the five *yamās*.

Non-anger (*akrodha*) means the absence of resentment even when subjected to physical assault. Service to the teacher (*guruśuśrūṣā*) means obedience to the commands of the teacher and others, as well as faith in one's daily obligatory duties (*nityakarman*). Purity (*śauca*) means the cleansing of the body with earth and water, as well as purity of intention (*bhāvaśuddhi*). Contentment (*saṃtoṣa*) means...

Equanimity toward gain and loss; uprightness (*ārjava*) means the absence of crookedness. These are the five observances (*niyamas*). Knowledge, however, is of ten kinds; that will be explained in the section on liberation. Dispassion (*vairāgya*) likewise [consists of] the lack of satisfaction with the experience of all objects such as disease, as well as the internal and other forms of suffering.

The eightfold sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) consists of the powers beginning with *aṇiman* (atomicity) and so forth. [The tenfold power] is of ten types: that caused by the acquisition of wealth and other such miseries, the separation from loved ones, the perception of the faults of women, the insatiability of the body, and the knowledge of scriptural injunctions regarding acceptance and so forth; and that caused solely by the ripening of prior merit.

The definition of *tallakṣaṇa* (the characteristic of that) will also be made clear in the words to be cited hereafter. *Adharma* (unrighteousness) is also of ten kinds, distinguished as: violence, theft, false speech, sexual misconduct with those who should not be approached, doing harm, returning harm, envy, neglect of obligatory duties and so forth, impurity, lack of contentment, and crookedness. *Ajñāna* (ignorance) is also...

It is fivefold, distinguished as *tamas*, *moha*, *mahāmoha*, *tāmisra*, and *andhatāmisra*. Among these, *tamas* is the notion of selfhood in that which is not the self; it is tenfold, according to the various systems such as the Cārvāka and others. *Moha* is the pursuit of the eight supernatural powers (*siddhis*), beginning with *aṇimā*. *Mahāmoha*, however—
The determination of superiority (*paratva*) regarding the tenfold objects— sound and the rest— which are divided into divine and non-divine categories,

is [the affliction] *tāmisra*. The affliction named *andhatāmisra* is the torment resulting from the destruction of the tenfold objects— sound and the rest, distinguished as divine and non-divine— as well as the eightfold [siddhis] beginning with *aṇimā*.

Intolerance toward sound and other objects, as well as toward the supernatural powers such as *aṇimā* when they are being enjoyed by another, is non-detachment (*avairāgya*). Non-contentment (*atuṣṭi*) is of ten kinds due to its various forms; lack of sovereignty (*anaiśvarya*) is also of eight kinds.
This [lack of sovereignty] arises from incapacity (*aśakti*), and incapacity is numbered at one hundred and seventy-six.
Thus, dharma is of ten kinds; knowledge is eightyfold; dispassion is numbered as one hundred;
and sovereignty is of sixty-four kinds. Adharma is of ten kinds; ignorance is sixty-fourfold; lack of dispassion is one hundred; and lack of sovereignty is one hundred and eighty-four. In total—
The functions of the intellect (*buddhi*) number six hundred and twelve.
As it is stated in the venerable *Pauṣkara*:
"Dharma, knowledge (*jñāna*), dispassion (*vairāgya*), and sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) are the functions of the intellect."
In this context, three are proclaimed as the primary dharmas characterized by sattva.
Passion (rāga), however, belongs to the quality of rajas; the remaining [qualities] are proclaimed to be tāmasa.
Since these eight, beginning with dharma, bring about [their respective effects] from that source, [they are so designated].
The absences of the marks have been indicated; they are now recited in their proper order.
Among them, dharma is of two kinds: namely, yama and niyama.
The restraint of the mind therein is taught as *yama*;
it consists in the abandonment of actions not prescribed by the scriptures, even regarding those actions which are prescribed by the scriptures.

That which is taught by the scriptures as restraint (niyama)—namely, this control of the senses—and the fivefold discipline (yama): non-violence, truthfulness, and non-stealing; ||| indeed, these are [the observances].
Celibacy, freedom from deceit, and self-restraint—thus, restraint is fivefold:
freedom from anger, service to the teacher, purity, and contentment.
And straightforwardness—thus the discipline is proclaimed to be fivefold:
non-injury toward others is the non-arising of suffering, even through hundreds of acts of malice.
That violence which is enjoined by the scriptures should be understood as "non-violence";
however, that which is done out of distress or fear is not called true truth.
Even that which is untrue is true when it serves the purpose of one's guru or deity;
likewise, the taking of what is not given and the relinquishing of wealth acquired through unjust means [are true].
Even the treating as straw of what has been heard or seen constitutes non-thievery;
this applies through action, mind, and speech, whether by hearing or by seeing.

To always regard even a woman who solicits one as a mother—that alone constitutes true celibacy (*brahmacarya*); all others are mere mockery of a vow. It is purity, equanimity, and affection, even in the face of a hundred injuries.
Not tolerating turbidity or enmity—this indeed is called freedom from deceit. These five restraints (yamas) have been declared for ascetics whose nature is auspiciously serene.
One whose impurity is eternally destroyed has no anger even when struck by gods,
devotees of Śiva, parents, or even a teacher.
Through the constant observance of commands regarding optional and occasional rites,
as well as acts of charity, fasting, pilgrimages, and the hearing and study of the scriptures.
For men, service performed with faith is proclaimed as *śuśrūṣā*;
purification (*śauca*) is declared to consist of washing the body with clay and water.
Contentment is declared in the Tantra; one’s mind remains the same whether there is gain or loss.
O best of Brahmins, even though he knows this, he remains like one who is dull-witted and likewise mute.
Abstaining from harming others and possessing faith from the depths of one's being—this is declared to be his uprightness; thus, the observance (niyama) is fivefold.
That knowledge which consists of the intellect (buddhi) has as its object the gunas and that which lies beyond the unmanifest (avyakta);
from that comes the perfect attainment of liberation—thus is its accomplishment described.
And that [number] has been proclaimed in brief as eighty in number (*Pau Puṃ Pa* 49–67).
Now, the classification of detachment (*vairāgya*) is also briefly stated here.
Afflicted by disease and other such ailments, he feels detachment even toward his own body;
content in all undertakings, he loathes [the world] due to his lack of desire.
Detachment from internal and other forms of suffering will certainly arise from that which pertains to the acquisition,
protection, and theft of wealth by thieves.
For one who considers that [separation] to be suffering, detachment arises suddenly,
as he is being separated from what is dear, weeping and tormented by pain.
Thinking that affection is the cause of suffering, one becomes dispassionate;
yet a lustful man, upon seeing a woman, perceives some cause for detachment.
One immediately attains dispassion, which is the cause for the attainment of the highest good;
the body is sustained by wholesome food, water, and so forth, and not otherwise.
Even a single laugh causes exhaustion in the lower abdomen at that very moment;
for this reason, it is difficult to satisfy, and thus detachment arises.
In some cases, one attains detachment through the renunciation of receiving gifts and the like;
in other cases, someone becomes detached spontaneously due to the power of their merit.
Thus, the contentments have been declared as tenfold in the teaching of Śiva;
O best of the twice-born, all other contentments are included within these very ones.

And these contentments, because they lead to the realization of the principles beginning with the elements and ending with the unmanifest, amount to one hundred in number when combined, according to the teaching of Śiva.
Now, the differentiation of sovereignty is also briefly observed;
sovereignty, established through the distinction between the intellect and the self, is eightfold.
For a wise person who is devoted to knowledge, established in the dharma, and desirous of dispassion,
one should generate the sattva of the Buddha through the power of the will for the sake of the atom's sovereignty.
Aṇimā is the state of being subtler than even the most minute atom;
laghimā is the possession of swift velocity and the ability not to sink even in mud and the like.

Māhātmya (greatness) is the pervasive state [of existence] through a vast body, sense organs, and so forth; the third is sovereignty (aiśvarya), consisting of powers such as aṇimā, which is established from its effects.
The five qualities, beginning with attainment (prāpti), arise from the instruments of the yogin.
Attainment is the abode of qualities, wherein the desired object is accomplished by means of the mind.

She who, by swiftly attaining the power of pleasure at will, creates thousands of women and issues commands even to Brahmā and the other gods, is considered the Sovereign (Īśitā) and the object of their worship.
"Subjugation (vaśīkṛti) would be mastery (vaśitva), as well as the creation of the world;
for one who enjoys [these] through dharma and so forth, weightiness (garimā) is considered to consist in being unassailable. Thus [it is said].
(From Pauṣkarapārameśvara, Puṃsūkṣma, verses 87–103) 65) This sovereignty of the Piśācas consists of eight qualities of earth.
That of the Rākṣasas consists of sixteen qualities of earth and water. That of the Yakṣas consists of [twenty-four] qualities of earth, water, and fire.

The [smell] of the Gandharvas possesses twenty-four qualities. That of the gods consists of the earthly, aqueous, fiery, and aerial [elements], possessing thirty-two qualities. That of Indra consists of the earthly, aqueous, fiery, aerial, and ethereal [elements], possessing forty qualities. [That] of Soma—
The aggregate of the earth, water, fire, air, ether, and mind belongs to Prajāpati and possesses forty-eight qualities.
That of Prajāpati, however, includes the ego (ahaṃkāra) in addition to the earth, water, fire, air, ether, and mind, and thus possesses fifty-six qualities. As for that of Brahmā:
The sixty-fourfold qualities consist of those pertaining to earth, water, fire, air, ether, the mind, the ego (ahaṃkāra), and the intellect (bauddha). And it is said in the *Śivadharmottara*:
"In that regard, the eightfold sovereignty of the flesh-eaters is of the nature of earth."
And for those men who have attained union with Him, it is remembered as being equal to that.
The earthly and watery [elements] of the Rākṣasas are sixteenfold;
this is twofold, and among the Yakṣas it is entirely different, consisting of light.
The Vāyavya weapon is for the Gandharvas, and the entire Yākṣa weapon is likewise remembered;
that of Indra consists of the five elements and possesses forty great qualities.
The divine mind of Soma, as well as that which is below consisting of the five elements,
is the station of Prajāpati arising from the lunar principle and endowed with the qualities of ego.
The supreme sovereignty of a Buddha, which is of the nature of Brahmā, possesses sixty-four qualities. Thus it is said.
Likewise, in the illustrious Pauṣkara: "The eight qualities beginning with *aṇiman*, as previously specified for the Piśācas,
should be known to be twofold for the Rakṣasas and threefold for the Yakṣas."
The Gāndharva soma possesses four qualities, while that of Indra possesses five;
the soma of Prajāpati possesses six qualities, and that of Soma possesses seven.
The sovereignty of a Buddha is recorded as being sixty-four times that of Brahmā;
from that, the sovereignty [of a Mahābrahmā] is considered to be sixty-four times greater.
Then, even while remaining among sense objects through the enjoyment of sovereign power,
they move about with their karma exhausted in the houses of the pure and the prosperous.
Then, agitated by wealth, sleep, and intoxication, they apply themselves to what is called "dharma" through violence, theft, or even false speech.
Even in the case of approaching the wife of one's teacher, in retaliation for an injury, in anger, in the constant omission of obligatory rites, or in impurity, there is indeed atonement.
Those with blinded vision constantly engage in dishonesty;
these ten types of unrighteous conduct are as previously enumerated.

Then the Great Lord subjects that [individual], who has turned toward unrighteousness and possesses a subtle lack of knowledge within their continuum, to such a state that the fool does not perceive it.
Tamas, moha, mahāmoha, tāmisra, and andhatāmisra—
these five are considered the functions of ignorance.
That which is the conception of a self in what is not-self is proclaimed as darkness (tamas),
[extending] from the elements up to the unmanifest (avyakta), according to the distinctions in the vision of reality.
Delusion (tamas) is said to be tenfold, while infatuation (moha) is considered to be eightfold;
this is because, even when powers such as atomization (aṇimā) have been attained, there arises the realization of superiority [over others].
That determination of superiority regarding all ten objects, beginning with sound, through the distinction between the divine and the non-divine, is proclaimed as *mahāmoha* (great delusion).
Or else, it is due to the distinction between divine and non-divine regarding the ten [objects] beginning with sound,
or due to a deficiency in the accomplishment of the eightfold [siddhis] beginning with *aṇimā*.
The torment arising from the loss of things already acquired is proclaimed as *tāmisra*;
likewise, when sound and so forth, as well as the powers such as *aṇimā*, are being enjoyed by another.
The effort to bring about that happiness is tāmisra, and that which precedes it is andhatāmisra;
thus, this division of ignorance is considered to be of sixty-four kinds.
And there is a hundredfold lack of dispassion due to the reversal of the [ten] satisfactions;
at that time, humans feel no revulsion or similar sentiments toward any objects.
The eightfold lack of sovereignty consists in the reversal of sovereignty;
that [lack of sovereignty] arises from incapacity, which is one hundred and seventy-sixfold.
Because they consist of ignorance and contentment, there are one hundred and sixty-four [forms of contentment];
and the incapacity of the intellect regarding the cause constitutes twelve forms of contentment.
Thus, in brief, there are one hundred and seventy-six [varieties of] incapacity.
In this way, entities such as merit (dharma) and so forth reside within the intellect in the form of latent impressions (vāsanā).

They are said to be of the nature of cognitions sequentially, according to the distinctions in their modifications; they cause the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) to cognize, and for that reason they are remembered as "cognitions" (pratyaya).
Dharma is considered to be tenfold, knowledge numbering one hundred and eighty,
detachment eightfold, sovereignty eightfold, and adharma tenfold.
Ignorance consists of sixty-four types, non-detachment is one hundred;
lack of sovereignty is eightfold, and [the remaining afflictions] are three hundred and thirty-six.
The power [of the intellect] is considered to be one hundred and seventy-six in number;
when combined, the functions of the intellect amount to six hundred and twelve.
Thus, the intellect, consisting of eight states, has been briefly described;
they wander again and again within this great eight-spoked wheel.
"By means of those [views], persons do not see the end of those very persons. Thus it is said.
(Chapter on Purity, Male, and Purity; Verses 104–128) 67) [Objection:
But how can entities such as merit (*dharma*) and so forth, which are mutually contradictory, arise from a single cause? It is said: Merit and the others are not mutually contradictory.
They exist because they consist of conditions (*pratyaya*). Therefore, the absence of knowledge is not ignorance (*ajñāna*);

rather, it is simply a form of erroneous knowledge (*anyathājñāna*). Consequently, since even non-dharma and the like possess the nature of knowledge, there is no contradiction due to their relationship as general and particular. And it is said in the *Pauṣkara*:
The eight entities, beginning with dharma, are mutually contradictory;
likewise, the qualities such as sattva and the rest—how could they have a single cause?
Īśvara says:
Attributes such as dharma and the rest are not contradictory, because they consist of cognition.
Here, the absence of knowledge is not ignorance; otherwise, it would simply be wrong knowledge.
Therefore, all those [particulars] such as dharmas and so forth are established within that specific cognition;
for particulars are never contradictory to the universal. Thus it is said.

(From the *Pauṣkarabhāṣya*, verses 44–46) 68) From this very principle of intellect (*buddhitattva*), the principle of egoity (*ahaṃkāra*)— which initiates the sense organs and so forth and, by means of its own superimposition, serves as the cause for the notion of "I" (*ahaṃbuddhi*) within the self— is produced.
From its activity proceeds the movement of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth. As for the proof of its existence, it is precisely the following inference:

the determination (*adhyavasāya*) in the form of "I" must have some cause, because it is an effect, like [any other] agreed-upon effect. Nor can this be accounted for by the intellect (*buddhi*) alone; for the intellect...

The effect, namely determination (*adhyavasāya*), possesses a form that is distinct for each respective object and a form that grasps the object; however, the determination in the form of "I" possesses a single uniform form and a form that grasps the subject. This is because it is distinct from the determination that is the effect of the intellect (*buddhi*).

Furthermore, if the superimposition of the "I" (ahaṃ-adhyāsa) were the cause [of cognition], it would follow that the "I" would be colored [as an object] in every apprehension of an object. Nor can it be argued that the coloring or non-coloring of the "I" in the apprehension of an object is explained by the entry or non-entry of the causal complex for the manifestation of the Self (ātman); for the conjunction of the Self [with the internal organ] is [present in all cases].

Because there is no absence of penetration [of the ego] everywhere due to its universal entry; however, in our view, attachment and non-attachment are logically established through the activity and non-activity of the ego (ahaṃkāra), so there is no inconsistency whatsoever. Thus, the existence of the ego is proven by its being the cause of the determinative cognition (adhyavasāya) in the form of "I."
69) This has been stated in the venerable Pauṣkara:
"Henceforth, the principle of ego (ahaṃkāra-tattva) is described in brief.
It is determined for each individual soul and is well-known as having the nature of 'I'."
The mind is the primary underlying reality from which [the ego] arises;
for the sages,
the conviction here below is "I am," since it consists of the nature of determination.
"Therefore, let there be only the intellect (buddhi); what is the use of this [ego]? Tell me, O Lord. The Lord:
"That which is the determination of objects, existing as distinct for each respective object,"
Everything characterized as "this" is reckoned by the term "intellect" (buddhi).
But I am the Self, of a single nature, established everywhere;
how could this intellect, whose essence consists of the determination of the grasper, exist?
The intellect is directed toward objects, while "I" am the grasper of objects;
O Brahmins, how can the identity of these two, which are utterly distinct, be asserted?
The Sages said:
Since the notion of "I" must be sought as one for all who possess the self,
because that cognition arises [identically], how could it be restricted to each individual self?
Īśvara:
First of all, the cognition "this" arises everywhere;
yet one cannot assert its oneness on that basis alone, because it is contradicted by perception.
Furthermore, in all jars, the cognition "jar" alone arises;
yet no unity among all those jars is perceived.
The ego-sense, determined for each individual, functions with the thought "I am going," and likewise, there arises in another person the awakening of the intellect in the form "I see."
Otherwise, the notion of "I" would be of one and the same kind for both [the self and the body];
let it be understood that the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) is distinct and universally recognized as such.
"If the ego were non-different [from the Self], then the notion of 'I' would arise even in Devadatta, and it would arise in others as well; therefore, the oneness of the Self is not established."

(Pau Puṃ Pa Ślo 129–140) 70) Furthermore, this *ahaṃkāra* is first of all threefold, distinguished as *jīvana*, *saṃrambha*, and *garva*. Among these, *jīvana* is that which sustains the five vital breaths (*prāṇavāyu*). *Saṃrambha* is...
Effort (*prayatna*). Pride (*garva*) is the determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*) of the subject as "I. And it is said in the *Tattvaprakāśa*:

"Ahaṃkāra is threefold, through the distinctions of vital impulse (*jīvana*), exertion (*saṃrambha*), and pride (*garva*). In the *Mṛgendra*: "The five bodily winds (*vāyu*) exert themselves through its [the ahaṃkāra's] exertion (*saṃrambha*) and so forth."
And elsewhere:
"Agitation is the function of the ego. Thus it is said.

Furthermore, this [ahaṃkāra] is threefold according to the distinction of *sāttvika* and so forth. Among these, the *taijasa* is designated as *sāttvika*, the *rājasa* is called *vaikārika*, and the *tāmasa* is named *bhūtādi*.
From the *taijasa* ahaṃkāra, the five organs of cognition (the sense-faculties), such as the eye and so forth, arise.
From the *vaikṛta* ego (*ahaṃkāra*), the five organs of action, beginning with speech, arise.

From the *bhūtādi* ego, the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*), beginning with sound, arise. Among these, the principle that is the cause of conceptualization and discrimination is the mind (*manas*). When an object has been perceived by the eyes and other senses, this—

The determination that "this is a Brāhmaṇa" and so forth is *saṅkalpa* (conceptualization), because it consists in the mental construction of an object through the proper relation of qualifier and qualified. Doubt (*vikalpa*), such as "Is this a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya? regarding such an object, is conceptualization (*vikalpa*), because it consists in various constructions. As for the proof of its existence:

The cognition [of the self] has conceptualization and discrimination as its conditions and possesses a cause, because it is an effect. Furthermore, this is neither produced by the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) nor by the intellect (buddhi); for those two—the intellect and the ego-sense—are established as the causes of the determinate cognition and the notion of "I," respectively. Nor is this [cognition] sensory; for an object perceived by the eyes and other senses is apprehended by the mind alone.

Because it ascends into the intellect; otherwise, upon seeing a jar, there would also be the certain cognition of a cloth. Nor should it be argued that the desire to know (*bubhutsā*) itself is the regulator of that [cognition], for desire, being of the nature of volition, is produced by the mind. Therefore, the mind is established as the cause of conceptualization and deliberation.

72) And this mind (*manas*) is large. [Objection: Is it not rather minute (*aṇu*), since objects are manifested sequentially? If it were large, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that all objects would be manifested at all times. [Reply: Not so.
Even if the mind is large, knowledge arises only through dependence on a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) due to the power of karma, and also because of being overcome by darkness (*tamas*).
Because [the perception of objects] occurs sequentially. Furthermore, if the mind were atomic in size, only atomic-sized objects would be manifested;

for it is observed in the case of lamps, the sun, and so forth, that an object is manifested only to the extent that its cause has pervasion. Nor should it be argued that it is illogical for a large [cause] to grasp a small [object].
Because there is no contradiction. Therefore, it is established that the mind (*manas*) is the Great One (*mahat*). And that [mind] is restricted to each individual self (*pratyātmaniyata*).
As it is stated in the venerable *Pauṣkara*:
"And that is declared to be threefold; among them, the first is the Taijasa."
The second is the Vaikārika, and likewise the other is the Bhūtādi.
That which has sattva as its predominant portion is here called taijasa;
that which has rajas as its predominant portion is vaikṛta, and that which has tamas as its predominant portion is bhūtādi.
From the taijasa ego arise the mind and the organs of cognition;
from the vaikṛta ego, however, the five organs of action arise.
From the ego-principle (ahaṅkāra), however, arises the aggregate of the subtle elements (tanmātra) originating from the primary matter (bhūtādi);
this is the internal cognition of men, whose nature consists of conceptualization and discursive thought.
He is neither characterized by egoism nor is he a Buddhist, due to the difference in activity;
rather, in this tantra, the ocean of liberation, he is intended to be purely mental.
O Brahmins, that which causes an object perceived by the eye to enter the range of the intellect is here designated as the mind (manas).

Otherwise, even upon seeing a cloth when one has previously perceived a jar, there would be a certain determination [of it as a jar]; furthermore, having experienced the word "cow" in reference to a body possessing a dewlap and so forth, [one would not subsequently recognize it].
Furthermore, when something similar to that is seen, the mind— which is caused by the utterance of the word "cow" and consists of conceptual cognition— is described in the Tantra as such.
Some maintain that the mind is atomic because objects appear sequentially;
for if it were large, there would be simultaneous cognition of all objects at all times.

That is incorrect; for the arising of knowledge in humans occurs gradually due to the power of karma, owing to the dependence upon a collection of causal conditions, and also because of the suppression by darkness (ignorance).
If the mind were atomic, it would always be capable of grasping only atomic substances;
for as far as the pervasion of the grasper extends, so far is the grasped apprehended.
If it is thought that the mind is small because it perceives only a limited object— just as perception occurs through a lamp or through the rays of the sun;
Therefore, even from that which is great, a small portion is perceived;
yet the principle of the mind is truly vast and is restricted to each individual self. Thus it is said.

(From *Pauṣkarapārameśvara*, verses 140–153) 74) Furthermore, these— mind (*citta*), intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṃkāra*), and mind-stuff (*manas*)— are internal organs (*antah-karaṇa*) because they lack the capacity for the perception of external objects. And thus it is not...

Like the ear and the other senses, they do not grasp only the present, but rather grasp both the past and the future as well. The sense organ (*indriya*) is a principle (*tattva*) originating from either the *sāttvika* or *rājasa* ego (*ahaṃkāra*).
It is of two kinds: the faculty of cognition (*buddhīndriya*) and the faculty of action (*karmendriya*). Among these:
The organ of cognition (*jñānendriya*) originates from the *sāttvika* ego (*ahaṃkāra*), because it is illuminating.

The organ of action (*karmendriya*) originates from the *rājasa* ego, because it generates activity. Among these, the organ of cognition is fivefold, distinguished as the ear and so forth. Among these, the organ that perceives sound is—
The ear; the skin, which perceives touch; the eye, which perceives form; the nose, which perceives smell;
and the tongue, which perceives taste. And it is said in the venerable Pauṣkara:
"The sense organs of cognition are said to be the ear, the skin, and the eye."
The tongue, the nose, and the five [senses]—these are well known.
"Since they are established as objects of direct perception, no further arguments are stated;
they are born from the sāttvika aspect of the ego. Thus [it is said].

(Verse 158, 159) 75) Objection: Let it be that the ear-cavities and so forth, which are considered the substrata of the auditory organ and the rest, are themselves the perceivers of sound and the other objects. What is the use of separate sense organs such as the auditory organ? And it is not the case that...
It is logical that one must accept a sense organ distinct from its physical locus on the grounds of its functioning through contact (*prāpyakāritva*);
for it is established that the skin and other such loci do indeed function through contact, and because the functioning of the eye and ear through contact is not proven. Nor is this so...

There would be the undesirable consequence of perceiving even that which is obstructed by walls and the like; for since the absence of walls and such is also a cause in that case, it is logical that there is no perception of it when a wall or similar object is present. Furthermore, we observe things even when they are separated by crystal and other transparent media. Moreover, if [the sense organ] functions by reaching its object, the simultaneous perception of the branch and the moon would be impossible.

Therefore, one should not assume a sense organ distinct from its physical basis; do not say so. For if the eye did not function by reaching its object (*prāpyakāritva*), it would follow that even an object obstructed by a wall or similar barrier could be perceived. Nor is the wall the actual impediment; for if the wall were the direct impediment, [the light] would have to exist outside the wall.

For even in the case of one standing between a wall and a person, it would follow that [the object] is not perceived; therefore, one must accept that its status as an obstacle occurs precisely through the disruption of sensory contact (*saṃnikarṣa*). Nor is it an obstacle by virtue of being situated between the grasped and the grasper, since [this applies to] the state of being in the middle as well.

This is because [the contact] must be required precisely for the sake of breaking the proximity; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that an object situated behind one would be perceived just as easily as one standing directly in front, since there is nothing else between the perceiver and the perceived. Furthermore, the objection regarding the non-perception of objects separated by crystal is equally applicable to you as well.

In your view as well, there exists an intervening object that acts as an obstacle; since that opaque object serves as an impediment, it can equally be stated in my view that it is precisely that which obstructs the contact. Therefore, it is the eye itself, when in contact, that is the perceiver. Nor [is this untenable] regarding the eyeball.

Since contact with objects such as jars is possible [only when the sense organ reaches them], one must accept that the eye is something entirely distinct, which has those [objects] as its substrate and possesses the properties of contraction and expansion. Furthermore,
even when there is an obstruction by a person or other things in between, the rays of the eye do not fail to reach contact with the jar and so forth.
