It must be said that its perception would occur because there is an absence of the destruction of the substratum or of the motion of either [the object or the sense organ], which are the causes for interrupting the proximity [of the sense organ to the object]. For here too, just as in the case of the sunbeams inside a window when it is closed— where they either perish or depart— either perishing or departing is possible.
Because it is only the dissolution of conjunction that is logically possible.

76) [Objection: But how can there be a connection between the auditory organ (*śrotra*) and its object? For, unlike the activity of the eye, the activity of the ear does not involve going outside [the body], and thus a connection is not possible. Furthermore, it would follow that a low-pitched sound could be perceived just as easily as a high-pitched one, even when located at a great distance. [Response: This is not so, because [the perception occurs] through a continuous series (*santati*), according to the analogy of waves upon waves.

Because the perception of sound produced in the region of the ear is logically established. Nor should it be argued that, just as with sound produced in the region of the ear, there would be perception by means of inherence (*samavāya*) in the space conjoined with the auditory organ even for sound produced at a distance;
for it is only inherence in the space delimited by the ear that functions as the perceiver. [Objection: But if this were so...

If it is argued that there is no evidence for an additional sense organ because, by accepting the production [of sound] according to the analogy of waves and ripples, the contact occurs with the ear itself, we reply: this is not so, because even when the ear is present, a deaf person does not perceive sound; therefore, another [organ] must be admitted as having that [ear] as its substrate.

Therefore, it is established that the auditory organ (*śrotrendriya*) has as its substrate a portion of space delimited by the ear-cavity (*karṇaśaṣkulī*). And this [organ], through a continuous series (*santati*) according to the analogy of waves and ripples, is the grasper of sound produced in the region of the ear. Consequently, even a sound produced at an extreme distance [is perceived].

It is incorrect to claim that sound would be produced in the location of the auditory space through a continuous series; for if that were the case, there would be no distinction between perceiving sounds as near or distant based on the difference between low (*mandra*) and high (*tāra*) pitches.
Therefore, just as a single arrow falls at varying distances depending on the degree of its cause (the force applied), so too does it happen here.
Likewise, it is a single sound that reaches the region of the ear of a person standing at a distance or nearby due to the varying degrees of its causal conditions (*nimitta*).

Similarly, since touch and other sensations are not perceived when there is an impairment of the skin and so forth by leprosy (*kuṣṭha*) and other diseases, the sense organ (*indriya*) which has those [skin parts] as its substrate must be admitted. For if leprosy and the like were inherently defects [of the sense organ itself], [the perception would be obstructed regardless of the state of the substrate].
Because there is a lack of evidence [for such a distinction].

(77) Now, let it be that there is only one sense-faculty which, through the difference of its physical bases (*adhiṣṭhāna*), perceives different objects; what is the use of postulating a plurality of sense-faculties? Furthermore, the established conditions of blindness, deafness, and so forth, would also be accounted for simply by the destruction of the respective capacities of that single faculty.

If it is argued that this will be so, we say no; for by the very means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) stated which apprehends the subject (dharmin), the sense organs are established as being distinct. If non-difference were established by a means of valid cognition, then some kind of distinction in their powers (śakti-bheda) might be postulated to account for the observed functional arrangement; however, there is no such means of valid cognition in that regard.
Thus, the sense organs are distinct.
As it is stated in the venerable Pauṣkara:
"Now, some [hold] that the eye is merely the physical orb (golaka), along with its cause."
Because there is the perception of an interval [between them], and because the branch and the moon exist simultaneously.
And for the same reason, why is it not accepted that [the senses] grasp gross objects?
Īśvara says:
"The perception of objects at a distance is held to be due to the sense-organs being of the nature of the eyeball and so forth."
For in this way, the grasper would be perceived as being pervaded, just like a lamp; such is the view held.
Because it does not pervade the eyeball, the visual nature of that [light] is effectively excluded;
whereas its grasping of large objects is consistent with its being pervasive.
If there were not the perception of an entity as small as a ball,
then at one and the same time there would be the perception of both the branch and the moon, owing to its all-pervasiveness.
In reality, however, the perception of the moon and its branches does not arise at one and the same time;
it is merely a misconception due to rapid succession, like the [illusory] piercing of a thousand petals.
The Sages said:
"Is it not the case that the eyeball itself is accepted as the locus of the eye?
For wherever there is the existence of a locus, there the located object is established."
That existence which is all-pervasive is considered to be ineffective;
just as the soul, though all-pervasive, does not provide cognition within the space of the sky.
But how does the eye grasp an object situated at a great distance? The Lord [answers]: Because the eyeball is externalized by virtue of its being composed of light (*taijasa*).
Just as a lamp, the eye perceives that which has been placed before it, but not what is extraordinary.
The eye is assisted by a lamp, and the collection of objects [is perceived] despite the darkness;
therefore, the objection regarding [the perception of] smell and so forth, as previously stated, is effectively refuted.
Is it not because of the activity of the eyeball, which serves as the support for the eye,
that even when the ocular rays have issued forth and joined together?
The object would be perceived immediately after the [eye's] contact, because it does not perish quickly,
like the light of a lamp situated inside a jar when it is covered by a lid.

If the visual organ were merely the physical eyeball, there would be perception of objects not in contact with it; and if it could perceive what is not in contact, then it would perceive even objects obstructed by a barrier.

Therefore, the eye must be admitted to be all-pervasive in order to perceive distant objects; if this were so, however, the skin and other sense organs would likewise reach their objects and grasp them.

If this is argued, it is not so; for these [senses] do not grasp objects by traveling to the domain presided over by the elements such as air, but rather they cause the attainment of the object once it has reached them.
The sages said:
If the ear, like the eye, does not go out to grasp the sound,
then how is it that the word-sound, as conditioned by its direction and location, is apprehended here?
Īśvara says:
Due to the momentum of that [sound], the sound arrives at the ear through a continuous series;
like the flight of an arrow or similar objects, it immediately allows one to infer the direction and location.

Therefore, the inference of the drum and so forth, which occurs through prior experience alone, apprehends only an object already present; hence, it is established that the sense organs [apprehend what is proximate].
"One sense-faculty cannot be admitted, because there is no cognition of [both] the eye and visible form, etc. Thus [it is said].

(Pau Puṃ Pa Ślo 173–191) 79) But how can these [organs] be derived from the *ahaṅkāra*? For it is more appropriate that they be elemental (*bhautika*), since they apprehend specific qualities. Just as, for example, the ear and the other organs have as their material cause the substrata of sound and the other objects.

Because it manifests that [quality]; for whatever manifests something is of the same nature as the substrate of that thing, just as clarified butter (ghṛta) manifests the fragrance of saffron. This is not so; because the argument is inconclusive due to the visual organ (cakṣus), which manifests blue color but is not of the same nature as its substrate, earth. Now, regarding these...

If it is asked, "In the absence of a difference in material cause (*prakṛti*), how is there a restriction of objects?"—it is not that the restriction of objects is caused by a difference in material cause. What then? It is caused by a specific necessity (*niyati*). Furthermore, what is the nature of this restriction of objects? Is it that whichever sense organ has whatever as its material cause, it perceives only the quality (*guṇa*) of that [cause]?

Is it that [an organ] does not perceive anything other [than its own quality]? Or is it that whichever sense organ is of a certain nature perceives only that specific quality and not something possessing a different quality? The first alternative is not tenable, because it would entail the consequence that the eye could not perceive blue and other qualities belonging to earth.
The second is not tenable either, because it would entail the consequence that action, generality, and so forth could not be perceived. But surely the sense organs [perceive] those respective...

If it is argued that [the elements] have the nature of their respective substrates because they manifest each of those specific subtle elements (*tanmātra*) among the five beginning with sound, we say no; for there is no corroborating example (*dṛṣṭānta*) for the claim that [air] manifests sound alone.
Likewise, regarding the claim that [water] manifests taste alone, [this is not the case] because water manifests the odors of new earthenware and the like.

In the illustrative example, there is a deficiency of the probans (*sādhanavaikalya*). Alternatively, in all cases, [the reason] is non-conclusive (*aprayojaka*) and is sublated by scripture (*āgama*) which establishes that [the senses] are derived from *ahaṅkāra*. Therefore, it is established that the sense organs are not elemental (*bhautika*), but rather are derived from *ahaṅkāra* (*āhaṅkārika*).
80) This has been stated in the venerable Pauṣkara:
The Sages said:
"That which manifests something must indeed be of the same genus as that thing."
Just as in the case of a substance that has been overcome by a foul odor, such as neem bark and sandalwood.
The auditory organ, which manifests sound, is composed of space alone;
in the same way, the nature of the skin and other organs is to be inferred—how then can they be said to be derived from the ego-principle (ahaṃkāra)?
Īśvara:
Because they are composed of the elements, the senses possess material form like a jar or other objects;
they are objects of perception by other senses and do not abide anywhere [as independent entities].
Furthermore, there is no grasping of corporeal objects by means of obstruction to other corporeal things;
for the eye would not fail to perceive an object situated inside a crystal.
Or even [the eye] within water; therefore, the eye is not composed of light (taijasa).
The Sages said:
"If this is so, then even for an object placed behind a wall..."
[Objection: There would be perception [of sound] because it is formless and because it arises from the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra).
[Response: The Lord [says]: That is not so, because of its insubstantiality and because walls and the like obstruct its movement.
As for the claim that the suggested meaning and the suggester are of the same genus,
that too is not tenable, because action and genus are objects of visual perception.
Therefore, its object is exclusively visible form, and its luminous nature is not thereby lost;
for if it were otherwise, the perception of objects at a distance would be impossible.
It is never observed that anything is perceived without being reached due to some kind of obstruction;
rather, every sense organ perceives only what it has reached, just as the skin does.
Furthermore, if [the sense organs] were limbs of the body, it would follow that the mute and others could not exist;
yet the mute and others are observed to possess parts such as the nose and so forth.
Therefore, the eye is held to be all-pervasive in the perception of distant objects;
the ear and the other [senses] are mentioned in sequence, as are their five respective objects.
The scripture is the apprehender of the words associated with the five elements;
therefore, among the remaining elements, touch is held to be perceivable by the skin.
In this way, it should be understood for the others as well; those to be grasped are five, in sequence.
The sequential arising of the ear, skin, eye, and so forth has thus been declared. Thus [it is said].

(pau puṃ pa ślo 160–172) 81) The organs of action (*karmendriya*), however, are speech, feet, hands, the anus, and the genitals. Their functions (*vyāpāra*), moreover, are speaking, grasping, moving about, excretion, and sexual pleasure. And these...
Even though they are considered to be the locations (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the sense organs, [the functions] do not arise in certain cases;
therefore, the sense organ is established as something distinct from its location. As it is said in the Pauṣkara:
"The organs of action are speech, feet, hands, the private organ, and the anus."
"The causes of speech, grasping, movement, pleasure, and emission. Thus [it is said].
82) The principle originating from the *tāmasa* ego is the *tanmātra*. It is fivefold:
the *tanmātra* of sound, the *tanmātra* of touch, the *tanmātra* of form, the *tanmātra* of taste, and the *tanmātra* of smell. Among these—

The general property of sound (*śabdasāmānya*), devoid of specific qualities such as resonance, articulation, high pitch, and low pitch, is the subtle element of sound (*śabdatanmātra*). The general property of touch (*sparśasāmānya*), devoid of distinctions such as cold and heat, is the subtle element of touch (*sparśatanmātra*). The general property of form (*rūpasāmānya*), empty of specific qualities such as whiteness and so forth, is [the subtle element of form].

The subtle element of form (*rūpatanmātra*) is that which is devoid of distinctions such as color. The subtle element of taste (*rasatanmātra*) is the generality of taste, free from divisions such as sweetness and so forth. The subtle element of smell (*gandhatanmātra*) is the generality of smell, not yet reached by specific qualities such as fragrance and so on.

83) [Objection: But what is the proof for the existence of those *tanmātras*? First of all, the inference that "the elements such as space (*ākāśa*) are not originated from material causes (*upādāna*), because they are effects" is not a valid proof; for this would entail the fallacy of proving something already established (*siddhasādhana*), since [space] is distinct from the *tāmasa-ahaṅkāra* or from atoms (*paramāṇu*). Nor are the specific objects such as stars [proof].

The inference that "particulars are preceded by a universal because they are particulars" is contradictory, since particulars such as the 'lumpy' and the 'hornless' lack the property of being preceded by the universal 'cow'. Therefore, there is no means of valid cognition for the existence of that [universal] alone; but this is not so.

If the tamasic ego were the cause of ether and the other elements, then the increase in successive qualities found in ether and the others would have to be caused by unseen merit and demerit (adṛṣṭa) alone. Therefore, because they are caused by visible factors, it must be admitted that they are caused by the subtle elements (tanmātras) of sound and so forth. For in this way, [the properties of] ether...

Sound possesses the quality of sound because it is composed of the subtle element of sound (*śabda-tanmātra*). Air possesses two qualities because it is composed of the subtle elements of sound and touch (*sparśa-tanmātra*). Fire possesses three qualities because it is composed of the subtle elements of sound, touch, and form (*rūpa-tanmātra*). [The same applies to] water...

Because it is composed of sound, touch, form, and taste, earth is the substratum of four qualities. Since it is composed of the subtle elements (tanmātras) of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell, it is logical that earth is the substratum of five qualities. And it is not...

It is logical that these [gross objects] possess the status of being substrata for their respective qualities because they have atoms— which themselves are substrata for those respective qualities— as their material cause (*upādāna*); for while it is possible for a subtle quality itself to be the cause, there is no justification for postulating a subtle substratum of the quality as the cause when the quality alone can suffice.
Out of respect [for the tradition]. Therefore, it must be accepted that the *tanmātras* alone are the material causes (*upādāna*) of the elements.
As it is said in the venerable *Pauṣkara*:
"The *tanmātras*, which have now been reached in their proper sequence, are likewise described."
Because it possesses qualities that are discernible by the external sense organs, it is a composite of the primary elements.
Since for people such as ourselves, perceptibility is established as being preceded by causes,
that which is the cause therein, O brahmins, is indeed an aggregate of those subtle elements (tanmātra).
Furthermore, because sound and the other [objects] possess particularity, and because those [particulars] are preceded by universals,
one should contemplate that which is the universal even there as being "mere" (tanmātra).
The aggregate of the subtle elements (tanmātras) possesses one, two, three, four, and five qualities respectively;
for this very reason, there is a progressive application of the qualities to the gross elements.
"The distinction between them is caused by grossness and subtlety, just as there is a distinction between the gross elements and their subtle counterparts. Thus [it is said].
85) The *tattva* (principle) beginning with the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) is the *bhūta* (gross element).
Alternatively, it is the substratum of qualities (*guṇa*) belonging to the class of those perceptible by the sense organs. And that [is divided] by the distinction of ether (*ākāśa*) and so forth.

It is of five kinds. Among these, space (*ākāśa*) is the reality whose function is to provide room. Alternatively, it is that which is derived solely from the subtle element of sound (*śabda-tanmātra*), while not being derived from the subtle elements of touch and the others. Its quality is sound alone. Its status as a quality is to be inferred by its being subject to degrees of intensity and diminution. Now, regarding sound...

If it is asked, "How is space established, given that qualities such as sound belong to the drum and other instruments?", we say no; for space is established as the material cause (*upādāna*) with respect to sound by way of reaching the auditory organ, according to the analogy of the falling arrow.
The drum and so forth are not the material cause, but rather merely the efficient cause (*nimitta*). Now, one might ask: "In what sense is sound alone the quality of this [space]?"

If it is argued that color also exists because of the experience "the sky is blue," and that the inference of its being colorless— based on its lack of tangibility and so forth— is sublated by direct perception, we say no; for in the very same location where there is the perception of blue from a distance, one perceives its absence upon approaching nearby.

This is because that cognition is determined to be an error, as it is produced by defects such as distance. Nor should it be argued that the postulation of this [space] as a distinct category of reality is useless, since its existence can be accounted for as the mere absence of all corporeal substances; for if that were so, it would follow that sound—which has space as its quality—would be without a substratum. This is because [if space were merely an absence], there could be no substratum for the absence itself.
Furthermore, because the existence-dharma (bhāvadharma) consisting of being the substratum for the granting of space to all beings and for coming and going is untenable;
as it has been stated in the venerable Pauṣkara:
The great elements (mahābhūtāni) arise in succession from the five subtle elements (tanmātrapañcakāt),
known by the names ether (ākāśa), wind (pavana), fire (tejas), water (toya), and earth (bhūḥ).
O bulls among sages, you should accept that space is the cause of those activities such as going and coming which occur for human beings when it exists.
If that space called "the intermediate region" did not exist, where would living beings dwell?
For the coming and going of creatures is never observed within the interior of the earth.
Therefore, space must be accepted as the cause of accommodation.
Furthermore, sounds such as "intense" and so forth depend upon a substratum, because they are qualities.
It has been stated that space possesses qualities, yet it is beyond the senses of ordinary men.
The sages said:
"But surely space is perceptible, for one sees birds flying through it."
If that which is beyond the senses were not visible, such as the flight of birds in the sky;
[then] Īśvara says: "In this way, space would be a material entity due to its association with qualities such as touch."
For one who speaks in this manner, it is exceedingly beautiful to determine the true nature of one thing by means of the effect of another, through the analogy of the earth.
For the conjunction of light and space is indeed perceived in the sky;
however, the notion that "the sky is blue" is false, being based on factors such as distance.
"Space is merely a collection of subtle elements (tanmātra) due to its extreme distance.
The sages said:
"There is no such thing as space; it is merely a designation for that which provides room."
Others say that the space of earth and so forth is indeed of the nature of non-existence; let a resolution be provided regarding this.
Īśvara:
Non-existence possesses the properties of existence, and likewise, existence resides within that [non-existence].
If non-existence did not possess those properties, then the absence of a jar would belong to a cloth.
If this non-existence were a property (dharma) of the object, like the horn of a hare, it would never be perceived; therefore, this objection is not valid.
For non-existence is indeed non-apprehension, and that is dependent upon its effect;
being the effect of that cause, it exists through the predominance of tamas.
Non-existence is the persistence [of a thing] from its state of potentiality in the form of an existent effect;
therefore, existence and non-existence are not accepted as coexisting in a single entity.
Since the absence of a material object is itself an absence, it is established only within material objects;
how then could this absence of such an object be space here?
"Whatever property belongs to something, its existence in that substratum is logical here;
moreover, this very space is seen to be all-pervading everywhere. Thus [it is said].
(Pau Puṃ Pa Ślo 279–294) 87) Wind is that which is not originated from the subtle element of form (*rūpa-tanmātra*), yet is originated from the subtle element of touch (*sparśa-tanmātra*);
its qualities are sound and touch. [Objection: But sound is not a quality of wind, because it is perceivable by the auditory organ; for...

That quality of air is not perceived by the sense of hearing, just as touch is not; or rather, air does not have sound as its quality because it is other than ether (ākāśa), since the inference that "whatever has sound as its quality is ether" establishes the certainty that sound is not a quality of air— how then [can it be so]?

If it is argued that sound is a quality of air, we say no; for since sounds such as *śaka-śaka* are perceived as residing in the air, the two types of inference [proposing sound as a quality of space] are sublated by perception. Likewise, because sounds such as *dhamadham*, *chalachal*, and *khaḍakhaḍa* are experienced as residing in fire and so forth, [the same applies to] light and other elements.

It has sound as its quality. Furthermore, this [air] is an object of sensory perception produced by the sense of touch (*tvagindriya*), because of the experience "I am touching the air" and because it possesses manifested touch (*udbhūtasparśavat*). Nor is it correct to ask how that which lacks color (*nīrūpa*) can be an object of sensory perception; for color is the necessary condition only for visual perception (*cākṣuṣatā*).
88) Fire is that which is not originated from the subtle element of taste (*rasatanmātra*), but is originated from the subtle element of form (*rūpatanmātra*).

Its qualities (*guṇa*) are sound, touch, and form. Although it is appropriate that fire, by virtue of its luminous nature, should be originated from the *sāttvika* ego-constituent (*ahaṃkāra*)—just like the organs of cognition (*jñānendriya*)—nevertheless...

It should be understood that although it is a manifestor in relation to objects such as a jar, it is a manifested object in relation to the sense organs; therefore, its being produced from the *tāmasa* ego is stated by way of a mediated succession.
89) Water is that which is derived from the subtle element of taste (*rasa-tanmātra*), provided that it is not derived from the subtle element of smell (*gandha-tanmātra*). Of this—

Taste is also a quality. Its sound is *chalachala*, its touch is cold, its color is white, and its taste is sweet; for the perception of differences in taste in wells and other locations is caused by the difference in their substrata.

90) Earth is originated from the subtle element of smell (*gandhatanmātra*), and its quality is also smell. Here, color (*rūpa*) is divided into the distinctions of white, blue, yellow, green, red, and brownish-red. Taste (*rasa*) is also divided into the distinctions of sweet, sour, salty, bitter, pungent, and astringent. Touch (*sparśa*) is neither hot nor cold.
Odor is both fragrant and foul-smelling; it is further divided into two types: that produced by cooking (*pākaja*) and that not produced by cooking (*apākaja*).

Its sound is *khaḍakhaḍa*. These elements, beginning with the primary nature (*prakṛti*) and ending with earth, are designated as the "impure category of objects" (*aśuddhabhogyakāṇḍa*). As for the sense organs and so forth, [their nature] is intrinsic...

Even in the absence of being an object of enjoyment (*bhogyatva*) in its own right, it is included within the category of the "enjoyable" (*bhogyakāṇḍa*) because, by means of perception (*ālocana*) and so forth, it presents the object to the intellect; thus, by producing the form of the intellect as delimited by the object, it functions as an object of enjoyment.
This inclusion is logically established.
91) This is stated in the venerable Pauṣkara:
"The sequential origination of wind and the other elements is now described:
wind, fire, water, and earth—this is the tetrad."
From the subtle element of touch, Anila (the wind) came into being, characterized by the nature of expansion;
it is beneficial as the cause of activities such as lifting and so forth.
Existing within the bodies of all living beings in ten ways,
it functions under the designations of prāṇa, apāna, samāna, vyāna, udāna, and so forth.
Fire is born from the subtle element of form (rūpatanmātra), characterized by the act of cooking;
it exists in the world in three ways, known by such names as Gārhapatya and the rest.
Therefore, the Śaiva fire is indeed distinct from that [ordinary fire]; it resides within the interior of the Bindu, and whatever this world eats is digested by this very fire alone.
Therefore, this fire is exceedingly beneficial to living beings;
from the subtle element of taste (rasa-tanmātra), water arose, which performs the function of cohesion.
By water alone the stability of this worldly substance is maintained;
and by this very element, the earth—which is inherently composed of dust—is indeed made firm.
The earth arose from the subtle element of smell, characterized by the function of supporting;
wind is not born from space, nor does fire originate from wind.
Water does not arise from fire, nor earth from that [water], because we observe an excellence of qualities [in each subsequent element].
Therefore, the transfer of qualities into effects is logical as being derived from their causes, and not spontaneously.
If the order of creation were such that [space arose from the five subtle elements], then space would possess five qualities;
for from the five subtle elements (tanmātra) is born the pentad beginning with space. Thus it is said.
Likewise, in the venerable *Matanga*:
"The subtle sound-tanmātra came into being; it is not perceived at all."
The word "only" (tanmātra) is used for the purpose of excluding any remaining objects.
From this arises the subtle element of touch (sparśa-tanmātra), accompanied by sound;
likewise, the subtle element of form (rūpa-tanmātra) is accompanied by sound and touch.
"Then there is another, the subtle element of taste, which is endowed with the triad previously mentioned;
likewise, the subtle element of smell is also endowed with a tetrad."
And in the venerable *Mṛgendra* (6.101–104):
"The pentad of elements consists of ether, wind, fire, water, and earth."
Sound and the other [elements] possess one additional quality each, and they have space and so forth as their substratum.
The qualities [of sound] manifesting as shaking, burning, flooding, and harshness reside in air and so forth;
in space, they consist of sounds and their corresponding echoes.
"Arrangement, providing space, cooking, and the grasping and holding [of objects]—these are the functions of air, ether, fire, water, and earth. Thus [it is said].
Elsewhere [it is said]: "Sound is a specific quality of space because it exists apart from its substratum. (Mṛgendra-pramāṇa 11.17–19)
This reason, as stated by the Vaiśeṣikas, is understood to be a fallacious reason (hetvābhāsa).
And that which is taught at an improper time is sublated by perception and scripture:
"There is a clanging sound in the earth, a splashing sound in water, and [a crackling sound] in fire."
A crackling, snapping sound, like the rustling of leaves, and an echo in the wind and sky—thus [it is said].
And in the *Śrīmālinīvijayottara*:
"Thus, among the five [elements], this [quality] is sound; touch exists in the four elements:
coldness and heat in earth and air, and coldness and heat in water and fire."
In fire, color is brilliant; in water, it is white; on earth, it is manifold, such as white and so forth. Taste exists in three [elements], being sweet in water; on earth, it is of six kinds.
Odor is considered by the wise to be of two kinds on earth: unpleasant and pleasant.
Furthermore, there are the functions of expansion, providing space, cooking, cohesion, and support.
The functions of air, space, fire, water, and earth [are found] in the body; and earth resides in the bones, flesh, hair, skin, nails, and teeth.

Water situated in the heart, in the digestive fire, or in the eyes [produces] urine, blood, phlegm, sweat, semen, and so forth; likewise, light [produces these] in the case of bile, because one perceives their respective properties therein.
"By means of the distinctions in its functions, such as prāṇa and so forth, the wind has indeed been described to you. Thus [it is said].

(Pratyabhijñā-hṛdaya 12.26–30) 94) Bodies composed of these thirty-one principles, beginning with *kalā*, serve as the instruments of experience for persons. However, that which is the cause for the movement to and from other worlds is called the *puryaṣṭaka*.
The subtle body (*sūkṣmaśarīra*). And that consists of the five *tanmātras*, the mind (*manas*), the intellect (*buddhi*), and the ego (*ahaṃkāra*).
As it is stated in the *Triśatika-kālottara*:
"Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth."
"Mind, intellect, and ego—this is declared to be the city of eight. Thus [it is said].

There is also an inference for its existence: the soul’s movement to the next world and so forth is accomplished by some instrument, because it is an action, like the action of the gross body. And since this cannot occur spontaneously for the all-pervading soul, it must be conditional (aupādhika).
Its establishment [is achieved] by means of "being expressible" as a limiting condition (*upādhi*).
Thus, it is established that the five fetters (pāśas) consist of the power of concealment (tirodhāna-śakti), limited agency (mala), māyā, and karma.

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Category of Bonds" (pāśapadārtha), in the *Śaivaparibhāṣā* composed by the venerable Jñānaśivācārya, the foremost lord of yogins devoted to Śiva and protector of the Śaiva tradition who transcends the distinctions of caste and stage of life.
The Fifth Chapter:

1) By not coming into contact with these fetters, this self gradually attains liberation, characterized by the manifestation of the bliss of Śiva through identity with Śiva. For instance: the Brāhmaṇa...

When a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, a virtuous Śūdra, or one born of the *anuloma* castes from a woman of the same or higher varṇa, becomes endowed with equanimity toward action and the ripening of past impressions (*saṃskāra*), then the supreme power of the Lord descends upon him. At that time,
faith arises in him for the knowledge of the highest good, and [this faith] is dependent upon perceiving the defects inherent in sense objects.
Dispassion arises. Having thus become dispassionate, he approaches the teacher’s household for the sake of knowing the supreme good (*śreyas*).

And from that teacher, having received the initiation into the rules (*samayadīkṣā*) based on his own qualification inferred through devotion and other qualities, he [observes] the duties of a *samayin*: the protection of the grove of Śiva, the sweeping of the temple of Śiva, and [the preparation of] materials for the worship of Śiva.

He performs the gathering of flowers and other offerings, the worship of Śiva’s devotees, the smearing of ashes, the application of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), the wearing of rudrākṣa beads, and so forth.

2) For one who practices in this manner, the descent of power (śaktipāta), which previously existed in a very mild form, becomes more intense. At that time, faith arises in him toward the worship of Śiva, the study of the Āgamas, and so forth. Subsequently, through a guru who recognizes the ripening of such faith, [he engages] in the study of the Āgamas, the worship of Śiva, and other [practices].
He receives the special initiation (*viśeṣadīkṣā*) which serves as the cause [for his status].

Immediately thereafter, faith arises toward the study of the scriptures and other practices taught by the Guru. He performs the duties of a *putraka*, such as the worship of Śiva and so forth; thus he follows both the duties of a *putraka* prescribed in the Āgamas and those of the Vedic tradition.
For one who practices the daily rites and so forth, the descent of power (śaktipāta), which previously existed only in a mild state, becomes intense.

Then, because the impurities have become thoroughly ripened, a desire to know the reality (tattvajijñāsā) arises regarding the meanings of the scriptures as they are initially understood, in accordance with their internal consistency from beginning to end. Immediately thereafter—

From that Guru who possesses such direct realization, he receives the initiation into liberation (*nirvāṇadīkṣā*), which destroys all accumulated karma that acts as an obstacle to the knowledge of reality. Immediately thereafter, he realizes that his own limited knowledge and other such qualities are produced by the impurity of karma and so forth, whereas omniscience and other such attributes are his natural state through identity with Śiva.

One proceeds by means of the teacher’s instruction; immediately thereafter, having established that very same reality through logical arguments, one meditates upon it without interruption. Thus, through uninterrupted practice, the knowledge of one's true nature (*svarūpajñāna*) is manifested by the grace of the teacher, aided by its own maturation. At that very moment, [it is also manifested] by means of the impurity (*mala*).

He becomes completely liberated. Thus, even though he is freed from impurity, he remains experiencing the bondage of the body due to *prārabdha* (commenced) karma. Likewise, although he has no further need for the karma that produced that [liberating] knowledge because he has attained perfected knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), he may sometimes perform it; at other times, he does not.

He renounces that [world]. Sometimes he performs even intense actions, yet he is not tainted by them. Thus he experiences the pleasure or pain that is the fruit of *prārabdha* karma; nevertheless, he does not become attached to it, nor does he despair. Abiding thus, at the end of the enjoyment of *prārabdha*, due to the absence of both impurity (*mala*) and karma—

Since even *māyā* cannot act as a binder through the medium of the body and so forth, one becomes unified and attains the non-worldly, marvelous, and ineffable bliss of Śiva, which consists of the undivided form of Being-Consciousness (*saccid-ātmaka*). This alone is the attainment of liberation (*mokṣa*). All of this is established in due order.
3) For instance, in initiation (*dīkṣā*), the four castes (*varṇa*) and the six *anuloma* [castes] are eligible. The *anuloma* castes include the *savarṇa* and others.
Among them, one born from a Brāhmaṇa father and a Kṣatriya mother is a *savarṇa*; likewise, one born from that same [Brāhmaṇa] father and a Vaiśya mother is a *savarṇa*.
The Niṣāda is born from that very same [Kṣatriya] father upon a Śūdra mother; the Pāraśava is born from that very same [Kṣatriya] father upon a Śūdra mother.
The Mahiṣya is born from a Kṣatriya father upon a Vaiśya mother; the Dauṣyanta is born from that very same [Kṣatriya] father upon a Śūdra mother.
The Ugra is born from a Vaiśya father upon a Śūdra mother. Apart from these ten, [there are those eligible for] initiation (*dīkṣā*).
They are not qualified [for other means]. Regarding their entitlement to hearing the Āgamas, Purāṇas, and so forth:
"Other Brāhmaṇas, O Viṣṇu, as well as kings, and likewise Vaiśyas, are qualified for the practice of knowledge according to their respective degrees."
For a Śūdra who serves [the higher castes], there is knowledge through the Purāṇas alone;
for all others as well, the practice of knowledge is prescribed.

Because [the scripture] prohibits listening to other languages by means of such passages as, "In time, even that [other language] may be beneficial to them," and so forth; and although the word *anya* (other) here also brings to mind those who are *anuloma* (of mixed caste), nevertheless...

Since the study of the Vedas, the hearing of the Bhāgavata, and so forth are mentioned in various places for those born in the natural order (*anuloma*), such as Jāmadagnya and Vidura, this [prohibition] refers to others besides them. And thus,
while there is no entitlement to the study of the Āgamas for those other than those born in the natural order of the castes (*varṇa-anuloma*),...

There is likewise no eligibility even for the initiation that is a constituent part [of the main rite], because eligibility for a subsidiary (aṅga) belongs only to one who is eligible for the principal (pradhāna). Even though it has been said:
"Initiation should indeed be performed for all those who are joined with the application of its power," [this does not apply here].
It applies to all three castes, but not to Śūdras or those of the lowest birth.
Thus, eligibility for initiation has been prohibited; nevertheless:
"But those Śūdras who do not drink liquor, who are devoted to purity, proper conduct, and ritual observances, and who are devotees of Śiva—for them initiation should be performed, and not otherwise."
Thus, since the prohibition has been established as referring to unworthy Śūdras,
the qualification belongs exclusively to the worthy Śūdra.
4) Likewise, the ripening of impurities and the equilibrium of karma are specific qualifications of the qualified candidate.
"Because of such statements as: 'The ripening of impurity itself is, however, the cause of grace.
O best of Brahmins, O twice-born ones, when that disciple's [karmic] actions have reached equilibrium..."
The Śāmbhavī power, a mass of consciousness, falls intensely into that.

And because of such statements as these: therein, "equality of karma" refers to two actions of equal strength that have contrary results—whether they are of the nature of merit, of the nature of demerit, or of the nature of both merit and demerit—simultaneously tending toward the production of their fruits. And this occurs by means of the removal of the power of concealment (*tirodhāna-śakti*).

The phrase "the cause for the descent of the power of grace" (*anugrahaśaktinipāte hetuḥ*) is an epithet of the qualified recipient (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*). Since, when there is an inequality of strength and when the fruits are not contradictory, the experience of that fruit is inevitable, the power of concealment (*tirodhānaśakti*) cannot be revoked; therefore, in that case, there is no "equalization of karma" (*karmasāmya*).
To exclude that [possibility], the qualifiers "having equal strength" (*tulyabalatva*) and "having contradictory results" (*viruddhaphalatva*) have been employed.

For the "maturation of impurity" (*malaparipāka*) is a specific state characterized by a tendency toward disjunction (*viśleṣaunmukhya*). Even the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) upon an eligible person (*adhikārī*) who possesses such maturation of impurity and so forth occurs only after that maturation and the like, whereas previously it was obstructed.
When maturation and the other stages have occurred, that [grace] is clearly manifest as a disposition toward bestowing favor.
The signs of this descent of power (*śaktipāta*) are aversion to worldly existence, the desire for liberation, devotion to Śiva, and so forth.
Only after recognizing the qualified candidate by these signs should initiation (*dīkṣā*) be performed by the Guru. And the Guru...

It concerns the four castes alone. Among them, the Brāhmaṇa is the teacher for the four beginning with the Brāhmaṇa and for the six *anuloma* [castes]. The Kṣatriya is the teacher for nine beginning with the Kṣatriya. The Vaiśya is the teacher for eight beginning with the Vaiśya. The Śūdra is the teacher for the Śūdra alone. Regarding the sequence of the stages of life (*āśrama*) as well, the renunciant (*saṃnyāsī*)...

The renunciant (*saṃnyāsin*) and the others constitute four [categories]. The forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) belongs to three, beginning with the forest-dweller. The householder (*gṛhastha*) belongs to two, the householder and the student (*brahmacārin*). As for the student, if he is a lifelong one (*naiṣṭhika*), then he belongs to three, excluding the renunciant. Of the aforementioned form...

In the absence of a [Brahmin] teacher, a Kṣatriya may be the teacher of a Brāhmaṇa; a Vaiśya may also be the teacher of a Kṣatriya; and a Śūdra may be the teacher of a Śūdra alone. A Śūdra can never be the teacher of one of a higher varṇa. Likewise, according to the sequence of the stages of life (āśrama), a forest-dweller (vānaprastha) may be the teacher of even an ascetic (saṃnyāsin), and a householder may be the teacher of both the forest-dweller and the ascetic.

Even among those who are celibate students (*brahmacārī*), householders (*gṛhastha*), forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*), or renunciants (*saṃnyāsin*), as well as those belonging to the four castes (*cāturvarṇika*), one who is endowed with conduct, age, lineage, virtues, physical form, and so forth, and is free from defects, is indeed a teacher (*guru*). Furthermore, a teacher is not one who possesses the nature of a beast; rather—

Having attained the state of Śiva through the direct realization dependent upon the ripening of hearing, reflection, and meditative absorption (nididhyāsana) regarding the Nigamas, Āgamas, and other scriptures;
and having assumed the form of the Teacher (Ācārya) by means of the fourfold descent of grace (śaktipāta).
The Blessed One bestows grace upon all of them as well.

"The teacher is indeed Śiva himself," as stated in such passages; for this reason, the acceptance of a figurative sense— that Śiva is the agent of grace through his presence in the teacher just as he is in the ritual jar (kumbha) and other implements— is [rejected].
Because it would be illogical if there were no sublation of the primary meaning; thus, the qualified candidate must first receive the *samaya-dīkṣā* from such a guru in the manner described.

5) The general definition of initiation (*dīkṣā*) is: the activity of Śiva capable of accomplishing either the entitlement to the scriptures of the Āgamas and so forth, or the entitlement to hearing the scriptures and so forth. Among these, both the initiatory rite of the rules (*samayadīkṣā*) and the specific initiation (*viśeṣadīkṣā*) consist of service to the abode of Śiva, worship of Śiva, and the daily rites and so forth.

The *nirvāṇadīkṣā* (initiation for liberation), however, brings about the qualification for hearing, reflecting upon, and so forth, the *āgamas*. The mention of "the activity of Śiva" is intended to exclude those activities restricted to the specific duties of the four castes (*cāturvarṇika*) and other fixed occupations. Furthermore, this initiation is distinguished by types such as the visual (*cākṣuṣyā*) and others.

It is sevenfold. Among these, the gaze with the intention of liberating from the bonds of *pāśa* is the visual initiation (*cākṣuṣī dīkṣā*). With that same intention, touching [the disciple] with the right hand is the tactile initiation (*sparśadīkṣā*).
With that same purpose, the utterance of the *saṃhitā* mantra is the vocal initiation (*vācikī dīkṣā*). This is the liberation from his *pāśas*.

Mental initiation (*mānasadīkṣā*) is the mental contemplation [by the teacher] with the thought, "Let it be so. Scriptural initiation (*śāstradīkṣā*) is the imparting of the scriptures with that same intention. Yoga initiation (*yogadīkṣā*) is the union with Śiva for that very purpose. The sacrificial initiation (*hautrī*) is characterized by the presence of the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*), the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), and other such requirements; it too is of two kinds: that which possesses knowledge (*jñānavatī*)...

And it is called "possessing action" (*kriyāvatī*). That [initiation] in which the ritual acts performed in the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), and so forth, are accomplished sequentially by means of the mind alone, is the "possessing knowledge" (*jñānavatī*) initiation.
This *jñānavatī* initiation is clearly explained in the *Śaivasannyāsapaddhati*; it should be consulted there. However, where...
Through physical activity, that [practice] is possessed of action (*kriyāvatī*). Even that which is possessed of action is of two kinds: seedless (*nirbījā*) and with seed (*sabījā*).

Among these, for those who are incapable—such as women, children, the elderly, and those afflicted by disease—the practice is "seedless" when it consists merely of purifying one's conduct according to the rules (*samaya-ācāra*), yet remains devoid of the actual conduct of the *samaya*. This too is of two kinds.

[There are two types: that which grants immediate liberation (*sadyonirvāṇadā*) and that which grants non-immediate liberation (*asadyonirvāṇadā*). That in which even *prārabdha* karma is purified is "that which grants immediate liberation. Although it is established in various places that *prārabdha* [karma] is destroyed only through experience (*bhoga*), nevertheless, that refers to the case of *prārabdha* with intense momentum. For *prārabdha* indeed...

It is fourfold, distinguished by the categories of intense-velocity (*tīvravega*), slow (*manda*), and dormant (*supta*). Among these, for those of intense velocity, there is no destruction [of the bond] without [experiencing] worldly enjoyment (*bhoga*). For the slow, there is destruction through the consumption of enjoyment, preceded by the conjunction (*saṃyojana*) and the generation (*sañjana*) [of the seed] during initiation (*dīkṣā*). But for the dormant, there is destruction even without the consumption of enjoyment. And thus, where...

Having recognized an extremely intense descent of power (*śaktinipāta*) residing in the disciple, as well as such a ripening of impurity (*malaparipāka*), and knowing that the *prārabdha* karma is weak or dormant, the most capable Guru effects its destruction either by means of the enjoyment of experiences (*bhogabhojana*) or without it; that [initiation] is the "bestower of immediate liberation" (*sadyonirvāṇadā*). In which [case]:
It does not involve the purification of *prārabdha* (karma already in motion), yet it bestows immediate liberation (*sadyonirvāṇa*).

When performed by those capable of following the rules of conduct (*samayācāra*), it is "with seed" (*sabījā*). This [initiation] is also of two kinds: that which conforms to the nature of Śiva (*śivadharmiṇī*) and that which conforms to the nature of the world (*lokadharmiṇī*). It is that wherein there is the purification of both dharma and adharma.
That is the *śivadharmiṇī* (the state characterized by Śiva). That in which there is the purification of mere unrighteousness (*adharma*) is the *lokadharmiṇī* (the state characterized by the world).

The *kriyāvatī* (active/initiative) initiation is of three kinds according to another classification: the *samayadīkṣā*, the *viśeṣadīkṣā*, and the *nirvāṇadīkṣā*. That in which one is joined to the state of Rudra is the *samayadīkṣā*.

That which effects union in the state of Īśvara is the *viśeṣadīkṣā* (special initiation). In both of these, there is no cutting of the topknot (*śikhā*). That which effects union in the state of Śiva is the *nirvāṇadīkṣā* (initiation of liberation). Where renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) follows the *nirvāṇadīkṣā*, there indeed is the cutting of the topknot.
Since it is taught that the purification of the paths (*adhva-śuddhi*) must be performed during the initiation into *nirvāṇa*, the paths are now described.
(6) Furthermore, the path is sixfold, distinguished by mantra, word (*pada*), phoneme (*varṇa*), world (*bhuvana*), principle (*tattva*), and energy (*kalā*).
Among these, each subsequent one pervades each preceding one. There are eleven mantras and eighty-one words.

There are fifty phonemes (*varṇa*), two hundred and twenty-four worlds (*bhuvana*), thirty-six principles (*tattva*), and five energies (*kalā*). Among these, within the energy of *nivṛtti* (retrogression), there is the single principle known as Earth (*pṛthivī*), and one hundred and eight worlds beginning with Kālāgni. Within that—

Within the casket of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), there are six [worlds]; ten in each of the ten directions beginning with the east; and two above. Thus, there are one hundred and eight worlds. There are two mantras called Sadyojāta and Hṛdaya; twenty-eight words (pada); and one phoneme (varṇa). [This concludes the enumeration] of the words and phonemes.
Its essential nature has been demonstrated elsewhere. Its color is yellow; its mandala is square;

its objects are smell and the rest; its cause is Brahmā. Within the *pratiṣṭhā* kalā, there are twenty-three principles (*tattvas*), which consist of those beginning with water and ending with primordial nature (*prakṛti*). There are fifty-six worlds (*bhuvanas*).

And those [mantras], beginning with Āmareśa and ending with Śrīkaṇṭha, are eight each in water, fire, air, and ether; and eight each in the ego-principle (ahaṅkāra) which contains the subtle elements (tanmātra), the sense organs, and the mind, as well as in the intellect (buddhi) and the unmanifest (avyakta).
The two mantras are Śiras and Vāmadeva. There are twenty-one words and twenty-three syllables. [The first] syllable...
[The kalā] Śuklā; the maṇḍala is in the shape of a half-moon; the objects [of experience] are taste and so forth; the cause is Viṣṇu.

In the category of Vidyā-kalā there are seven principles (*tattva*). These consist of those beginning with Puruṣa and ending with Māyā. There are twenty-seven worlds (*bhuvana*); these are those beginning with Vāmā and ending with Aṅguṣṭhamātra. Among them, there are six in Puruṣa.
In *rāga*, *niyati*, and *māyā*, there are five each; in the others, two each. The mantras are *śikhā* and *ghora*.
There are twenty *padas*. The syllables (*varṇas*) are seven. The color is crimson. The mandala is a triangle.
The objects (*viṣayas*) are form and the rest. The cause is Rudra. In the *śāntikalā*, there are three *tattvas*; these are...

The [realms] beginning with Śuddhavidyā and ending with Sadāśiva are eighteen worlds (*bhuvana*). These begin with Vāma and end with Sadāśiva. Among them, there are nine in Vidyeśvara, eight in Īśvara, and one in Sadāśiva.
The mantras are Tatpuruṣa and Kavaca; the words (*pada*) are eleven; the phonemes (*varṇa*) are three; and the mandala is...

The hexagon. The objects are touch and so forth. The cause is Īśvara. Within the *kalā* beyond peace (*śāntyatīta*), which consists of the two principles (*tattva*) known as Śakti and Śiva, there are fifteen worlds (*bhuvana*). These range from Nivṛtti up to Anāśrita. Among them, four are in the principle of Śakti, and eleven are in the principle of Śiva. [These are] Śiva, Astra, and Īśāna.
There are three mantras, one word, and sixteen phonemes. [The deity is] white in color, with the luster of crystal.

The mandala is circular. The object is sound. The cause is Sadāśiva. Thus, purification must be performed through the sequence of conjunction and so forth within the *kalās* that contain the five paths (*pañcādhvan*).

7) This being the case, having received the initiation into the *samaya* (pledge), one should practice the duties of a *samayin* as instructed by the Guru. The duties of a *samayin* include such things as serving the temple of Śiva and the devotees of Śiva, as well as wearing the *tripuṇḍra* mark and *rudrākṣa* beads. For him—
And this is the conventional designation for the path of the *samayin*.
Furthermore, this practice of wearing the triple horizontal mark (*tripuṇḍra*) and the rudrākṣa beads, and so forth, is not to be performed by the *samayin* alone;
rather, it must be performed by everyone as a constant duty (*nityakarman*), just like other obligatory rites. In the event of non-performance—

Because it is enjoined as obligatory through the hearing of [passages on] sin (*pātaka*) and so forth, through praise for the faith in its performance, and through statements regarding its necessity; for instance, in the *Skanda Purāṇa*, the sin incurred by non-performance is heard:
"In the case of the triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*), the smearing with ashes (*uddhūlana*), and so forth, as well as in the hearing of the rules concerning them..."
Those in whom no desire arises are possessed of great sin. Thus it is said.
In the Vāsiṣṭhalaiṅga: "O Brahmin,
those in whose hearts there is constant aversion toward sacred ash,
their lineage shall become mixed."
(Chapter 5, Verses 26–27) Those whose anger is constant upon seeing the ash on the forehead—
their mixed origin should be inferred by the wise. (Chapter 5, Verse 22)
"Those men who, upon seeing one who wears the sacred ash, revile him with words—
their birth from a Śūdra should be inferred by the wise" (Agni Purāṇa 5.23).
"Those men who, upon seeing one who wears the sacred ash, inflict physical blows..."
O Brahmin, it should be understood by the wise that their birth is from Caṇḍālas—those, O Sage, who never possess faith in the ashes prescribed by the Śrutis. (A 5, śloka 24)
"Regarding them, it is certain that the sacraments beginning with *garbhādhāna* do not exist. (A 5, śloka 25–26).
By such statements, it is heard that for those who do not perform [the rites], there is a confusion of births (*janmasāṅkarya*) and an absence of the sacraments of the twice-born.
Likewise, in the *Parāśara-upapurāṇa* (Chapter 3,
Verse 35): "Brāhmaṇas who are your devotees shall always be averse to the triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*) smeared with ashes, which is established in the Vedas and bestows liberation."
Thus, it is heard that the abandonment of this [practice] results in a curse. Likewise, in that same [text]:
"Faith toward the excellence of the Vedas, the excellence of Śiva, the excellence of the Vidyā, and likewise the excellence of the tripuṇḍra and the uddhūlana, shall belong to the meritorious."
For those who have attained perfection over many births and follow the injunctions of the Śruti and Smṛti,
the inclination toward the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) arises solely through the path declared in the Vedas.
Thus, faith in the *tripuṇḍra* and other such marks is praised as having the fruit of great merit. Likewise, in that same [text]:
"A Brāhmaṇa [should wear] the *tripuṇḍra* produced according to the rule with ash alone."
One should always wear the horizontal smearing of ashes upon the forehead.
(a. 5, ślo.

25–26) Thus, by means of the application of the word "eternal" (*nitya*), the injunction is seen [in the scripture] beginning with the Brāhmaṇa section: "The triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*) should be worn with ashes."
For this very reason, a Brahmin should always wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra).
"One should always wear the *tripuṇḍra* with ashes established by the Vedas" (Parāśaropapurāṇa, Chapter 5, Verses 27–28).
Thus, a prescription is seen through the use of the word "always. Furthermore, in that very same [text]:

"One should not, even out of delusion, abandon the application of ash—established by the Vedas—for marking the body with the triple line (tripuṇḍra), nor the worship of the Liṅga of Rudra. Thus it is said.
And in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"One should wear the tripuṇḍra with devotion; one should not transgress it even in thought."
Thus, renunciation is prohibited. 9) Likewise, the wearing of rudrākṣa beads is obligatory, because the fault incurred by its non-performance is proclaimed in such texts as the Skanda Purāṇa:
If a Brahmin, out of delusion, performs any Vedic rite while not wearing rudrākṣa beads, he will certainly fall into hell.
Thus, the fault in not wearing them is proclaimed in the *Bṛhannāradīya*:
"At the end of many births, by the grace of Mahādeva,
faith in wearing the rudrākṣa beads arises spontaneously."

Thus ends the statement regarding faith as having merit as its fruit. In the Skanda Purāṇa: "Endowed with supreme devotion, one should always wear a rudrākṣa on the neck, the head, as a sacred thread (upavīta), or on the ears or both hands."

Thus ends the discussion on the word "constantly" (*nitya*). In the *Vāyavīya* [Purāṇa], it is stated: "One should not wear the rosary without devotion; one should always wear it with devotion alone. This injunction should be understood as being connected with the word "always" (*sadā*). And this is a duty for the initiate (*samayin*).

If, in that very birth, one does not obtain the initiation for specific liberation (*viśeṣanirvāṇadīkṣā*) and so forth, [the rite] grants the fruit of *sālokya* (residing in the same world) and then produces liberation after an interval of two births or an interval of one birth.
As stated in the *Śivadharmottara*:
Now, those who constantly worship the Śiva-yogins with devotion attain great enjoyments and, in the end, the yoga of Śaṅkara.
Therefore, those who desire the attainment of enjoyments should worship the Śiva-yogins with shelter,
food, drink, beds, clothing, seats, and other such necessities.
Thus, whoever constantly practices devotion toward the Śiva-yogins shall attain yoga either in his second or third body.

Because it is established as such by statements beginning with these words; and although these rules of the initiate (*samayin*) are common to all *putraka*s and practitioners (*sādhaka*s), nevertheless, because they possess other non-common attributes, they are called "rules of the initiate. Thus...

Upon obtaining the qualification for the special initiation (*viśeṣadīkṣā*) through the performance of the duties of the initiate (*samayin*), one should perform the special initiation and then carry out the duties of a "spiritual son" (*putraka*), such as the worship of Śiva and the study of the Āgamas.
Thus, when the initiation of the initiate is specifically distinguished.
The disciple becomes fit for the knowledge of the fire-sacrifice and the scriptures.
Because the qualification for that [practice], consisting of the special initiation (viśeṣadīkṣā) endowed with the rules (samaya), has been established as existing;
therein, mental worship of Śiva is recommended. However, one who is unable to do so [should perform it] preceded by the fivefold purification.

One should perform the outer sacrifice (bahiryāga), which consists of consecration, adornment, offering, recitation of hymns, prostration, and so forth; likewise, one should also observe the duties of caste and stage of life (varṇāśramadharma),
because these serve as means for attaining the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna).

10) But let it be granted that these [rites] are indeed direct means for liberation, since they are so presented in the *Gautama-dharma*, the *Skandapurāṇa*, and other texts. Therein, in the *Gautama-dharma*:
"He who possesses these forty sacraments (*saṃskāra*) and the eight qualities of the self attains union with Brahman (*brahma-sāyujya*)."
"one attains residence in the same world"—thus it is established that ritual actions are direct causes of liberation. Likewise, in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"Liberation comes only from the proper observance of the duties of the social classes (varṇa) and stages of life (āśrama), and not otherwise."
Elsewhere also [it is said]: "Indeed,
Janaka and others attained perfection through action alone" (Bhagavad Gītā 3.20).
Thus it is heard [in scripture]. Nor is it logical to claim that because those [rites] are employed for other fruits, they have no connection with the fruit of liberation;

for if that were the case, it would follow that there is likewise an absence of connection between rites and the fruit of knowledge, since the nature of the rites is understood from their originative injunctions (*utpatti-vākya*) and [only subsequently related] by the two injunctions of qualification (*adhikāra-vākya*).

If it is argued that the connection with two separate results can be understood through the principle of "separateness of conjunction" (*saṃyogapṛthaktva*) by virtue of mutual independence, then it follows that in the present case as well, the connection with liberation as a result can likewise be stated; thus, the situation is identical.

11) If it is objected that it is not logical for ritual performance to be a cause of enjoyment by way of generating merit, we say no; for while those [actions] performed with a desire for enjoyment may indeed be causes of enjoyment, there is no contradiction in their producing liberation when performed with a desire for liberation. Otherwise, the same would apply to you as well.
For if they were practiced for the sake of producing knowledge, it would follow that they would produce [further] enjoyment;
nor is it logical that liberation could occur through mere ritual actions alone, since there is no means to terminate the accumulated karma acquired over many lifetimes except through knowledge.

Because they are to be discarded solely through the gateway of experience, by means of assuming a plurality of bodies dependent on the powers such as *aṇimā* (minuteness) and so forth, which are accomplished through yoga; and because, by the statement beginning with "merely from the conduct of the castes and stages of life," the causality of karma is also [established] by way of its exclusion from other factors.

Since it is appropriate to conceive of [action] as a means through an alternative (vikalpa), based on mutual independence, in order to avoid the contradiction between two statements; therefore, actions produce liberation directly and not by way of knowledge—do not say so. For it is said in the *Jñānatilaka*:
Neither by gifts, nor by austerities, nor by sacrifices, nor by fire-offerings, nor by restraints, nor by vows,
nor by the performance of ablutions at sacred fords is the supreme state attained.
By means of many accumulations of evil and many collections of merit,
they always bind themselves, just like worms in a storehouse.

This is because, through such arguments, it is established that actions are not the cause of liberation but, on the contrary, are the cause of bondage. Furthermore, liberation is not possible without the cessation of impurity (*mala*), since that which obscures the experience of the bliss of Śiva persists. Nor can there be the removal of impurity, which is of the nature of ignorance (*ajñāna*).
Cessation [of bondage] is possible only through knowledge;
that ignorance is removed by knowledge and not by ritual actions.
Having attained knowledge, one shall soon achieve union with Śiva.
Thus, because the *Śivadharmottara* establishes that impurity (*mala*) is removable by knowledge alone,

and because the destruction of accumulated karma is impossible in the absence of knowledge; for if it were destroyed through experience, the repeated acquisition of karma would remain unavoidable during the performance of ritual acts.
And because the incidental demerit does not cease; therefore, liberation is not attained through action alone.

12) Well then, let it be that knowledge and action together, as equally primary and combined, constitute the cause of liberation. For this very reason, even the sixfold set of faults resulting from the application of alternatives does not apply. Furthermore, the prohibition beginning with "not by gifts" is also justified as referring to actions performed without knowledge.
But in the case of a conjunction where there is equal primacy:
"Knowledge is primary, but not devoid of action;
action is primary, but not devoid of wisdom."
Therefore, the establishment of those two alone must occur;
for a bird does not fly on only one wing.
Just as food mixed with honey and honey mixed with food [are both superior],
so too are austerity and knowledge, when combined, a great medicine.
Such statements as these constitute the authoritative source [for this view]. Therefore, knowledge and action are the means to liberation with equal primacy. This is not so;
for indeed, no external ritual action is to be performed by that Great Soul.
"For one who is satiated by the nectar of knowledge and whose self is rendered helpless by devotion," as it is said in the *Śivadharmottara*:
"Neither the sectarian mark (*liṅga*) nor the conduct of the stages of life (*āśrama*) [is required] for one established in the Supreme Self."
Thus it is stated in the *Sarvajñānottara* (Vidyāpāda, verse 7):
"There is no meditation, no austerity, no worship, no fire-offering, and no ritual means."
And for him, O Maheśvarī, there is no need for rites such as the fire-sacrifice (agnikārya).
For him, there is no restrictive rule regarding the service of sacred fields, seats, and so forth; nor is there ritual worship, ancestral rites, pilgrimages, or religious vows.

Thus, in the *Devīkālottara*, because the prohibition of ritual action for one who has attained knowledge indicates that actions exist for the sake of knowledge, if actions were the direct cause of liberation— just like knowledge—
then they would have to be performed even after knowledge has arisen; however, if their status as a means is through knowledge, then [the door itself...]
Since that [knowledge] has been perfected, it is logical to prohibit actions for its sake, stating that such actions need not be performed.

Furthermore, since it is possible for actions to function through the medium of visible knowledge, it is improper to postulate that they function through an invisible (adṛṣṭa) medium. Even statements such as "knowledge is primary" are to be understood in light of the aforementioned prohibition.

Knowledge is primary; it is the direct cause [of liberation]. However, if that knowledge is deprived of its own generator—namely, action—it cannot produce its effect because it itself has not been brought into existence. Likewise, action is primary, as it must necessarily be depended upon for the production of knowledge. Therefore, by means of the intellect (*buddhi*), which serves as the medium...

That which is devoid [of the other] is not a producer. Therefore, it should be construed as being intent upon the conjunction of the means and the end—the state of being both door and doorway—in that liberation occurs only when both exist. 13) Regarding the production of knowledge by actions:
By the recitation of the Vedas,
by sacrifice, by study, by giving, by austerity, and likewise by fasting, [the gods are pleased].

"The wise man who desires to know is a sage (muni), and no other person"—this statement from the Skanda Purāṇa is the authoritative source. Nor is it correct to argue that because the words ending in the third case (*vedānuvacanāt* etc. are primarily construed with the verb "desires" (*icchatīti*), they can only serve as means for desire and not as means for knowledge.

In the expression "he wishes to go by means of a horse," although going is not the primary element in terms of the words, it is the primary element in terms of the sense; thus, by the principle stated in *Brahma Sūtra* 3.4.26— "And there is dependence on all [works] such as sacrifice,
because of the scriptural injunctions, just like the horse"— the Vedas, recitation, and so forth are connected to knowledge (*vedana*).
Even if one relies on primacy based on the literal expression (*śabda*), because the connection with knowledge (*vedana*) occurs through such a desire,

or even if one relies on worldly linguistic usage (*laukika-vyutpatti*), it is established that ritual actions (*karman*) are the means for attaining knowledge (*vedana*). However, in reality, when relying on the linguistic usage specific to the Mīmāṃsā system, the fifth mood (*liṅ*, optative) in the word "desires" (*icchatīti*) [indicates the injunction].

In connection with the injunctions such as the recitation of the Vedas (*vedānuvacana*), since these are prescribed for one who desires to know (*vividiṣu*), it is indeed understood from this very statement that ritual actions are the means to knowledge. Alternatively,
the statement "He for whom these forty sacraments (*saṃskāra*) exist" [establishes] that ritual actions are the means to knowledge.

Regarding the *māna* (means of knowledge): for the ritual acts (*saṃskāra*), like the impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and so forth, lack inherent capacity to produce a fruit and thus require a fruit-producing instrument that is to be assisted. In the present context, that which produces the fruit consisting of union with Śiva (*śivasāyujya*) is knowledge alone. Indeed, it is from knowledge alone—

The supreme Śruti states, "It is isolation (kaivalya)," and so forth, because [that state] is presented as the fruit of that [knowledge]. For it is more cumbersome to abandon what is present and imagine something not present; therefore, through knowledge assisted by the forty purificatory rites (saṃskāras), one attains union with Śiva.

Thus, by virtue of having this meaning—that "it comes to be"—the statement regarding purification (*saṃskāra*) serves as the authority for the fact that ritual acts are means to knowledge. Likewise, sacrifices and other such acts [are established];
for it is proclaimed: "Action (*kriyā*), practice (*caryā*), is the cause for the arising of knowledge."

By virtue of the scriptural statement, these [means] indeed produce knowledge. Likewise, even such things as dying in Kāśī are means for liberation only through the gateway of knowledge; for since impurity is removable by knowledge alone, liberation is impossible without it. Therefore, it is said in the Skanda Purāṇa:
The auspicious city of Śrī Vārāṇasī is eternally dear to me;
by the power of my compassion, for a living being departing from it with their life-breaths, [liberation is attained].
"I grant the saving knowledge of Brahman for your ultimate welfare, O Hari"—
thus it is established that [the Lord] is the means for that knowledge.
(14) Nor is it appropriate to ask how accumulated karma (*sañcitakarma*) is dissolved therein, because [it is dissolved] by knowledge.

For their cessation is possible through initiation (dīkṣā) performed by Śiva. Therefore, ritual actions (karmāṇi) are means to liberation only by way of knowledge (jñāna). Consequently, those seeking knowledge must perform both Vedic and Āgamic rituals; it is not only those prescribed in the Vedas and Āgamas that are to be performed.

Actions produce knowledge; moreover, even those transgressions that are neither enjoined nor prohibited therein, when performed as worship of Śiva, also become generators of knowledge. As stated in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"Those actions in the world which are prohibited and unenjoined..."
These constitute the supreme worship of Śambhu; this knowledge is the great sacrifice.
Whatever actions are entirely prohibited in the Śruti and Smṛti,
the knowledge that these are the means of propitiating Śambhu constitutes the Great Sacrifice (mahāmakha).

O you of excellent vows, even sinful deeds become utterly purified through the thought that they are for the sake of the Lord; this is indeed the truth, there is no doubt. Just as a great fire, having dried out wet wood, consumes it.
Likewise, sin committed with the thought that it is God becomes purified and bestows knowledge.
O twice-born ones, O best among those who know the meaning of the Vedas, even he who, having abandoned the Vedic and Tantric paths, follows his own intellect,
is declared by me to be a performer of sacrifice.
Everything accompanied by faith leads to the greatest welfare.
Because it is established as such by [the passage] beginning with "ityādi. And this is the dharma for those who have taken refuge (*prapanna*).

For one who has not taken refuge, only the dharmas of the [four] castes and stages of life (*varṇāśrama*) are to be practiced. Thus, while one is performing the duties of a *putraka*, when—by the power of fate—the initiation for *nirvāṇa* [occurs]...
In that case, it is impossible; rather, after experiencing the fruit of proximity, liberation occurs in a future birth.

However, when one obtains either the descent of the most intense or the more intense power and thereby receives the initiation into liberation (*nirvāṇadīkṣā*), then, through that initiation, there is the cessation of accumulated karmas and the removal of the impurities that obstruct the knowledge of reality.

One should engage in hearing [the scriptures] and other practices for the sake of knowing reality. This pure Śaiva Tantra should not be given nor revealed to anyone except to one who has been initiated, who is steadfast, and who is devoted to Śiva.
"Indeed, it is not praised to speak of this elsewhere than to one who is worthy of hearing it," because initiation is established as the prerequisite for the right to hear [the scriptures].
Although one who has studied the Āgamas may gain knowledge of the meaning merely through the mastery of words and their referents, [this alone is insufficient].

Nevertheless, if the intended meaning (*tātparya*) is not understood, then due to the immediate perception of contradictions between preceding and succeeding passages, the understanding would remain defiled by doubt and other such factors; therefore, for the sake of an undefiled comprehension, one must attend to *śravaṇa*, which consists in the thorough knowledge of the intended meaning. And this—
For as long as the knowledge of Śiva has not become firmly established within him,
for that long he must especially engage in hearing [the scriptures] and other such practices.
This has been prescribed by such passages as these.

16) Although the knowledge of the intended meaning (*tātparya-jñāna*) need not be enjoined— since it is already established through worldly experience as the cause for generating the knowledge of the sentence-meaning— nevertheless, this matter [is established] only through the investigation of the *Nigamas*, *Āgamas*, and so forth.
It is to be determined that [the object] is not [known] through the investigation of linguistic compositions and the like; thus, it is enjoined for the purpose of excluding others.

Consequently, like the injunction regarding threshing and so forth, this is a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*). And since there is no supreme *apūrva* to be accomplished by the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) resulting from the restriction in those cases, the status of being a restrictive injunction is appropriate; however, in this case—

It cannot be said that it is illogical because there is nothing to be accomplished by that [knowledge], for direct realization is logically established as being accomplished by it. For this very reason, the venerable Bādarāyaṇa stated: "And there is dependence on all [works], because of the scriptural texts concerning sacrifice and so forth, as in the case of the horse" (Brahma Sūtra 3.4.26), thus establishing that [liberation] is to be accomplished by all unseen forces (*adṛṣṭa*).

Thus, the nature of knowledge has been described. Knowledge arising from hearing likewise penetrates the non-difference between oneself and Śiva; it does not, however, penetrate difference through such relations as that of the controller and the controlled.
As it is said: "He who remembers, 'I am the Self, while Śiva is another, the Supreme Self' [is bound]."
Thus, whoever should cultivate this out of delusion shall not attain the state of Śiva.

"Śiva is one, and I am another; one should abandon the sense of separateness"—thus [it is said], preceded by the negation of the cognition of duality. (Sarvavīra-pāda, verse 39–40) — thus [it is said].
One should always contemplate non-duality, thinking: "I am indeed that which is Śiva."
By this statement from the *Sarvajñānottara* (verse 40), it is taught that the knowledge of non-duality alone is the means to liberation;
and this [knowledge] is [attained] from a Guru residing in the form of the Teacher, preceded by the initiation of liberation (*nirvāṇadīkṣā*).

[This applies] to all [the types of souls]. It should be understood that for the *vijñānākala* and *pralayākala*, initiation (*dīkṣā*) and knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) occur through the mere grace of Śiva, who is without substratum (*niradhikaraṇa*). Thus, when hearing (*śravaṇa*) has been accomplished, there follows the reflection upon its meaning by means of reasoning (*yukti*).

Meditation (*manana*) must be performed for the sake of stabilizing what has been heard (*śravaṇa*), by means of removing any unfitness [for such stabilization].
