Immediately thereafter, one must practice profound reflection (*nididhyāsana*), which consists of the continuous contemplation of the meaning of what has been heard, for the purpose of eliminating contrary impressions (*viparīta-bhāvanā*) and for achieving one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgrya*). For contrary latent tendencies (*vāsanā*), which have persisted since beginningless births, do not [subside] otherwise.

It is not removed by mere hearing once; rather, it is removed only by the latent impression (vāsanā) produced through meditation. When contrary impressions exist, direct realization (sākṣātkāra) is not possible. Likewise, without one-pointedness of mind (cittaikāgrya), there can be no direct realization of a subtle object, as is observed in the case of the direct perception of hair-nets and similar phenomena.
Therefore, for the cessation of contrary latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and for one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgrya*), one must practice meditative reflection (*nididhyāsana*). Furthermore,

when hearing (*śravaṇa*) and the other means are not sufficient for direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*), then, after experiencing the enjoyment of fruits by way of the path beginning with light (*arcirādi*), if there is the grace of Śiva at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*), liberation occurs right then and there.

In that case, in the absence of Śiva’s grace, liberation occurs in another birth through the Guru. But when [the practice] is complete, then, through the ripening of the Guru’s compassion, self-knowledge is manifested—just as by the proximity of the sun's rays. This very arising of direct realization is also the means to the fruit.

17) But surely, as long as the obscuring impurity (*mala*) exists, how can there be manifestation? Nor is it reasonable to say that manifestation occurs only after the cessation of the impurity, because you yourself accept that the cessation of the impurity is something to be accomplished by manifestation. Therefore, regarding manifestation and the cessation of the impurity...
To avoid mutual dependence, it must be admitted that impurity (*mala*) is indeed removable by initiation (*dīkṣā*).

And this is logical: since impurity is a substance (*dravya*), it must be removed by the activity of Śiva alone, just as defects such as those of glass are removed by medical treatment. Nor can impurity be [defined] merely as ignorance (*ajñāna*).

It is logical that [impurity] is removable by knowledge alone; for if the word "ignorance" (ajñāna) were to mean "error" (bhrānti), then since impurity lacks the nature of error, it would lack the property of being a predicate of the subject (pakṣadharmatva). Likewise, if it were to mean the "absence of knowledge," it would likewise lack the status of being a predicate of the subject.
Because there is a contradiction [in your position], as we observe that being brought to cessation by such an action applies only to substances that denote delusion (*bhrānti*).
Furthermore, if it denotes the individual soul (*āṇava*), then since that very soul constitutes the subject (*pakṣa*), there is no locus for grasping a concomitance (*sahacāra*).
Therefore, direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) is indeed the fruit; it is not a means. And thus, since the fruit is not something to be enjoined (*avidheya*), [the objection does not apply].
It should not be argued that the enjoinability of direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) is untenable; for this is an accepted consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*).

The injunction being heard, however, must be interpreted as meaning: "One should strive in such a way that direct realization is accomplished. Therefore, initiation alone is the means. For this very reason—
"Initiation alone liberates and leads one even to the supreme abode above"—
such statements as these are also consistent [with this view]. Therefore, direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) is not the means for attaining the fruit.
18) Not so;
for by such statements as "Indeed, that ignorance is to be removed by knowledge, not by ritual acts," the fact that ignorance is removable by knowledge is first established.

This is because it is denied that [impurity] can be removed by action; and because impurity, being of the nature of non-luminosity, must be removed by luminosity alone. Since the removal of darkness, which is of the nature of non-luminosity, is experienced through light and the like, there is no absence of a locus for observing concomitance. Nor [is this denied] on the grounds of its being a substance.

It cannot be argued that it is possible to infer either "being removable by action" or "not being removable by knowledge," because if "being other than ignorance" (*ajñānānyatva*) were cited as a limiting condition (*upādhi*), then "being other than the subject of the thesis" (*pakṣetaratva*) would also incur the status of a limiting condition.
This is not so, because [the inference] is sublated by scripture (*āgama*). Nor is there a mutual dependence between manifestation and the cessation of impurity.

For their absence is established just as it is in the case of darkness and light. For even there, since light does not arise while darkness exists, the cessation of darkness is required for the arising of light;

and the arising of light is required for the cessation of darkness—thus a mutual dependence (parasparāśraya) results. And that [dependence] is resolved by the fact that light arises only when darkness already exists.

Darkness ceases; or rather, it may be resolved that even between darkness and light there is indeed a co-existence for a mere moment, or that the cessation of darkness occurs through light existing at the same time; furthermore, causality does not consist in temporal priority, but rather in causal capacity (*śaktatva*). This same principle applies here as well.

Since this resolution is possible, there is no inconsistency whatsoever. Furthermore, the statement that "initiation alone liberates" refers merely to the necessity of initiation; it does not exclude the role of knowledge. Thus, there is no contradiction with that [other teaching]. Therefore, the removal of impurity occurs through direct realization alone. [The impurity] becomes manifest...

Direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) is indeed the knowledge of the true nature itself; it is not of the form of a mental modification (*buddhivṛtti*) or the like, because such a modification does not apply to the conscious principle (*cetana*), and because of the absence of a cause [for its production]. Nor is the word (*śabda*) itself the cause, since its inherent nature is to produce indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*), and thus it is incapable of producing immediate knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*).

It cannot be argued that because of a lack of capacity, the nature of the instrument (*karaṇa*) is not the determinant for [the status of] immediacy (*aparokṣatva*) and so forth, but rather the nature of the object (*viṣaya*). For if that were so, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that a sentence such as "this is a jar" could produce immediate knowledge regarding a jar situated in front of one. And this is not an acceptable conclusion.
For that [cognition] is universally accepted as producing knowledge of an object not present [to the senses] precisely with respect to one whose eyes are closed.

Furthermore, if it were the causal factor even for one whose eyes are not closed—who nonetheless possesses sense-object contact—then it would follow that such cognition would arise for anyone else as well. This is also the case in the instance of "You are the tenth," which arises from verbal testimony.

Immediately after indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*), direct sensory knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*) itself arises. It is not reasonable to ask for what purpose there is a dependence on words regarding sensory knowledge;
[for it serves] as that which completes the number ten.

Since the unity inherent in oneself does not appear in enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*), when it is made known by the statement "You are the tenth" that this inherent unity is indeed the completer of that number, its direct realization is appropriate.
For this very reason, [the realization] does not [occur] for one who knows that the unity inherent in their own self is not the completer of that number.
That statement is applicable. Therefore, a word does not possess the capacity to produce direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*).

19) Thus, one who is liberated through the direct perception [of reality] by virtue of knowing the nature [of the Self] as it has been manifested is called "liberated while living" (*jīvanmukta*). For such a person, there is no longer any action to be performed; nevertheless, from the arising of knowledge...

Due to the force of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) from the uninterrupted performance of actions in the past, he engages in the performance of action for the sake of exhausting his *prārabdha* karma and for the protection of the world; yet he is not bound by the merit produced by those actions. Nor is it the case that an action capable of generating merit [could not produce it in him].

It should be stated that this is because it does not produce [any result]. Just as fire does not burn one who possesses the power to paralyze fire, so too it is logical that even *karma* does not produce results for one who possesses knowledge of reality (*tattvajñānin*).
In this way, it is also logical that no demerit (*adharma*) arises even when one performs prohibited acts for the sake of experiencing what has already been commenced (*prārabdha-bhoga*).
The Nigamas, Āgamas, and other such texts, which inform us that action is the producer of that [result], are also a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*);

for they have as their purport the fact that action, when conjoined with the absence of the obstacle consisting in the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), is the producer of that [result]. This applies equally to prescribed and prohibited actions, and to friends and enemies.
And because there exists the capacity to produce merit and demerit;
for the statement establishing that [an action] produces merit or demerit residing in the agent or the object— which has a general scope—
is superseded by the specific case of an action performed by one who possesses the knowledge of reality, whether toward a friend or an enemy.
For it is logical that there should be a restriction [of the general rule] by means of Vedic statements which establish the meaning that [the performance of rites] produces merit and so forth.
20) But surely, immediately after the arising of the knowledge of reality, all karmas perish.
Just as a greatly blazing fire would consume even a mere log of wood,
so the fire of knowledge consumes both auspicious and inauspicious karma in an instant.
In the same way, the fire of knowledge reduces all actions to ashes.

This is because of such statements as [Bhagavadgītā 4.37]. And thus, since action no longer exists, experience is also impossible; therefore, the continued existence of the body for that purpose is not tenable. Or, let us grant that the *prārabdha* karma persists.

Even so, since one whose impurities have ceased possesses unobstructed knowledge, how could there be the experience of worldly pleasure, pain, and the like? For such experience is brought about by attachment and other passions, and in one who is stainless, attachment and the rest are absent. Therefore, it is illogical for a knower of reality to remain in the body.
"Liberation while living (jīvanmukti) is untenable"—do not say so.

For, according to such scriptural statements as "The prārabdha [karma] perishes through experience; the remainder is consumed by knowledge," the verse beginning with "Just as fire... refers specifically to karma other than that which has already begun to bear fruit (prārabdha).
Therefore, it must be admitted that *prārabdha* karma certainly persists.

Consequently, the persistence of the body is indeed required for the production of experience (*bhoga*) dependent upon that [karma]. Nor is it logical to ask how one who is pure could have experience governed by attachment and other such passions; for even in the absence of attachment and the like, [experience occurs].

For experience arises from the intention to exhaust the *prārabdha* (commenced) karma; or rather, experience arises through the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of passion and so forth. Therefore, even when the *prārabdha* karma is destroyed, experience is possible solely by means of that very latent impression.
21) Some, however, [quote]:
"Karma that has not been experienced does not perish even in hundreds of millions of kalpas" (Vāsiṣṭhalaiṅga, chapter 10, verse 33).

Because of such statements as these, they claim that all karma whatsoever is to be destroyed by experience (*bhoga*). They further maintain that even passages such as "the fire of knowledge" (*jñānāgni*) refer only to destruction by means of generating experiences through the assumption of a plurality of bodies (*kāyavyūha*), so as not to contradict the aforementioned scriptural declarations. This is not correct; for if everything were to be destroyed by experience, [it would lead to an absurdity].

Because there would be no distinction between *prārabdha* (commenced) and *aprārabdha* (uncommenced) karma, there would arise the contradiction of such scriptural statements as: "The *prārabdha* is destroyed through experience; the remainder is burnt away by knowledge. Furthermore, the statement "that which has not been experienced [is not exhausted]" is also explained by this very [reasoning].

Since it was stated that [the state] is communicated by means of words because it pertains to an object already commenced, there is no contradiction therein either. Furthermore, the definition of one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) is purity while being endowed with a body and so forth that are illusory (*māyika*). Moreover, this purity does not consist in the destruction of impurity (*mala*); for if impurity were a single entity, the consequence would follow that upon the liberation of one person, all would be liberated. Why? [Because they share the same impurity.]

Rather, it is the state of having the destruction of the conjunction with impurity (*mala*). Since this conjunction differs for each individual soul, even if it is destroyed in one case, it is not destroyed in another; thus, the aforementioned fault does not apply. Others, however, avoid the stated fault by distinguishing between the various powers of obscuration (*āvaraṇa-śakti*) corresponding to each [soul].
22) Furthermore, the signs of this one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) include laughter, weeping, leaping, and so forth.

Although these are common to those such as the insane, nevertheless, these signs are distinct from those caused by insanity and the like; they are produced by the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), compassion, and other such qualities. As it is said therein:

While the path taught in the Śiva-śāstras exists, people practice the path taught in the Paśu-śāstras out of ignorance. Alas! Such delusion has arisen even regarding a perceptible object—this realization is a source of laughter. [It arises] from the longing for the pleasure of the senses.

Compassion, which causes one to cry out, arises from the thought: "This person experiences great suffering; how can this be removed? The knowledge that one has crossed over the ocean of saṃsāra oneself is the cause for exultation.
As it is said in the *Tattvasāra*:
Endowed with fortitude and steadfastness, and ever enveloped in bliss,
he laughs and dances, and even weeps and leaps about.
Kārttikeya said:
You have described laughter and other such actions as the conduct of the lords of yogins;
I do not understand their meaning—O Lord, for what purpose do they perform these?
Īśvara said:
Having clearly corrupted [the path], people are devoted to the wrong way;
seeing them, the yogi laughs: "Alas! The world is utterly deluded!"
Having realized the unreality of existence, they sport within the midst of existence;
even while sporting, they are not defiled by it, and therefore the yogis dance.
Just as a fish greedy for flavor does not see the iron hook,
so too the world, greedy for pleasure, does not see the realm of Yama.
Deprived of the truth, he endures exceedingly terrible and great suffering;
therefore, that yogi cries out upon seeing the misery of worldly people.
"Thinking, 'I have indeed crossed to the far shore of the boundless ocean,' and being thus conceited, yogins prance about. Thus it is said.

In this very manner, the other signs mentioned in other scriptures are to be understood. Having ascertained someone to be liberated while living (jīvanmukta) by these signs, one should feel supreme affection for him and never any hatred. For if hatred is felt, sin would arise within oneself through that person's prohibited actions. And in such a case...

In the state of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*), because the veil has been removed through the direct realization of one's true nature (*svarūpasākṣātkāra*), the bliss of Śiva shines forth. Nevertheless, even pleasure and pain pertaining to sense objects may arise due to the force of mental distraction (*vikṣepa*). Therefore, supreme liberation alone is the highest human goal (*paramaḥ puruṣārthaḥ*).

23) Furthermore, proponents describe the nature of that supreme liberation in various ways according to their respective doctrines. For instance, the Cārvākas maintain that since the body alone is the source of suffering, with its destruction, suffering will no longer arise.

They say that liberation (*mokṣa*) is precisely the destruction of the self in the form of the body, which is the cause of all suffering. That is not so, because it would not be a human goal (*apuruṣārthatvāt*). Although the destruction of the root of suffering at the time of liberation is agreed upon by all disputants, nevertheless, that [destruction] cannot itself constitute a human goal. For indeed—

If it is argued that the avoidance of snakes, thorns, and so forth is indeed the human goal (puruṣārtha), and that the absence of suffering alone is the human goal—then is that the destruction of suffering, or the antecedent non-existence of suffering? Not the first, because as long as suffering has not yet arisen, its destruction cannot exist; and if it has already arisen, it is destroyed by the very knowledge of it.

Because human activity would otherwise be fruitless. Not the second [alternative], because the antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of suffering, being beginningless, cannot be something to be accomplished and thus cannot constitute a human goal (*puruṣārtha*). If it is argued that, in that case, let the destruction of the very cause of suffering be the human goal; we say no, because of the fault already mentioned. [This applies] to the self (*ātman*) as an enjoyer in the form of the body...

Furthermore, because it is non-existent at the time of liberation and is not being experienced, it cannot be a human goal (*puruṣārtha*), according to the principle that "a human goal is not something that is not known. Indeed, a human goal is such only when it is being experienced by one who desires it;
and the destruction of one's own self is not experienced by oneself, just as the body, being the source of suffering, is not [experienced as a goal].
Furthermore, since happiness as a source [of well-being] also exists, its destruction cannot be the intended goal.

Moreover, the doctrine that the body is the self has already been refuted. By this, the Madhyamaka position—that liberation is the cessation of the continuum of consciousness—is also refuted; for the destruction of consciousness cannot be the intended goal.

Furthermore, the doctrine of the momentariness of cognition has already been refuted. The Yogācāra position—that liberation consists in an uninterrupted stream of cognition free from affliction due to the absence of the coloring of objects—is also untenable, because of the absence of the body and other factors that serve as causes for cognition. Nor is it the case that the body functions as a cause only with respect to cognition as delimited by an object.
Because, for the sake of parsimony, its causality resides in cognition alone.

24) The Sāṅkhyas, however, declare that liberation (*kaivalya*)—which is *mokṣa*—consists in abiding in a state free from the superimposition of the effects of *prakṛti*, such as the *mahat* and so forth, upon the discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*) of *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*. For instance: *prakṛti* creates the *mahat* and so forth for the sake of the experience (*bhoga*) of the *puruṣa*.

It proceeds. Since enjoyment is impossible for the untainted *puruṣa* by its own nature, enjoyment must be said to arise solely from non-discrimination (*aviveka*) between the *puruṣa*, which has become the enjoyer, and the intellect (*buddhi*). And when non-discrimination between the *puruṣa* and the intellect ceases through the dawn of discrimination, enjoyment produced by non-discrimination becomes impossible; thus, [the *puruṣa*] remains in *prakṛti*.

It is argued that since the effects beginning with the Great Principle (mahat) are not produced, liberation (*kaivalya*)—which consists in abiding in a state devoid of those adjuncts—is possible. This is incorrect; for in this state of liberation, which is like the condition of a stone due to the absence of the light of consciousness, no desire can arise to abandon the enjoyments of the various worlds belonging to Sadāśiva and others.

If there were an unsurpassed happiness in liberation that was untouched by the sufferings of saṃsāra, then there would be a desire for it. However, since liberation consists merely in absolute isolation (kaivalya), which is opposed to all enjoyment, no one’s desire can arise for it. Therefore, absolute isolation is not the goal of human endeavor (puruṣārtha).
25) By this, the Naiyāyika position—that liberation (*mokṣa*) is the absolute cessation of suffering—is also refuted.

In their system, because the self (*ātman*) is devoid of specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) in the state of liberation, the absence of suffering is not cognized, and thus it fails to constitute a human goal (*apuruṣārtha*). [Objection: But surely, the absence of suffering...

The status of being a human goal (*puruṣārthatva*) belongs to [liberation] by its very nature (*svarūpeṇa*), and not by virtue of its being known. For activity does not proceed with the aim, "May I know the absence of suffering"; rather, it proceeds with the thought, "May suffering not be mine," or "May this suffering currently arising in me perish. This is true for pleasure and other goals as well; they are goals by their very nature alone.

If it is argued that [liberation] is for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*) and that knowledge is merely an invariable concomitant, we say no; for if the state of being free from suffering were not itself known, it would—like a swoon or similar states—not constitute a human goal (*apuruṣārthatva*). As it has been said: "Even the absence of suffering is not desired as a human goal if it is not cognized."
For a wise person is never seen to engage in activity for the sake of states such as fainting and the like. Thus [it is said].
By this, the view of certain Naiyāyikas— that liberation is the absolute destruction of the means of suffering— is also refuted.
26) The followers of Bhaṭṭa, however, say that liberation is the manifestation of eternal bliss. That too is not tenable:

is this manifestation something produced (*janya*) or unproduced (*ajanya*)? In the first case, is the manifestation the removal of an obscuration (*āvaraṇanivṛtti*) or knowledge (*jñāna*)? If you say it is the removal of an obscuration, that is our own position, and thus you would be guilty of contradicting your own tenets (*apasiddhānta*).

If it is argued that [liberation] is knowledge, then by the principle that "whatever is produced is impermanent," its perishable nature would entail the consequence that liberation is non-eternal. Furthermore, if manifestation were unproduced, it could not be accomplished by the person (puruṣa), and thus it would be unfit to be the goal of the person.
27) According to the Arhatas, however, liberation consists solely in the soul’s perpetual upward movement. Its upward movement occurs through the severance of bondage;
whereas in the state of transmigratory existence, there is downward movement despite the soul being naturally light.

It is argued that for one who has become heavy through the bondage of karma, it is logical that upward movement is impossible—just as it is for a gourd placed in water while remaining inside an iron cage; and that even upward movement would be logical only upon the dissolution of the bondage of karma and the breaking of the iron cage, just like the gourd. But this too is incorrect.
Because the atomic and intermediate dimensions of the self have been refuted, it is impossible for that which is all-pervasive to undergo movement;
furthermore, upward movement is not a human goal (*apuruṣārtha*), as it is distinct from both pleasure and the absence of pain.
(28) It is also not tenable to claim that liberation is the attainment of the status of Rudra, Viṣṇu, Indra, and so forth, because of that... [text truncated]
Because it is subject to destruction; for even those statements in the Purāṇas and other texts that establish its nature as liberation are intended only in a figurative sense of liberation.

29) Some, however, say that liberation is simply the release of the *sattva*. For it is thus: the Puruṣa’s state of being an enjoyer of *prakṛti* is beginningless. If it were to have a beginning, then since there would be no evidence for the existence of the Puruṣa prior to that [beginning], it would follow that the Puruṣa itself must also have a beginning. Furthermore, one cannot conceive of the cessation of that which is beginningless.

This is logical, for otherwise the cessation [of experience] would apply to the *puruṣa* as well. Therefore, even in the state of liberation (*mukti*), this [prakṛti] alone remains the enjoyer. However, there is this distinction: in the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), prakṛti—whose nature is pleasure obscured by pain and delusion—is the object of enjoyment through the power of karma; whereas in liberation...
The claim that primordial nature (*prakṛti*), consisting of *sattva* and characterized by unsurpassed bliss, is the object of experience because of the absence of karma—
this too is refuted by the very same refutation of the Bhāṭṭa view through the dilemma of whether [the state] is produced by experience or not.

30) Even identity with Śiva is not liberation. That identity occurs in four ways: through birth (*utpatti*), transition (*saṅkrānti*), immersion (*samāveśa*), and manifestation (*abhivyakti*). Among these, those who observe the Great Vow (*mahāvratin*) attain identity through birth. For instance, regarding liberation:
To that extent, there is equality with Śiva; and that [equality] consists in the nature of omniscience and so forth. Moreover, that arises only at that [final] moment;
otherwise, it would follow that it already existed previously. Therefore, equality with Śiva occurs precisely through the arising of qualities similar to the qualities of Śiva.

31) The Pāśupatas maintain that [the liberated soul] attains equality through transference (*saṅkrānti*). For instance, just as the fragrance of musk and the like transfers to cloth and other materials, so too do omniscience and other qualities residing in the Lord (*īśvara*) transfer to the liberated person. Therefore, there is equality through the transference of Śiva’s qualities.
32) The Kāpālikas attain equality through immersion (*samāveśa*); for it is thus: just as planetary spirits enter into men, so do the qualities of the Lord enter into those who are liberated.
Therefore, there is equality through the immersion in the qualities of Śiva.
33) Those who hold that [the soul] is a part of the Lord attain equality through manifestation. For instance:

just as with Śiva, omniscience and other attributes already exist in the souls from the very beginning; however, in the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), they do not shine forth because they are obstructed by impurity (*mala*). But in liberation, however—
It is manifested through the removal of impurities; therefore, there is equality with Śiva by virtue of the manifestation of one's own qualities.
34) In that regard, first of all, the position that [omniscience] arises simultaneously [with liberation] is untenable.
Since the body and other factors that produce knowledge are absent in liberation, the arising of omniscience is not possible;
for if it were subject to arising, it would follow that it is impermanent, and it would further follow that there is no distinction between liberation and [the attainment of] heaven and so forth.

35) The position that [liberation] consists in the equality of transition is also untenable. For instance: does "transition" mean the attainment of another substratum by abandoning one's own substratum, or without abandoning it?
Not the first; for if the transition of God’s knowledge into the liberated soul were admitted, [it would follow that] God...

Because it would entail the consequence of the non-existence of knowledge. Nor is the second [alternative] tenable, because since knowledge is partless, its transition by means of a part is impossible. Furthermore, there is a lack of evidence for the existence of such a consciousness.
This is established by the inference: "The knowledge of Śiva does not transfer elsewhere, because it is a quality (*guṇatvāt*)."

And because the absence of transmigration is established; nor is there a lack of logical necessity [for this argument]. For if a quality were to depart elsewhere while abandoning its substrate, it would follow that the identity between the quality and the qualified entity (guṇin) is destroyed, which renders the very nature of being a "quality" untenable. As it has been said:
"Qualities do not leave their own possessor to go to another possessor;
and for those things that do move, this established rule of entities is contradicted. Thus [it is said].
Indeed, by censuring brahmins and virtuous men, or by serving sinners,
evil is transferred to men and their own merit departs.
In one who is patient and does not revile others, merit transfers to men through their dwelling with the virtuous; likewise, evil departs from them to others.
Thus, in the Smṛtis and other texts, the transference of merit, demerit, and so forth is established. Likewise,
the transference of knowledge residing in the teacher to the disciple is heard in the *Svāyambhuva* and other works during the initiation of the teacher (*ācāryābhiṣeka*).
"This authority which has been transferred by me to you today must be exercised by you until it has been transferred to another. Thus [it is said].

And if it is argued that, in this way, the previously stated reason (*hetu*) "being a quality" (*guṇatva*) is inconclusive (*vyabhicāra*), we say no; for in the case of memory and so forth, a statement teaching the "transference" (*saṅkrānti*) of merit and demerit intends rather the production of something of that same nature.

Likewise, even a statement teaching the "transference" of knowledge intends [the production of a similar cognition] through the teacher’s instruction, such as in the exposition of the teacher's words and so on.
Because [the text] is intent upon establishing independence (*svātantrya*), there is no primary transference (*saṅkrānti*) in that case.

Nor is there a deviation [from the rule] because the fragrance of musk and the like is seen to transfer onto cloth; for even there, it is only the particles of the musk itself that are transferred. And in that instance, this is because [fragrance] lacks the status of being a quality (*guṇatva*).

Because there is no logical reason [for such a transfer]. Nor should it be argued that there is a deviation [in the inference] because the heat residing in fire is not observed to be transferred into water; for otherwise, burning would not occur in the hand or other parts upon contact with water. Even in that case, it is precisely the fire residing within the water—possessing unmanifest color—that acts as the burner. Thus, there is no [transfer] of a quality.
It is established that there is a transition elsewhere than from its own substratum; therefore, the position that the transition is identical [to the original] is indeed untenable.

36) Nor is there an identity with possession (*āveśa*); for if that were the case, it would follow that [the practitioner] lacks independence—just like one possessed by a spirit—and thus it would be unfit to be the goal of human endeavor (*puruṣārtha*).

37) The position that [liberation] consists in the equality of manifestation is also untenable. For that which consists in the manifestation of the activity of cognition cannot, by its very nature, constitute a human goal (puruṣārtha), since it is not distinct from the absence of pleasure and pain. Nor is the absence of pain at that time a human goal, because of its...
Because you do not accept [liberation] as liberation; for you admit that only the manifestation of knowledge and action,
denoted by the term "state of equality" (sāmyapada), constitutes such [liberation],
since it involves an equal balance of gain and loss through the abandonment of the various enjoyments of those respective worlds.

Furthermore, it is because [liberation] would lack the status of being for the sake of the person (puruṣārtha). Moreover, if the liberated one—who is distinct from Śiva yet equal to him—were to cease his dependence on Śiva, it would result in the subversion of Śiva’s sovereignty as the Lord of all. Upon the cessation of the liberated ones' dependence, [Śiva] himself, by virtue of possessing the power that is the cause of the world, would also...

Furthermore, it would entail the creation of the world [by the liberated soul]. Moreover, since there is no basis for differentiation between the liberated soul and Śiva, their distinction is not tenable. If liberation consists in equality with Śiva, is that liberation an equality in one respect or an equality in every respect? In the first case, since some degree of equality exists even for those who are bound, [liberation would be indistinguishable from bondage].

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that there is no distinction between the bound and the liberated. Even in the second case, if the liberated one lacks parts, then since there would be no differentiator between such a liberated one—who is partless, endowed with qualities such as omniscience, and independent—and Śiva, the liberated one would be Śiva himself; he would not merely be equal to Śiva. This is because of the liberated one’s...
If one accepts that [the self] possesses parts (*sāvayavatva*), then "possessing parts" must be defined as nothing other than being joined with a body such as the *bindu* and so forth;

for no other kind of "having parts" is possible. And if that were the case, it would follow that there is no distinction between the liberated (*mukta*) and the bound (*baddha*). Furthermore, absolute equality results in nothing but non-difference (*abheda*).
Therefore, liberation is not identity with Śiva.

38) Furthermore, liberation is precisely the experience of the bliss of Śiva through the state of oneness with Śiva. This is because, as taught in the *Śrī-sarvajñānottara* and other scriptures, the knowledge of one's own non-difference from Paramaśiva is the cause of liberation. Indeed, it is stated thus in the *Sarvajñānottara*:
The verses:
"That God who is all-pervading, the self of all, whose face is everywhere,
consisting of all principles, inconceivable, and established above all."
Transcending all principles and devoid of speech, mind, and name—that is I; thus one should worship with a non-conceptual mind.
Thus, this knowledge is fruitless, eternal, constant, and imperishable;
it is free from conceptual construction, indefinable, and devoid of causes and examples.
Without marks, imperishable, peaceful, beyond the range of sense-objects, inconceivable, and free from doubt—that is I; there is no doubt in this.
I alone am the supreme deity, Śiva, who consists of all mantras;
yet I am also beyond all mantras and free from creation and destruction.
All this—visible and invisible, moving and unmoving—is pervaded by me;
I alone am the Lord of the World, and from me everything proceeds.
The entire multitude of worlds, differentiated by manifold forms,
from Śiva down to the earth— all that is established within me.
Whatever is seen or even heard in this world,
all of that— distinguished by the division of external and internal— is pervaded by me.
"He who, out of delusion, contemplates thus: 'I am the self, Śiva is indeed another, the Supreme Self,' shall not attain the state of Śiva."
"Śiva is one and I am another"—one should abandon such a sense of separation.
"He who is Śiva, that indeed am I"—thus one should always contemplate non-duality.
Endowed with the contemplation of non-duality and established in the Self everywhere, he perceives that which is all-pervading and resides within all bodies; of this there is no doubt.
Thus, for the yogin who abides in the state of a single self and is free from conceptual construction, omniscience is fully realized.
He who is indeed recited in all the scriptures as the unborn Lord.
The Self is indeed bodiless and devoid of qualities; I am that, without a doubt.
When unawakened, it is a bound soul (paśu), having resorted to the nature of manifestation.
"Once known, he is eternal, pure, and auspicious; of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, the self should always be known by the wise after thorough investigation. Thus it is said.

In our commentary on the *Sarvajñānottara*, we have demonstrated that the alternative interpretations of the partialists (*ekadeśin*), which— with great effort— attempt to establish a dualistic meaning by resorting to a figurative sense for these statements, are not tenable.

39) But surely, how can the identity of the all-knowing, eternally liberated Śiva with the limited-knower, bound *paśu*, be possible? For contradictory attributes can only exist in distinct entities; otherwise, if there were no difference between the *paśu* and Śiva, the attribute of bondage belonging to the *paśu* would [reside] in Śiva.

It would follow that the nature of Śiva’s dharma and his state of eternal liberation would apply to the bound soul (paśu). Nor should it be argued that contradictory attributes—such as omniscience and limited knowledge—can coexist in a single locus, just as the colors dark-blue and red can exist in a single jujube fruit at different times; for if that were the case, [the following would ensue]:
For it would follow that Śiva himself, by falling into a state of bondage during his condition as a *paśu*,

would contradict the accepted doctrine of his eternal liberation (*nityamukta*). Precisely for this reason, [the analogy] of the space within a jar (*ghaṭākāśa*) when the jar is destroyed does not apply to Śiva, as it would entail the possibility of Śiva having both bound and liberated states.

The position that the soul's identity with Śiva upon the removal of bondage such as Māyā is like the identity of the great space [of the pot] when the pot is destroyed is also refuted. Furthermore, it is not tenable to claim that the identity of bound souls (paśus) with Śiva upon the disappearance of bondage such as Māyā is like the identity of rivers with the ocean through their dissolution therein; for in dissolution, there is a merging into oneness, and in oneness...

Furthermore, because dissolution (*laya*) is impossible [for the soul], and because one who has dissolved cannot experience the goal of human existence (*puruṣārtha*) which is liberation (*mukti*). Nor should it be argued that the mention of "dissolution" regarding bound souls (*paśu*) here does not mean dissolution of their essential nature (*svarūpa*), but rather the dissolution of the state of being a bound soul (*paśutva-avasthā*);
for even in the case of rivers merging into the ocean, it is only the river-state that dissolves, not the essential nature of the river itself. And so it is.

Regarding the statement that those waters which previously existed in the form of rivers, having abandoned their former river-state, have become one with the ocean— what is intended by this? Does it mean that the former waters, having merged with the former ocean, originate some new composite whole (*avayavin*)?
What is intended? Is it a conjunction by virtue of being of the same genus?

Or is it the production of non-difference through the dissolution of the prior difference? In the first case, just like that [example], the consciousness of the individual soul (*jīvacaitanya*), by merging with Śiva, would have to be the originator of some composite whole (*avayavin*); and yet, that is not so.

It is accepted as such. In the second position, even if the conjunction (*saṃśleṣa*) of Śiva and the individual soul (*jīva*) is established, their non-difference (*abheda*) remains unestablished. In the third position, because difference is eternal, its destruction is impossible;
furthermore, if non-difference were produced, its inevitable destruction would entail the contingency of liberation being non-eternal. Moreover:

In the view that non-duality arises through the destruction of difference, it must be stated that at the stage of liberation, only one entity exists. This being the case, is the entity existing in liberation Śiva or the individual soul (jīva)? In the first case, since only Śiva exists, there would be the undesirable consequence of an absence of anyone to experience the fruit of liberation. In the second case, since only the jīva exists...

Otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence that the bliss of Śiva as an object of enjoyment could not exist due to the absence of Śiva's nature. Therefore, it is not possible for the individual soul (jīva) to have identity with the essential nature of Śiva; rather, it is like the expression of "identity with gold" when copper attains the state of gold through the process of alchemical transmutation by means of mercury, jaggery, and so forth, upon the removal of its blackness.

Just as there is the statement of identity with a Brahmin when the sage Viśvāmitra attained Brahminhood through the power of his asceticism and the consequent disappearance of his Kṣatriyahood, so too, through the power of knowledge, the individual soul (jīva) attains the manifestation of its own inherent Śiva-nature— which is the attribute of Śiva— upon the disappearance of its state as a bound animal (paśu).
If it is argued that this must be accepted as the statement of identity with Śiva, it is replied:

40) Just as between a quality (*guṇa*) and its possessor (*guṇin*), or between illumination (*prakāśa*) and its locus (*tadāśraya*), identity consists precisely in a slight difference. For this very reason, the systematic distinction between the bound (*baddha*) and the liberated (*mukta*), and so forth, is established. For instance, even though there is non-difference between a quality and its possessor, it is the quality—such as color—that alone possesses the nature of being a property (*dharma*) and is perceptible solely by the eye, whereas the possessor...

The systematic arrangement— that only a jar or similar object possesses the status of a subject (dharmin) while also being perceptible by the sense of touch— is thus established, because there exists a distinction between those two. In exactly the same way, although there is identity between Śiva and the individual soul (jīva), the individual soul alone possesses limited knowledge and is subject to bondage and so forth, whereas Śiva alone possesses omniscience.

Thus, the systematic arrangement—including the conjunction with the state of eternal liberation—is established, because the difference between Śiva and the individual soul (jīva) is also accepted. Furthermore, that identity does not arise at the stage of liberation;
for if it were so, it would follow that it is perishable. Consequently, identity indeed exists even during the state of transmigratory existence (saṃsāra).

However, due to the power of obscuration (*āvaraṇa*), it remains unmanifest at that time; upon the removal of obscuration, it becomes manifest in liberation (*mukti*). Just as fire, though existing in a state of identity within pieces of wood such as the fire-drill (*araṇi*) and so forth, is concealed by the form of the wood, later becomes manifest through the act of friction once the covering has been burnt away—
It is manifested in the form of wood through the nature of its solid, liquid, earthy, and watery constituent parts; it is just like that.

And it should not be argued that, this being the case, just as when the form of the obstructing threads placed upon a cloth has departed, manifestation itself takes the form of an origination, so too here, upon the removal of the obstruction, manifestation must likewise take the form of an origination; for if that were so, the defect of the consequence that liberation is non-eternal would remain just as it was. [This is because] where there is a cause—

In cases where [a thing] is covered by a particular state of the substratum (*āśraya*) and is manifested by the removal of that state, there is "origination" (*utpatti*); however, where it is covered by another substance residing in the substratum and is manifested by the cessation of that [covering], there is "manifestation" (*abhivyakti*).
This is because a distinction between origination and manifestation is accepted. [This applies to] the cloth, which is the substratum...

Even though manifestation is of the nature of origination upon the removal of the veil consisting of the state of being a thread, in the present case, because [the self] is enveloped by another substance in the form of impurity existing within the Self which serves as its substratum, when that veil is removed— just as when grass, moss, and the like are cleared away from a well— the oneness with Śiva, which was already previously present...

Since manifestation, like that of water [in a seed], does not consist in origination (*utpatti*), there is no consequence of the fault of impermanence. By this, the objection that "if identity with Śiva already exists previously, human effort directed toward that end would be useless" is also refuted; for when the impurity (*mala*) that conceals it is removed, the purpose culminates in being achievable through action (*kṛtisādhyatva*). And thus:

The declarations of unity found in the Vedas and Agamas— based on the analogies of the space within a jar and the great space, and the analogy of the river and the ocean— refer solely to the commonality of identity (*tādātmya*), which consists of non-difference containing within it a subtle trace of difference. They do not, however, refer to absolute non-difference or the elimination of the pre-established aspect of difference.

In that context, it is the intended meaning of both the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the thing illustrated (*dārṣṭāntika*). For it is not intended that there be identity in every respect between the example and the thing illustrated; otherwise, due to the consequence of their non-distinction, the very relationship between the example and the thing illustrated would be destroyed. And thus, the previously mentioned fault does not apply.

42) One might object: even so, mere identity with Śiva is not liberation, because it lacks intrinsic status as a human goal (*puruṣārtha*), being neither pleasure nor the absence of pain. Nor does it possess the status of a human goal through the experience of bliss, for there is no evidence for the actual existence of such bliss.

If it is argued that when bliss (*ānanda*) exists as an object of enjoyment (*bhoga*), it would entail the state of being a transmigrating soul (*saṃsāritva*) because enjoyment is of the nature of superimposition (*adhyāsa*), and that the scriptural mentions of bliss and so forth in certain places actually refer to fullness (*pūrṇatva*) and other such qualities—[we reply]: No. For [it is said]:
"That happiness which one finds in the Self when it has become free from the *tattvas* and devoid of parts..."
It is free from conceptual construction, inconceivable, and devoid of causes and examples.
That bliss is declared to be supreme, absolute, and incomparable;
having cast aside attachment to sense objects, one should abandon the fluctuations of the mind.
"When one attains the state of *unmanī*, then that is supreme bliss"—
since bliss is established by this statement found in the *Sarvajñānottara*,
the interpretation of some who claim that bliss here consists merely in the cessation of suffering is [refuted].
Since there is no reason for abandoning the primary meaning of the word "sukha" (happiness), [the claim that it refers to something else] is untenable.

43) Nor is there an impossibility of bliss because of the rule that it must be produced; for if that were so, it would follow that even knowledge does not exist. Since eternal knowledge is accepted on the strength of valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is no contradiction in accepting eternal bliss as well. For this very reason, being a enjoyer of bliss does not entail the state of a transmigrating being (*saṃsāritva*).

This is refuted by the word "syāt" (it might be). For it is accepted that one is a transmigrating being (*saṃsārin*) precisely when one is an enjoyer of impermanent pleasure; otherwise, by virtue of possessing knowledge and so forth, one would incur the status of a transmigrating being. Therefore, there is no consequence of being a transmigrating being through the enjoyment of eternal, auspicious bliss (*śivānanda*).

44) Nor should it be argued: "Since the individual soul (jīva) has attained oneness with Śiva and is itself of the nature of bliss, let there simply be the experience of the bliss that constitutes the nature of liberation; what is the point of accepting the experience of Śiva’s bliss?
For just as the sense organ of taste, although itself possessed of flavor, perceives only the flavor residing in a substance other than itself.

But it does not [perceive] itself. Or, for example, although the visual faculty possesses luminosity, it does not perceive the light of the sun and so forth by means of its own luminosity; for if that were the case, there would be the undesirable consequence that objects such as jars could be perceived even without the light of the sun and so forth. Rather, the eye perceives [objects] precisely through the light of the sun and so forth.
And so, just as the light of the eye is utilized in the experience of the light of the sun and other luminaries,
even so, for one liberated while living (jīvanmukta), it is the very nature of the bliss of knowledge that is utilized in the experience of the bliss of Śiva;
it is not the experience of pleasure residing within one's own self— such is the tradition.

45) By this [argument], the view that "just as the power of poison is obstructed by the potency of mantras, medicines, and so forth, so too by knowledge (jñāna) only the power of ignorance—which is the obscuration of knowledge—is obstructed, but its cessation is not brought about by knowledge"—is refuted. For if that were the case, the attainment of identity with Śiva would not occur; yet, if it is attained, [the obstruction must cease].

Because ignorance would also follow for Śiva; for the statements in the Śiva-āgamas regarding the eternality of ignorance refer to its beginninglessness and its persistence over a vast duration of time.

46) Therefore, when the direct realization of reality arises in the manner previously described, and there is no contact with impurity (*mala*) nor contact with future karma (*āgāmika-karman*), and when accumulated karma (*sañcita-karman*) has been removed through initiation (*dīkṣā*) and the karma already set in motion (*prārabdha*) has been exhausted through experience, then, due to the absence of both impurity and karma—

By the destruction of the power of the two-fold *māyā* to produce future bodies and so forth, through the exhaustion of *prārabdha-karma*, and by the removal of the fetters (*pāśa*) that oppose the experience of Śiva-bliss upon the dissolution of the present body and so forth,
one attains oneness with Śiva and [reaches] the supreme— consisting of the experience of extraordinary, unsurpassed Śiva-bliss.
Thus it is established that one attains liberation.

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Liberation," in the *Śaivaparibhāṣā* composed by the venerable Jñānaśivācārya, the foremost among the lords of yogins devoted to Śiva, the protector of the Śaiva tradition, and the preeminent teacher who transcends the distinctions of caste and stage of life (*ativarṇāśrama*).
